articles.title: Turning Point USA announces Charlie Kirk memorial on university campus where he was shot
articles.summary: Turning Point USA announced that its co-founder Charlie Kirk will be honored at a Sept. 10 event on the Utah Valley University campus, just feet from where he was shot. The event is titled “Freedom Built to Last” and will feature remarks from Turning Point USA spokesperson Andrew Sypher, conservative talk show host Glenn Beck…
articles.body:
Turning Point USA announced that its co-founder Charlie Kirk will be honored at a Sept. 10 event on the Utah Valley University campus, just feet from where he was shot.

The event is titled “Freedom Built to Last” and will feature remarks from Turning Point USA spokesperson Andrew Sypher, conservative talk show host Glenn Beck and Christian apologist Frank Turek.

“Utah Valley University seeks to foster healing for our community following the assassination of Charlie Kirk,” the university said in a statement sent to Nexstar, The Hill’s parent company.

“While campus operations will be closed that day to provide time and space for reflection, service, and connection, the UCCU Center will remain open. Turning Point USA has engaged Utah Valley University to use the UCCU Center on September 10 for a private event,” they added.

The UCCU center is a five-minute walk from the place where Kirk was assassinated in front of a crowd of students, supporters and Turning Point USA staff.

His wife, Erika Kirk, has continued her husband’s mission of spreading conservatism on college campuses by participating in a nationwide tour entitled “This Is the Turning Point Tour” after Kirk was killed during a stop on the “American Comeback Tour.”

Next month’s event honoring Kirk will kick off the “All-American Comeback Tour,” which will consist of additional stops on college campuses.

“UVU will continue listening, collaborating, and taking the time to thoughtfully support the needs of our campus community,” the university said in a statement ahead of the Sept. 10 event.

Talks are ongoing about holding a consistent memorial for Kirk in future years.

articles.title: Jennings shrugs off reports about interest in press secretary job: ‘I don’t know what’s gonna happen’
articles.summary: Scott Jennings on Sunday downplayed reports that he is a favorite to succeed Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary. “I don’t know what’s going to happen,” Jennings said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” The CNN contributor added, “I don’t have anything to say about it this morning,” before calling Leavitt “one of the…
articles.body:
Scott Jennings on Sunday downplayed reports that he is a favorite to succeed Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary .

“I don’t know what’s going to happen,” Jennings said on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

The CNN contributor added, “I don’t have anything to say about it this morning,” before calling Leavitt “one of the best press secretaries in the … modern era.”

CNN reported Thursday that Jennings, who worked for former President George W. Bush and has advised Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), was an early favorite for the press secretary gig.

During the 2024 presidential campaign and throughout President Trump’s second term, Jennings has frequently defended the president’s policies and decisions during appearances on CNN and while hosting his eponymous radio show.

Jennings and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles recently met at Mastro’s Steakhouse in Washington, D.C., according to CNN . The outlet noted that multiple White House staffers believe Jennings has backing from Wiles.

While Jennings deflected about his interest in the job, he praised Leavitt and Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), as the latter was Trump’s press secretary during his first term.

“Whoever does that job [has] big shoes to fill,” he said.

CNN reported Thursday that Trump has told his team he is not in a rush to decide on a replacement for Leavitt, who will depart her role at the end of the month.

Leavitt said Friday she will return to Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC after leaving the administration. She was a spokesperson for the group before joining the president’s 2024 campaign.

On Friday, Trump claimed he had “never seen so many job applications” for the press secretary role and complimented Jennings .

“Scott Jennings is good,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

articles.title: Barrasso: Monday will be ‘D-Day for the economy in Iran’
articles.summary: Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said that Monday will be “D-Day” for the economy in Iran as the Trump administration and U.S. military vow to exert maximum financial and militaristic pressure on Tehran to end the war overseas. “Their economy is in shambles. And they’re still dangerous. So, the president’s right to focus on…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said that Monday will be “D-Day” for the economy in Iran as the Trump administration and U.S. military vow to exert maximum financial and militaristic pressure on Tehran to end the war overseas.

“Their economy is in shambles. And they’re still dangerous. So, the president’s right to focus on it. And now he’s going even further economically. And as you said, tomorrow is D-Day for the economy in Iran,” Barrasso told guest host Jason Chaffetz during a Sunday appearance on Fox News’s “ Sunday Morning Futures .”

The Wyoming senator said he believes the new pressure will cause the Iranian regime to fold — opening the Strait of Hormuz and agreeing to not having a nuclear weapon.

Iran’s decision to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic ruptured the consistent flow of oil from the Middle East through a waterway responsible for carrying a fifth of the world’s oil transports daily.

The Trump administration’s primary component for an “economic D-Day” includes the aggressive use of secondary sanctions, meaning the U.S. will severely penalize any foreign nation, bank or business that acts as an economic lifeline to Iran.

Meanwhile, the Treasury Department has significantly ramped up enforcement on digital exchanges, freezing an estimated $500 billion in Iranian-linked cryptocurrency assets.

The U.S. Navy is also hunting down unregistered tankers and oil smuggling networks to drive Iranian crude exports to absolute zero while federal enforcement cracks down on alternative banking mechanisms, including currency swap lines, cash transfers and underground exchange houses, as reported by CBS .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to reveal the exact, detailed mechanics of the expanded Operation Economic Fury plan during a press conference on Monday.

On Sunday, Bessent said the impact of “economic D-Day” would be forceful.

“We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary. The Islamic Republic has subsisted by dressing extortion as security guarantees,” the Treasury Secretary wrote in a post on X.

“It has drawn strength from a calculus that regards Iranian retaliation as certain and American enforcement as negotiable. Under President Trump, that era is over. And those who fear the danger of defying Tehran ought not to discount the cost of testing Washington,” he added.

Despite efforts to ramp up punishment on Iran, their leaders say it’s a self-defeating mechanism that will only cause U.S. national debt to increase as the war drags on.

“The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister of Iran, wrote on social media Thursday.

“Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians,” he added.

articles.title: This week on the Hill: Georgia, South Carolina special elections draw focus
articles.summary: Lawmakers are fanning out across their districts and states for fundraisers, local events and campaign stops as the midterm elections heat up, while national party leaders are increasingly wading into races that could help shape control of Congress. In Georgia, voters are heading back to the polls Tuesday for a special election runoff to fill…
articles.body:
Lawmakers are fanning out across their districts and states for fundraisers, local events and campaign stops as the midterm elections heat up, while national party leaders are increasingly wading into races that could help shape control of Congress.

In Georgia, voters are heading back to the polls Tuesday for a special election runoff to fill the vacancy left by the death of longtime Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.), who died in April at age 80.

The runoff pits the late congressman’s daughter Marcye Scott (D) against Everton Blair Jr. (D), former Gwinnett County School Board chair. Marcye Scott garnered roughly 48 percent of the vote in the July primary, while Blair received about 35.6 percent, sending the two Democrats into Tuesday’s runoff, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The political spotlight will also turn to South Carolina, where Republicans are set for a closely watched Senate primary runoff between interim Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) and Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

Darline Graham — who was appointed to fill the seat belonging to her late brother, GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham (S.C.), and is running for a full term — has been in the spotlight in recent days after she said during a debate last week that she’s “not that informed on national security.”

And on the courts front, expect President Trump’s hush money conviction to be back in the spotlight. The judge mulling the president’s long-running bid to move his appeal out of New York’s state courts has newly indicated he expects to rule by Friday.

Trump wants to fight his conviction in federal court in the hopes of ultimately tossing it on presidential immunity grounds.

Democratic candidates vie in Georgia special election runoff: Marcye Scott, the late Rep. David Scott’s (D-Ga.) daughter; and Everton Blair Jr., former Gwinnett County School Board chair; will go head-to-head Tuesday.

President Trump backs Darline Graham: Trump is hoping to use his influence to convince GOP primary voters to choose Sen. Darline Graham over Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Senate primary runoff.

Federal district judge to decide on hush money case: A federal judge will determine whether to move Trump’s appeal out of the New York state courts.

Georgia special election runoff puts late congressman’s daughter in focus

Marcye Scott previously told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution that she saw the special election to fill her late father’s seat as a way to carry on his legacy.

Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.) was first elected to Congress in 2002 and rose to prominence in 2021 when he became the first Black lawmaker to serve as chair of the House Agriculture Committee. He has been hailed by members of the Congressional Black Caucus, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who characterized Scott as “a trailblazer” on Capitol Hill.

Georgia’s 13th Congressional District, a blue stronghold that David Scott had easily defended for decades, covers portions of six counties in the Atlanta metropolitan area.

The winner of the Aug. 25 runoff will represent the seat through the end of 2026.

Marcye Scott and Blair were two of three Democrats on the ballot in July, alongside former Judge Carlos Moore. Two Republicans also ran for the seat: Caesar Gonzales and Fayth Park. A fourth Democrat, Tony Brown, appeared on the ballot but had been disqualified.

Marcye Scott has been endorsed by Democratic Reps. Nikema Williams (Ga.) and Maxine Waters (Calif.), while Blair has been endorsed by Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

Both candidates have centered their campaigns around affordability, a key issue in the midterms amid rising grocery prices, gas costs and inflation.

Blair wrote on social media that he launched his campaign because he believes in building a district “where housing is affordable, healthcare is accessible, schools are fully funded, and families aren’t stretched thin just trying to get by.”

Marcye Scott, meanwhile, has championed infrastructure investment, protection of veteran programs and benefit, and workforce development.

Graham, Norman go head-to-head in South Carolina runoff

Trump-backed Darline Graham is set to face off against Norman, who’s been endorsed by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R), in the Senate primary runoff Tuesday.

Questions about whether Darline Graham is experienced enough to serve in the Senate roared to life after she flubbed a national security question. Norman told Kellie Meyer of NewsNation that Darline Graham’s debate response was “serious.”

But Darline Graham later told Fox News that, “I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician.”

Trump stumped for Darline Graham in Myrtle Beach, which is home to former Senate candidate Rep. Russell Fry’s (R-S.C.) district. Fry did not advance out of the initial Republican primary election to replace Lindsey Graham, making his support base critical for both Norman and Darline Graham.

Graham has been backed by other prominent Republicans, including Sen. Tim Scott (S.C.) and the state’s lieutenant governor, Pamela Evette.

Sanford, meanwhile, endorsed Norman last week, arguing that “the stakes are simply too high as our nation really is at a financial tipping point.”

“I have seen first hand his experience in legislative circles, matched by a conservative voting record and conservative stands. And all of this brings me to a binary choice, not only on the bigger question of less government and more freedom, but on who do I believe holds the best shot at holding the line on government spending, our debt and its accompanying deficits? I am freaked about this issue given our crossing of the $40 trillion federal debt mark this week. It has heinous implications for all of us,” the former South Carolina governor wrote on social media.

Norman, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, wrote in a social media post that “the Senate has become a place where good legislation goes to die, and as we elect our next U.S. Senator, we NEED a PROVEN conservative to take up the mantle and fight!”

“I’m the only candidate in this race with the experience and the resume to take on this job, and I look forward to representing the Palmetto State in the United States Senate!” he added.

Trump hush money case in the spotlight again

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein indicated last week that he expects to issue a decision on whether to move Trump’s appeal in his hush money case out of the New York state courts.

Trump wants to move the case so he can try to convince a federal judge that the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling compels tossing the jury’s 34-count guilty verdict.

Trump was convicted of falsifying business records in connection with a hush money scheme to keep quiet his alleged affair with porn actor Stormy Daniels ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

Trump has long argued he cannot get a fair shake in New York’s state court system and has repeatedly attacked the judge and jury that decided the case.

A three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit ruled November last year that it “cannot be confident” a lower judge adequately considered Trump’s arguments as he sought to move the case.

“The court bypassed what we consider to be important issues bearing on the ultimate issue of good cause,” the panel wrote.

The panel emphasized it has no view on whether Trump’s strategy should ultimately succeed, only that the lower judge needs to reconsider his prior ruling.

“We leave it to the able and experienced District Judge to decide whether to solicit further briefing from the parties or hold a hearing to help it resolve these issues,” the panel wrote then.

articles.title: Pressure mounts on Ethics Committee to speed up misconduct probes as midterms loom
articles.summary: Democrats and Republicans are pressing the House Ethics Committee to move more quickly on investigations involving allegations of sexual misconduct or domestic abuse, as a string of high-profile cases and the looming midterms have renewed scrutiny of the secretive panel’s process. Investigations into Reps. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Cory Mills (R-Fla.) and Max Miller (R-Ohio) —…
articles.body:
Democrats and Republicans are pressing the House Ethics Committee to move more quickly on investigations involving allegations of sexual misconduct or domestic abuse, as a string of high-profile cases and the looming midterms have renewed scrutiny of the secretive panel’s process.

Investigations into Reps. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Cory Mills (R-Fla.) and Max Miller (R-Ohio) — involving allegations of sexual harassment, dating violence or domestic abuse — have dominated headlines in recent weeks, prompting lawmakers to argue that the Ethics Committee needs to find a way to expedite such cases.

The debate comes as two lawmakers known to be under investigation are seeking reelection, leaving the public in limbo over the status of the allegations against them and whether they will face any consequences before voting begins in the midterms.

“One of the long-standing problems of House Ethics investigations is that they simply take too long — staff, the public, and the Members need the investigations and reporting to be quicker and responsive,” Democratic Women’s Caucus Chair Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (N.M.) said in a statement.

Leger Fernández — who has partnered with Rep. Kat Cammack (Fla.), chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, to combat sexual misconduct on Capitol Hill — added, “Right now we’re talking with staff to finalize proposals that put staff voices and experiences first, but ultimately our work is about changing a culture that has allowed perpetrators to abuse their power without accountability.”

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) also argued on the social platform X earlier this month that there is a “massive problem with current Ethics Investigation process,” adding that “slow rolling investigations to protect party numbers is not due process. It is a cover up.”

The Ethics Committee announced Monday it was investigating allegations that Gomez violated House rules by “engaging in inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer.” Gomez told The Hill in a previous statement his actions “were consensual in nature and haven’t violated the law or House Ethics rules.”

But two attorneys said Wednesday their client told the House Ethics Committee that Gomez sexually harassed and assaulted her.

The Democratic Women’s Caucus quickly called on the Ethics Committee to “release the status of their investigation, while protecting survivor privacy, before the 60-day blackout period ahead of Election Day.”

Gomez advanced from his primary in June and is set to face progressive Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election.

Cammack said in a statement the committee “should move with urgency, and if these allegations are substantiated, Representative Gomez must resign and any criminal conduct must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

She added that the woman “showed real courage” in telling the committee about her experience and that she “deserves a process that is fast, fair, and fearless.”

“Due process must be respected, but it cannot be used to run out the clock,” she said.

Miller, who is facing Democratic opponent Brian Poindexter in November, has been in a similar hot seat . His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of hurling hot water at her, pointing a gun at her head and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. Miller has denied the allegations and vowed not to drop his reelection bid.

The House Ethics Committee announced in early August that it was investigating Miller over domestic abuse and illegal drug use allegations.

The Ethics panel has also been investigating Mills since November 2025 over a wide swath of allegations, including whether he violated campaign finance laws, received special favors in his position, engaged in sexual misconduct, and misused congressional resources.

A state judge in October granted an ex-girlfriend of Mills a restraining order after she said he harassed her and threatened to release explicit images of her. Another woman Mills was dating initially told police he assaulted her in February 2025 before recanting. He has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.

Mills has previously faced calls to resign or be expelled. The Ethics investigation was still open when he lost his primary this month to Republican Ryan Elijah, a former news anchor for WOFL-TV in Orlando whom Luna and Rep. Mike Haridopolos (R-Fla.) both endorsed.

“Cory Mills is still in Congress a year and a half after criminal investigations [and] abuse, and we need real reform that’s going to ensure that members of Congress are actually held accountable,” Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.) told CNN earlier this month.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) regularly points to the Ethics Committee when asked about allegations against lawmakers. In response to a question about Mills and Miller before the House left for its August recess, he told reporters the “key word there is allegation” and said to wait for the process to “shake out.”

Liccardo, however, told CNN that while he’s glad the investigation is happening, “the problem we’ve seen too often and the reason why Congress has been a safe haven for too many abusers is these investigations take far too long.”

Other lawmakers have resigned from Congress with probes into their conduct still pending, resulting in the committee ending the investigations.

Former Reps. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) and Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), who had both been accused of sexual misconduct, were under investigation when pressure to resign from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle contributed to their departure from Congress in April.

Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.), on the other hand, dropped his reelection bid this month after the House Ethics Committee recommended that he be formally censured following an investigation that found he violated the “spirit” of the chamber’s policies on sexual harassment against staff. Cammack said in a statement that the House should follow through with the censure.

The Hill has reached out to the Ethics Committee’s leadership for comment.

House Ethics Committee Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) told Bloomberg News back in April that the committee would be “receptive” to changes that would expedite investigations.

“If leadership wishes to change the Ethics process and the fact of additional resources, additional jurisdiction, I think that is a decision for the Speaker and the minority leader to make in conjunction with one another,” Guest said at the time.

Investigations into Reps. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Cory Mills (R-Fla.) and Max Miller (R-Ohio) — involving allegations of sexual harassment, dating violence or domestic abuse — have dominated headlines in recent weeks, prompting lawmakers to argue that the Ethics Committee needs to find a way to expedite such cases.

The debate comes as two lawmakers known to be under investigation are seeking reelection, leaving the public in limbo over the status of the allegations against them and whether they will face any consequences before voting begins in the midterms.

“One of the long-standing problems of House Ethics investigations is that they simply take too long — staff, the public, and the Members need the investigations and reporting to be quicker and responsive,” Democratic Women’s Caucus Chair Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (N.M.) said in a statement.

Leger Fernández — who has partnered with Rep. Kat Cammack (Fla.), chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, to combat sexual misconduct on Capitol Hill — added, “Right now we’re talking with staff to finalize proposals that put staff voices and experiences first, but ultimately our work is about changing a culture that has allowed perpetrators to abuse their power without accountability.”

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) also argued on the social platform X earlier this month that there is a “massive problem with current Ethics Investigation process,” adding that “slow rolling investigations to protect party numbers is not due process. It is a cover up.”

But two attorneys said Wednesday their client told the House Ethics Committee that Gomez sexually harassed and assaulted her.

The Democratic Women’s Caucus quickly called on the Ethics Committee to “release the status of their investigation, while protecting survivor privacy, before the 60-day blackout period ahead of Election Day.”
Gomez advanced from his primary in June and is set to face progressive Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election.

Cammack said in a statement the committee “should move with urgency, and if these allegations are substantiated, Representative Gomez must resign and any criminal conduct must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
She added that the woman “showed real courage” in telling the committee about her experience and that she “deserves a process that is fast, fair, and fearless.”
“Due process must be respected, but it cannot be used to run out the clock,” she said.

Miller, who is facing Democratic opponent Brian Poindexter in November, has been in a similar hot seat . His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of hurling hot water at her, pointing a gun at her head and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. Miller has denied the allegations and vowed not to drop his reelection bid.
The House Ethics Committee announced in early August that it was investigating Miller over domestic abuse and illegal drug use allegations.

The Ethics panel has also been investigating Mills since November 2025 over a wide swath of allegations, including whether he violated campaign finance laws, received special favors in his position, engaged in sexual misconduct, and misused congressional resources.

articles.title: Sullivan endorses Sullivan against Sullivan in Alaska
articles.summary: Three Dan Sullivans are wading in on Alaska’s Senate race but only one Dan Sullivan has earned the support of a former lawmaker with his namesake. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) was endorsed by former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan (R) last Tuesday as he prepares to face off against Dan J. Sullivan and Rep.…
articles.body:
Three Dan Sullivans are wading in on Alaska’s Senate race but only one Dan Sullivan has earned the support of a former lawmaker with his namesake.

Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) was endorsed by former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan (R) last Tuesday as he prepares to face off against Dan J. Sullivan and Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) in November.

“As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan. He’s been great for Alaska,” the former mayor of Anchorage wrote in a Facebook post last week.

The post comes after Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign faced legal challenges , as Dan S. Sullivan and the National Republican Senatorial Committee accused him of launching a Senate bid to create confusion for voters seeking to elect the incumbent lawmaker.

Carol Beecher, a registered Republican and the director of the Alaska Division of Elections, attempted to remove Dan J. Sullivan from the primary ballot and disqualify his campaign, citing his logo’s similarities to the incumbent senator’s.

However, Dan J. Sullivan challenged the measure in court, and in June, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled that Dan J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot for the state’s primary on Aug. 18.

Republicans Dan J. Sullivan and Dan S. Sullivan advanced to Alaska’s general nonpartisan election in November alongside Democrat Peltola (Alaska), who Dan. J. Sullivan has said he voted for twice in previous elections.

The race is considered a toss-up by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report while Decision Desk HQ has Peltola favored to win due to her past success in statewide races and status as a moderate Democrat who hires Republican staffers on the Hill.

Some Republicans have accused Dan J. Sullivan of being a Democratic plant and entering the race to siphon votes away from the incumbent senator with the same name.

Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, has denied those accusations.

articles.title: Bernie Moreno says Natalie Harp discourse has been ‘super misogynistic’
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) on Sunday said discussions regarding White House aide Natalie Harp in recent days have been “super misogynistic.” Democrats and former White House staffers have said Harp’s relationship with President Trump has been inappropriate, citing reporting from The Daily Beast that unveiled letters to Trump in which she professes her allegiance to…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) on Sunday said discussions regarding White House aide Natalie Harp in recent days have been “super misogynistic.”

Democrats and former White House staffers have said Harp’s relationship with President Trump has been inappropriate, citing reporting from The Daily Beast that unveiled letters to Trump in which she professes her allegiance to him.

“You are all that matters to me,” Harp wrote to Trump in one letter. “I don’t want to ever let you down.”

In a separate letter, she wrote, “And please, when I fail, will you tell me? You have the absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more.”

In response to comments alleging an inappropriate relationship between Harp and the president, Moreno told reporters , “That’s super misogynistic.”

“I mean, the reality is she’s a very talented person. She’s very smart at what she does. She helps the president make sure he’s communicating. And the fact that if it was a guy, nobody would say that,” he added.

Moreno said rumors are arising because Harp is “a woman” and “obviously … pretty.”

“When the reality is she’s very talented, she’s very, very smart. I happen to know her very well. It’s also obviously a very kind person. She went through bone cancer in her 20s,” Moreno said.

“I mean, look at the other day, I’ve always said, let’s just keep personal issues out,” he added.

Harp is affectionately referred to as the “human printer” in the White House and is often seen at Trump’s side on Air Force One flights and high-level meetings to provide news clippings and comments for the president on demand.

She campaigned for him in 2024 after she credited Trump for saving her life by signing the Right to Try Act, which gave her access to medical treatments that cured her of cancer.

Following the campaign, Harp transitioned from a television host on One America News Network to a key West Wing aide and executive assistant to the president.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) recently said Trump “doesn’t want to do the job” of president and would rather focus on the White House ballroom project and “travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.” Ossoff made the comments during a campaign rally two weeks ago, referring to the newer Air Force One jet , causing pushback from the White House.

Eric Trump also stepped in to defend Harp , writing, “Natalie is an incredible young woman — a cancer survivor, a genuinely good person, and arguably one of the hardest-working people in the White House. She’s deeply committed to my father, to her job, and to this country,” in a post on the social platform X.

articles.title: ‘Radical’ has become the political word of the summer
articles.summary: As campaigns prepare for the crucial fall stretch ahead of the midterm elections, the word “radical” is being slung against candidates on both sides of the aisle. It’s happening as both parties are pulled from the political center, and it’s being used by Republicans against Democrats and Democrats against Republicans to make the same argument:…
articles.body:
As campaigns prepare for the crucial fall stretch ahead of the midterm elections, the word “radical” is being slung against candidates on both sides of the aisle.

It’s happening as both parties are pulled from the political center, and it’s being used by Republicans against Democrats and Democrats against Republicans to make the same argument: My opponent has moved outside the mainstream.

Republicans, often on their heels because of negative headwinds from the economy and the war in Iran, have used the term regularly as a weapon against “radical” Democrats.

From President Trump down to congressional campaigns, the GOP is eager to shift attention to how the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the left rank of the Democratic Party in general is “radical” or “extreme.”

Democrats, for their part, have used “radical” as a way to describe Trump and his MAGA movement, arguing it is time to put a curb on the GOP.

“Radical is the current word of choice in the framing battle to set the agenda for the 2026 elections,” said Tobe Berkovitz, a communications professor emeritus at Boston University who has served as a political consultant. “The Democrats and Republicans both use it to position their opponents as far out of touch with current social and political norms.

“For framing to succeed, words must be used repeatedly to sink into the minds of the voter,” Berkovitz added. “‘Radical’ certainly fits that criteria.”

For both Republicans and Democrats, “the partisan struggle to define ‘radical will be a very important part of the campaign cycle,” said Julian Zelizer, a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University.

The race to define the meaning of the word has been at the forefront of political battles around the country.

In Florida, GOP Rep. Byron Donalds, who is campaigning for governor, has been using the word in a political ad against his opponent, Democrat David Jolly, who used to be a Republican House member.

“How radical is David Jolly on the trans agenda?” the 30-second spot begins.

It continues by saying that Jolly is “radically liberal, radically wrong.”

“The only way you defeat crazy is stand up to it,” Donalds says in the conclusion of the ad.

The use of radical extended to the back-and-forth between the White House and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who is up for reelection in November, after Ossoff slammed Trump for not prioritizing his job as president.

“He golfs and trades stocks. … He wants to build a ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar,” Ossoff said at a rally last weekend, referencing White House aide Natalie Harp and beginning a days-long feud with the White House.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung responded by slamming Ossoff for being “a radical, extremist” Democrat.

Trump has time and again referred to Democrats as “radical” or “the radical left,” but he refrained from using the rhetoric when he was asked about Ossoff by a reporter in the Oval Office. The president simply called him “Pee-wee Herman” after the comic personality played by the late actor Paul Reubens.

Democrats — from individual campaigns to EMILY’s List, the Democratic PAC that helps elect women — have also made radical part of their regular vernacular.

Earlier this month, for example, the Democratic Governors Association released an ad highlighting Rep. Tom Tiffany’s (R-Wis.) “radical agenda.” Tiffany is facing off against David Crowley in the closely watched Wisconsin gubernatorial race.

“Pandering politician Tom Tiffany pretends he’s anything but a congressman with a MAGA agenda,” a narrator says. “The truth? Tiffany’s agenda is so radical that even Republicans say he’s part of a group of legislative terrorists in Congress.”

In Illinois, Gov. JB Pritzker, up for reelection, has been knocking his opponent Darren Bailey for being too radical. In a new ad called “Too Extreme,” Pritzker targets his opponent’s views opposing abortion, including in cases of rape and incest, as well as his loyalty to Trump and his “radical” pro-gun rhetoric.

Political observers say the word perfectly describes the polarization of the moment.

“It means more now than it ever did before,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “It’s actually more reflective of where both parties are now.”

“It’s an exclamation point on the ideas, and it’s shorthand for out of the norm,” Del Percio added.

But Del Percio, who does not support Trump, said using the word in a broad-sweeping way is “ineffective.”

“It’s laughable in some cases because someone like David Jolly is anything but radical,” she said. “He’s a former Republican and is much more independent minded. You can’t take the DSA movement and their ideas and impose that on David Jolly.”

She suggested it’s much more effective for Republican Mike Rogers to use the label on someone like Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race. “His policies are associated with radical ideas,” she said.

But Republican strategist Brian Seitchik said the word resonates with voters because “it transforms Democratic policy disagreements into a warning about the people proposing it.”

“It makes Democrats not just wrong but willing to remake the world with their policies that are not mainstream, that do not resonate with the American people,” Seitchik said. “We are not a socialist country. We are not Europe, despite the socialist agenda that is taking over the Democratic Party.”

Still, Seitchik cautioned, “You can’t just point and say ‘radical.’ You have to have some meat on the bones. And thankfully Democrats are giving us plenty of opportunities to do that.”

Michael Eric Dyson, the renowned historian and author, called the rhetoric the Red Scare 2.0, particularly for Republicans — and even for some moderate Democrats — who have seen the rise of candidates like Zohran Mamdani in New York, El-Sayed in Michigan, and Angie Nixon in Florida.

As the races heat up, he and others predicted, the rhetoric will only ramp up.

“It’s definitely a scare tactic,” Dyson said. “When you ain’t got much to say you got to do that. You got to play the card you got. And it’s a joker.”

articles.title: Iowa Senate candidates zero in on cancer crisis as key race tightens
articles.summary: Candidates for Iowa’s open Senate seat are zeroing in on the state’s high rate of cancer diagnoses as the race emerges as one of the most unexpectedly competitive contests this cycle. The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst…
articles.body:
Candidates for Iowa’s open Senate seat are zeroing in on the state’s high rate of cancer diagnoses as the race emerges as one of the most unexpectedly competitive contests this cycle.

The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R). The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election analyst, last week moved the state’s Senate contest from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.”

Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in basketball, is emphasizing his bipartisan record, trying to pitch himself as an independent voice. His latest ad notes that he has voted with Republicans in the statehouse 700 times. Hinson, a former broadcast journalist, is leaning on her record leading bipartisan bills and overseeing appropriations in the House. She also carries an endorsement from President Trump.

But an X factor is each candidate’s approach to Iowa’s cancer rates, which are some of the worst in the country. Iowa has the second-highest incidence rate for cancer in the nation, behind only Kentucky, and that rate is rising while most of the country’s incidence rates are stable or decreasing.

Kerri Johannsen, the senior director of policy and programs at the Iowa Environmental Council (IEC), said knowing many people with cancer was common around the state when she and her team started researching the crisis last summer.

“We all knew a lot of people, of course, who had cancer,” Johannsen said. “But I think that there was an idea that it was kind of just normal.”

The biggest culprits, according to IEC’s research, are environmental contaminants, especially PFAS, nitrates, radon and pesticides — the levels of which are higher in Iowa than other states.

“You can’t ever say like, ‘This thing caused this cancer,’ but we do have what we call kind of a skyscraper of risk factors,” Johannsen said. “And when you start to say, okay, well, maybe you have radon in your home. That’s a carcinogen. On top of that, perhaps you’ve had exposure to pesticides or nitrate in your drinking water. Each of those things, when they stack on top of each other, increases the risk of developing cancer.”

The prominence of pesticides and nitrates, in particular, are due to the heavily agricultural economy that makes Iowa run.

Johannsen said those spreading awareness of the issue have to carefully thread a needle between discussing solutions and not demonizing the agriculture industry that is the backbone of the state.

“I’m a farmer’s daughter,” Johannsen said, noting that while she understands “this is a tough thing to talk about,” the IEC has found that “the elephant in the room when it comes to this issue is: What part is our industrialized agricultural system playing in this crisis?”

“Many people in Iowa already were feeling and suspecting this was a part of the problem,” she continued.

The candidates for political offices are taking that balance seriously.

Turek has been talking a lot about cancer as he travels the state. He has told stories about his grandmother, who died of pancreatic cancer; his father, who was exposed to Agent Orange and had a variety of health complications including cancer; and his sister, who was diagnosed with Stage 2 breast cancer the day Turek launched his campaign for Senate.

His message is focused on cracking down on insurance companies so patients have more access to care they can afford.

“I talk a lot about healthcare as a human right, and that if I’m able to get to the U.S. Senate, I want to fight for a public option to make sure that every single American has access to a baseline level of healthcare coverage,” he said in an interview with Ability Magazine published earlier this month.

Hinson, in a statement to The Hill, said she supports efforts to address the growing cancer rate by expanding access to detection and care.

“I’m proud to co-lead legislation that would improve access to mammogram machines, mobile cancer screening tools, and other preventative equipment in rural areas,” Hinson said. “We’ve got way more to do – I’ll keep fighting for results that help families fight cancer and save lives.”

Hinson also introduced a bill recently that would redirect revenue from existing taxes on tobacco into cancer research, and a spokesperson pointed to her involvement in passing the Rural Health Transformation Fund as part of last year’s Republican reconciliation package, the One Big Beautiful Bill.

The focus on cancer rates comes as the race for Senate tightens.

A red stronghold for the past decade, the agricultural prairie state has taken a heavy hit from Trump’s tariffs and rising fertilizer prices. At the same time, Republican candidates nationwide are bogged down by the Trump administration’s low approval ratings.

In announcing the seat’s shift to “toss-up,” the Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote that “the political environment is uniquely challenging for the GOP” in Iowa.

An Emerson College poll earlier this month found Hinson leading Turek, 48 percent to 45 percent, within the poll’s credibility interval. Six percent of respondents were undecided.

The Cook report also shifted the governor’s race from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.” And the gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn, have made a central issue of addressing the cancer crisis.

Sand this week took it a step further, using headlines about a new mRNA treatment for melanoma to bash Lahn over his skepticism of mRNA vaccines.

Lahn, speaking at an American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network roundtable on Tuesday, singled out water quality as a cause for colon and ovarian cancer rates rising and said addressing contaminants in Iowa’s food and water supply is a “major, major focus.” He has also talked about his father’s battle with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Timothy Hagle, a professor of political science at the University of Iowa, said he’d seen the cancer crisis showing up in races all across the ballot, including the three competitive House races. In particular, Democrats are hitting Republicans over their votes to cut cancer research and funding for care in the reconciliation bill last year.

“I did see at least a couple of ads, not from Turek directly, but from some of the PACs that are advertising against Hinson, that kind of were chastising her for votes that she took in Congress, and so it’s sort of an indirect way to get at some of these medical issues,” Hagle said.

Turek has said as much on the campaign trail.

“Looking at a state with a legitimate healthcare crisis,” Turek said in June. “Only state with a growing cancer rate. Closed 250 more healthcare clinics than we’ve opened and what has she [Hinson] done? She has voted to see 110,000 Iowans lose their healthcare.”

But Hagle predicted the race will mostly turn on more conventional issues, like name recognition. Turek is still trying to introduce himself to voters, Hagle said, while Hinson as a U.S. representative is better-known. It’s the reverse in the governor’s race, though, where Sand as state auditor cut an outsized profile and is making pains to distinguish himself from other Democrats.

“The hope is that to the extent that Sand might actually win, that he’ll cause the other Democrats and the other competitive races to do better, which is probably one of the reasons why some people think that the Senate race is a toss-up at this point,” Hagle said. “But I’m just not buying it, at least not yet.”

The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R). The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election analyst, last week moved the state’s Senate contest from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.”

Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in basketball, is emphasizing his bipartisan record, trying to pitch himself as an independent voice. His latest ad notes that he has voted with Republicans in the statehouse 700 times. Hinson, a former broadcast journalist, is leaning on her record leading bipartisan bills and overseeing appropriations in the House. She also carries an endorsement from President Trump.

But an X factor is each candidate’s approach to Iowa’s cancer rates, which are some of the worst in the country. Iowa has the second-highest incidence rate for cancer in the nation, behind only Kentucky, and that rate is rising while most of the country’s incidence rates are stable or decreasing.

Kerri Johannsen, the senior director of policy and programs at the Iowa Environmental Council (IEC), said knowing many people with cancer was common around the state when she and her team started researching the crisis last summer.
“We all knew a lot of people, of course, who had cancer,” Johannsen said. “But I think that there was an idea that it was kind of just normal.”
The biggest culprits, according to IEC’s research, are environmental contaminants, especially PFAS, nitrates, radon and pesticides — the levels of which are higher in Iowa than other states.

“You can’t ever say like, ‘This thing caused this cancer,’ but we do have what we call kind of a skyscraper of risk factors,” Johannsen said. “And when you start to say, okay, well, maybe you have radon in your home. That’s a carcinogen. On top of that, perhaps you’ve had exposure to pesticides or nitrate in your drinking water. Each of those things, when they stack on top of each other, increases the risk of developing cancer.”
The prominence of pesticides and nitrates, in particular, are due to the heavily agricultural economy that makes Iowa run.
Johannsen said those spreading awareness of the issue have to carefully thread a needle between discussing solutions and not demonizing the agriculture industry that is the backbone of the state.

“I’m a farmer’s daughter,” Johannsen said, noting that while she understands “this is a tough thing to talk about,” the IEC has found that “the elephant in the room when it comes to this issue is: What part is our industrialized agricultural system playing in this crisis?”
“Many people in Iowa already were feeling and suspecting this was a part of the problem,” she continued.

articles.title: Four states where Democrats are running away from their own brand
articles.summary: A party confident in its own name doesn’t need to find ways not to use it.
articles.body:
When Democrat David Roth suspended his U.S. Senate campaign in Idaho on July 28, he did not mention the man his exit was intended to benefit. Todd Achilles, a former Democratic state representative, is now running as an independent against Sen. Jim Risch (R-Idaho). When he called it a two-person race, he didn’t mention Roth either.

Neither man wanted to draw attention to what had just happened.

That silence was notable, because this wasn’t an isolated incident. It’s the third time this cycle a Democratic Senate nominee has stepped aside to let a supposedly independent candidate — or at least someone without an official “D” next to his name — take the field alone against a Republican incumbent.

Individually, each case looks like a local story about a longshot candidate fizzling out. Together, though they look like a nationwide Democratic strategy — something the party would certainly never admit to, and one that says more about the state of the Democratic brand than its leaders likely want to discuss.

In Nebraska, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in May after openly promising she would drop out if she saw no path to victory. She kept that promise on July 17, exiting the race just as independent Dan Osborn qualified for the ballot by petition. This set up a one-on-one race against Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.). The secretary of state had already tried to remove Burbank from the ballot for not being a “good-faith candidate.” She sued her way back on, then dropped out to help Osborn, exactly as expected.

In South Dakota, Democrat Julian Beaudion dropped out in early August after months of insisting he’d never quit the race. A former state trooper, Beaudion looked like an ideal Democratic candidate on paper. But the challenge to Sen. Mike Rounds (R-N.D.) will now fall to independent Brian Bengs, a former Democrat who was trounced by Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) in 2022.

In Idaho, the Ada County Democratic Central Committee — covering Boise, the state’s Democratic stronghold — sent Roth a public ultimatum in early July: Raise real money and produce a new plan, or the party would consider endorsing Achilles instead. Roth had raised just over $8,000 to Achilles’ $700,000 and Risch’s $3.5 million. Roth called the demand “ridiculous” and vowed to stay in, but three weeks later, he dropped out without explanation.

The same conversation is happening in Montana. Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead (D) has so far refused pressure to withdraw in favor of independent Seth Bodnar, even after the state party chair was found to have quietly solicited legal advice on handling a potential vacancy.

Four states, four Republican-held Senate seats, four Democratic parties pulling or considering the same maneuver of vacating their own ballot line so that a technically unaffiliated candidate can run without the baggage of the Democratic label.

None of this is illegal, and it’s not new — Angus King and Bernie Sanders have caucused with Senate Democrats for years without anyone calling it a scandal. What’s new is the intentionality. National Democrats aren’t just tolerating friendly independents anymore; in at least two of these races, state party infrastructure actively worked to clear the field for them.

It makes a certain amount of sense. In states like these, “Democrat” is usually a losing brand in statewide races, regardless of a candidate’s actual positions. An independent can absorb anti-incumbent energy and deep-red dissatisfaction with national Republicans in ways a Democratic nominee simply cannot, no matter how moderate that nominee might be.

Timing matters, too. These withdrawals are landing just as centrist Democrats panic over the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America. The New York Times recently reported that Third Way and other centrist organizations are preparing for what one leader called the “next war” — not against Republicans, but against the party’s own socialist wing, newly emboldened by Senate primary victories by Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed (D) and Florida’s Angie Nixon (D).

Democrats are purging their brand from red-state ballots and bracing for a civil war over that same brand everywhere else. When a party isn’t sure what it stands for, it is easier just not to say anything.

Idaho Democrats had made a habit of swapping candidates on their own ballot line, but the legislature closed that loophole in 2025, declaring that the winner of the primary must be the candidate in November, barring death or disqualification. Simply withdrawing in favor of an independent does not violate that law, but it is still a betrayal of the party’s own voters.

How voters respond to this nationwide strategy remains to be seen. The independents in these four races still trail their Republican opponents in the polls and in fundraising. But the strategy tells on itself. A party confident in its own name doesn’t need to find ways not to use it. Is that shrewd coalition building? Or a quiet admission of brand failure? It depends on which Democrat you ask.

Brian Almon is chairman of Idaho’s District 14 Republican Party, a trustee of the Eagle Public Library Board, and editor of the Gem State Chronicle.

articles.title: Canadian anger reaches fever pitch over Trump’s tariff war
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Canada pledges tit-for-tat tariffs ▪ Jeffries, Kushner meet ahead of midterms ▪ Economic ‘D-Day’ for Iran ▪ House Ethics Committee under pressure Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new…
articles.body:
▪ Jeffries, Kushner meet ahead of midterms

Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new 50 percent tariffs took effect.

Carney told reporters at a press conference in Ottawa that his government will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.” Retaliatory tariffs are set to take effect on Sept. 8.

Carney said he broke off negotiations reluctantly because he knows the tariffs will result in higher costs for Canadians.

“But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada,” he said.

“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” Carney added. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”

Canadian politicians across the political spectrum have backed Carney’s move, including opposition leader Pierre Poilievre of the Conservative Party.

“Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses,” he wrote on the social platform X after talks broke down. “Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade.”

Provincial premiers struck a similar note.

“I’m sure there is a desire to get back to the table, but we should recognize that the Trump administration and the president are deeply flawed. He’s got two more years left in office. We should be prepared to duke it out for two years. And then hopefully sanity will return to America,” Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told reporters .

“It will be painful, but we have a strong, vibrant, diversified economy,” said Ontario Premier Doug Ford , who has led Canada’s opposition to Trump’s trade policies.

“We have to use every tool in our toolbox to make sure as Donald Trump is trying to inflict pain on every Canadian that we inflict pain right back,” he added in remarks to reporters.

Conservative Alberta Premier Danielle Smith expressed concern about the impact of a trade war but said the U.S.’s terms in negotiations were “untenable” for Canada to accept.

Trump is not enjoying similar unity behind his trade policies, which have been among the most controversial aspects of his second term.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a moderate who is in the midst of a tough reelection battle, urged the administration to “consider the negative impact” of engaging in a trade war with Canada. She said the tariffs would result in higher costs for Mainers.

“Ever since the tariffs were first announced, I have heard from many businesses, farmers, and lobstermen concerned about the cost of navigating the tariffs, the lack of domestic supply chains, and the likely imposition of retaliatory tariffs by Canada,” she said in a post on X . “I urge both sides to return to the negotiating table.”

Democrats were predictably furious over the development, with figures including Sen. Amy Klobuchar , who is running for governor of Minnesota, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul warning that prices would go up for U.S. consumers.

The U.S. and Canada had seemed to be approaching a deal that would stave off the 50 percent tariffs from going into effect on more than $20 billion worth of Canadian goods through much of last week.

The tariffs affect a wide range of goods, including wine, cement, plywood, furniture and hockey sticks.

Carney said “significant progress” was made in recent weeks but accused the U.S. of seeking to change the terms at the last minute.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued in an interview with The New York Times that the U.S. proposal would have given Canada the most preferential treatment of any trading partner.

He said the Trump administration would have eliminated a 10 percent tariff on softwood lumber and reduce a 25 percent tariff on cars that were imposed last year. He said the U.S. also offered to lower tariffs on metals, including steel and aluminum.

Carney said at the press conference that Canada agreed to many U.S. demands, including lifting various retaliatory tariffs and convincing Canadian provinces to lift bans on the sale of U.S. liquor. But he said the U.S. refused to include exemptions for some Canadian trucks and subsidies for French culture.

Trump showed no signs of backing down Sunday, alleging Canada wants the “benefits of being a state, without being one.”

“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” he said on Truth Social.

▪ The Hill : Sean Duffy says Carney will ‘come to the table.’

▪ Politico : Inside the 72 hours that cratered the U.S.-Canada deal.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has called off settlement talks with Paramount over the state’s lawsuit against its planned acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Bonta, one of 12 state attorneys general suing the company, accused Paramount of leaking details of a meeting they held Friday and misrepresenting the talks.

U.S. Southern Command carried out an airstrike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the East Pacific, the first known such strike in two months. Southcom said two people were killed in the attack. More than 200 people have been killed over the past year and a half of U.S. strikes in the Pacific and the Caribbean.

Sean Grayson, the former sheriff’s deputy convicted of fatally shooting Sonya Massey at her home in Illinois in 2024, has died in prison at age 32 after just six months into his 20-year sentence. He was previously denied early release as he was suffering from advanced colon cancer.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill, on July 13, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana )

MEETING OF THE MINDS : House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met in private in recent weeks to discuss possible areas of common ground, five people with knowledge of the meeting told The New York Times .

The meeting is being interpreted as a sign of the administration’s acknowledgement of the likelihood that Democrats win back control of the House in November.

The Decision Desk HQ forecast model currently gives Democrats roughly a 2 in 3 chance of winning a majority this fall.

Two people told the Times that Jeffries and Kushner discussed housing, immigration and the cost of living as potential areas of progress, and Kushner suggested Jeffries could meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles .

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the significance of the meeting during an appearance on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing,” noting that Kushner doesn’t have an official position within the administration. Kushner has served as an informal envoy for the president in talks to end the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran.

Trump and Jeffries have often clashed since the president’s return to officer. However, Trump told Punchbowl News earlier this month that he believes Jeffries is a “nice guy” with whom he could do business.

The Times reported that Kushner has told Trump’s advisers that if any bipartisan accomplishments are to get done in Congress, Jeffries, a fellow New Yorker, is the most serious person among Democratic leaders.

▪ The Hill : ‘Shocking’ fake poll firm puts industry under the microscope.

▪ The Hill : ‘Radical’ has become the political word of the summer.

‘D-DAY’ ARRIVING : Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said Monday will be economic “D-Day” for Iran as Trump has vowed to inflict maximum economic pressure on the country to force it to agree to end the war.

“Their economy is in shambles. And they’re still dangerous. So, the president’s right to focus on it. And now he’s going even further economically. And as you said, tomorrow is D-Day for the economy in Iran,” Barrasso said on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures.”

The Trump administration’s main tool for the economic offensive is the use of secondary sanctions, in which the U.S. will penalize foreign nations, banks and businesses that work with Iran economically.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to reveal the full details of the plan at a press conference today.

“We are now entering the endgame,” Bessent wrote on X, teasing an article he wrote for The Financial Times . “At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

Iran has warned its neighbors in the region against joining the U.S. in an “economic war” against Tehran, saying it will “retaliate in a seismic manner” if Trump takes action.

▪ The Hill Insider : Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ on Iran puts China in the crosshairs.

▪ The Hill : Mike Pence says more U.S. strikes against Iran ‘inevitable.’

▪ PBS : Iran’s president says U.S. memorandum is best way out of war.

RUNWAY CLEAR : The Trump administration has begun deportation flights of migrants previously protected under temporary protected status (TPS) after the last roadblock was lifted.

A federal judge lifted the final stay that barred immigration authorities from carrying out deportations to Ethiopia last week, the last of various court cases from TPS recipients challenging the elimination of their protections.

There are 13 countries formerly part of TPS that past administrations deemed not stable enough because of civil unrest or natural disasters to safely return migrants. Rebecca Beitsch reports for The Hill’s Insider that the designations for four other countries still part of TPS are set to expire soon, meaning more than 1.3 million migrants either have or will likely soon lose their protected status.

“Effectively, this signals the end of the program,” Nayna Gupta , policy director at the American Immigration Council, told Beitsch.

The moves come after the Supreme Court’s ruling in June that courts didn’t have the power to review the administration’s decision to end protections for citizens of Haiti and Syria.

▪ The Hill : Florida Republican ‘working’ with Haiti to stabilize government.

▪ The Hill : Federal judge rules against Trump’s 75-country visa ban.

The president will participate in a Rose Garden event at 2:30 p.m. He will participate in two telerallies at 6 p.m. and 7 p.m.

The House will convene at 9 a.m. for a pro forma session.

The Senate will meet at 12:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) arrives for new member orientation check-in and program registration in Washington, Nov. 13, 2022.

HURRY UP : Democrats and Republicans are calling on the House Ethics Committee to move more expeditiously in its investigations into members accused of sexual misconduct or domestic violence.

The probes into Reps. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), Max Miller (R-Ohio) and Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) have dominated headlines for weeks and left the public in limbo as the latter two are seeking reelection in November. Mills was defeated in his primary last week.

“One of the long-standing problems of House Ethics investigations is that they simply take too long — staff, the public, and the Members need the investigations and reporting to be quicker and responsive,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fern ández (D-N.M.), the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi .

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) argued on X earlier this month that the current Ethics process has a “massive problem,” saying “slow rolling investigations to protect party members is not due process. It is a cover up.”

The Democratic Women’s Caucus urged the panel to give an update on the status of their investigation into Gomez before the 60-day “blackout period” ahead of Election Day, which starts at the end of next week.

House Ethics Committee Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) told Bloomberg in April that the panel would be “receptive” to changes to speed up investigations.

▪ The Washington Post : The police investigation into how Miller’s daughter got hurt.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky looks on during his meeting with President Trump on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

NOT NOW : Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected a call from his former defense chief for the country to hold new elections, saying that doing so during wartime would “split Ukraine apart.”

Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for an election last week in the aftermath of his firing from his role overseeing the country’s armed forces. Fedorov was popular and credited with helping modernize Ukraine’s forces with new technology and drone warfare, but Zelensky ousted him as Fedorov clashed with Ukraine’s top military commander.

Zelensky told reporters that holding elections now, still in the midst of war with Russia, would “pose enormous risks.”

“I believe elections during a war like this would generally pose enormous risks. Holding elections right now would be a tsunami for the state that would split Ukraine apart,” he said, according to The Associated Press .

Zelensky noted it was not the first such call but said no one has come up with a plan for holding elections safely, legitimately and democratically. Holding elections now would be complicated by the Ukrainian territory and citizens currently under Russian occupation, the Ukrainians who have fled abroad and those currently fighting on the front lines.

Trump and his allies have also previously called for Ukrainian elections, with the president even calling Zelensky a dictator. Ukraine noted the remarks seemed to echo a Russian disinformation campaign.

Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new 50 percent tariffs took effect.
Carney told reporters at a press conference in Ottawa that his government will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.” Retaliatory tariffs are set to take effect on Sept. 8.
Carney said he broke off negotiations reluctantly because he knows the tariffs will result in higher costs for Canadians.
“But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada,” he said.
“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” Carney added. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”
Canadian politicians across the political spectrum have backed Carney’s move, including opposition leader Pierre Poilievre of the Conservative Party.

“Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses,” he wrote on the social platform X after talks broke down. “Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade.”
Provincial premiers struck a similar note.

“I’m sure there is a desire to get back to the table, but we should recognize that the Trump administration and the president are deeply flawed. He’s got two more years left in office. We should be prepared to duke it out for two years. And then hopefully sanity will return to America,” Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told reporters .
“It will be painful, but we have a strong, vibrant, diversified economy,” said Ontario Premier Doug Ford , who has led Canada’s opposition to Trump’s trade policies.
“We have to use every tool in our toolbox to make sure as Donald Trump is trying to inflict pain on every Canadian that we inflict pain right back,” he added in remarks to reporters.
Conservative Alberta Premier Danielle Smith expressed concern about the impact of a trade war but said the U.S.’s terms in negotiations were “untenable” for Canada to accept.
Trump is not enjoying similar unity behind his trade policies, which have been among the most controversial aspects of his second term.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a moderate who is in the midst of a tough reelection battle, urged the administration to “consider the negative impact” of engaging in a trade war with Canada. She said the tariffs would result in higher costs for Mainers.

“Ever since the tariffs were first announced, I have heard from many businesses, farmers, and lobstermen concerned about the cost of navigating the tariffs, the lack of domestic supply chains, and the likely imposition of retaliatory tariffs by Canada,” she said in a post on X . “I urge both sides to return to the negotiating table.”

Democrats were predictably furious over the development, with figures including Sen. Amy Klobuchar , who is running for governor of Minnesota, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul warning that prices would go up for U.S. consumers.
The U.S. and Canada had seemed to be approaching a deal that would stave off the 50 percent tariffs from going into effect on more than $20 billion worth of Canadian goods through much of last week.
The tariffs affect a wide range of goods, including wine, cement, plywood, furniture and hockey sticks.
Carney said “significant progress” was made in recent weeks but accused the U.S. of seeking to change the terms at the last minute.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued in an interview with The New York Times that the U.S. proposal would have given Canada the most preferential treatment of any trading partner.

He said the Trump administration would have eliminated a 10 percent tariff on softwood lumber and reduce a 25 percent tariff on cars that were imposed last year. He said the U.S. also offered to lower tariffs on metals, including steel and aluminum.

Carney said at the press conference that Canada agreed to many U.S. demands, including lifting various retaliatory tariffs and convincing Canadian provinces to lift bans on the sale of U.S. liquor. But he said the U.S. refused to include exemptions for some Canadian trucks and subsidies for French culture.
Trump showed no signs of backing down Sunday, alleging Canada wants the “benefits of being a state, without being one.”
“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” he said on Truth Social.

MEETING OF THE MINDS : House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met in private in recent weeks to discuss possible areas of common ground, five people with knowledge of the meeting told The New York Times .
The meeting is being interpreted as a sign of the administration’s acknowledgement of the likelihood that Democrats win back control of the House in November.
The Decision Desk HQ forecast model currently gives Democrats roughly a 2 in 3 chance of winning a majority this fall.

Two people told the Times that Jeffries and Kushner discussed housing, immigration and the cost of living as potential areas of progress, and Kushner suggested Jeffries could meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles .

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the significance of the meeting during an appearance on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing,” noting that Kushner doesn’t have an official position within the administration. Kushner has served as an informal envoy for the president in talks to end the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran.

Trump and Jeffries have often clashed since the president’s return to officer. However, Trump told Punchbowl News earlier this month that he believes Jeffries is a “nice guy” with whom he could do business.

The Times reported that Kushner has told Trump’s advisers that if any bipartisan accomplishments are to get done in Congress, Jeffries, a fellow New Yorker, is the most serious person among Democratic leaders.

“Their economy is in shambles. And they’re still dangerous. So, the president’s right to focus on it. And now he’s going even further economically. And as you said, tomorrow is D-Day for the economy in Iran,” Barrasso said on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures.”

The Trump administration’s main tool for the economic offensive is the use of secondary sanctions, in which the U.S. will penalize foreign nations, banks and businesses that work with Iran economically.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to reveal the full details of the plan at a press conference today.

“We are now entering the endgame,” Bessent wrote on X, teasing an article he wrote for The Financial Times . “At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”
