articles.title: Trump’s Taiwan two-step
articles.summary: South Korea is not a happy country. It was unwilling to help President Trump’s team keep the Strait of Hormuz open. So the petulant president decided it was time to rekindle his love affair with North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jung Un, and punish the South by cutting short joint exercises. One wonders if the logical consequence will…
articles.body:
South Korea is not a happy country. It was unwilling to help President Trump’s team keep the Strait of Hormuz open. So the petulant president decided it was time to rekindle his love affair with North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jung Un, and punish the South by cutting short joint exercises.

One wonders if the logical consequence will be the South’s acquisition of nuclear weapons, as it can no longer trust the Trump administration to honor its defense commitments to Seoul.

What happens when China’s President Xi Jingping meets with President Trump next month? Suppose a Trump Taiwan two-step tango takes place and Trump decides there is no reason for the U.S. to go to war or to defend Taiwan, should China invade.

Trump’s argument, before his ill-advised war with Iran, could have been that about two thirds of Americans would not support going to war over Taiwan. But after the bungled Iran “excursion,” opposition to a war with China must surely be greater.

Taiwan’s internal politics reinforces that preference. Taiwan has the resources to create a “ Porcupine Defense ” that would make any Chinese invasion very costly and thus unlikely. But it has not done so. Taiwan still depends on the U.S. for its ultimate defense.

Of the 113 seats in the Yuan , Taiwan’s Parliament, 52 are held by the Kuomintang party, which supports some form of reconciliation with the mainland; 51 are held Democratic People’s Party, whch wishes to remain separate; and there are 10 other seats. That is one reason why a full Porcupine Defense has not been implemented.

China probably is taking the long view — that at some stage, Taiwan will chose to be absorbed.

Trump could expedite that process, working out a deal with Xi, just as he may negotiate a modus operandi with Kim. In that case, the U.S. would not be prepared or required to defend Taiwan if Xi makes a promise or commitment not to invade. Perhaps he would even help to resolve the war with Iran, greatly easing demands on the U.S. military.

The U.S. National Defense Strategy sets as a top priority to deter China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, not confrontation, to prevent access to the first island chain. The strategic reality is that China has set up a powerful perimeter to prevent its being denied access . With its longest range missiles and aviation units, its weapons engagement zone extends more than 1,500 miles from China’s borders.

In unclassified war games, this zone holds any surface forces at sea and ashore at substantial risk, meaning that high casualties are quite possible in any conflict.

But the U.S. has a better alternative. For much of the Cold War, it maintained the ability to wage war to defend NATO at the conventional and nuclear levels, for which it maintained substantial tactical or battlefield nuclear weapons and strategic forces through it bomber, ballistic submarine and land-based missiles.

Trump could state, as his insurance policy, that the U.S. has both conventional and nuclear forces ready to make any invasion of Taiwan a disaster. Although the analogy with NATO lacks the Article Five commitment — that “an attack against one shall be considered an attack against all” — such a threat should suffice to keep China from making a big mistake.

From Trump’s perspective, this would be a trifecta. Whether North Korea and China would be helpful in allowing him to extricate himself from Iran, that could occur. While this approach may not alter the war in Ukraine, it would permit Trump to defuse potential tensions in Korea, alter the commitment to Taiwan and improve U.S.-China relations.

It would not be so bad if Trump could execute this Taiwan two step tango. But I would not bet the future on an administration with such a poor record of execution.

Harlan Ullman is senior adviser at Washington’s Atlantic Council, chairman of a private company, and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former UK chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos. “

articles.title: New York supermarkets sue over Mamdani’s municipal grocery stores
articles.summary: A group of grocers in New York City filed two separate lawsuits on Monday against Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration following the proposal of municipal grocery stores across the Big Apple. Plaintiffs united under the Multicultural Business Coalition sued Mamdani in state court, alleging their civil rights will be violated if city-run grocery stores are opened. …
articles.body:
A group of grocers in New York City filed two separate lawsuits on Monday against Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration following the proposal of municipal grocery stores across the Big Apple.

Plaintiffs united under the Multicultural Business Coalition sued Mamdani in state court, alleging their civil rights will be violated if city-run grocery stores are opened.

The second lawsuit alleges Mamdani’s administration didn’t engage in a proper analysis of the impact municipal grocery stores with reduced prices will have on current grocers.

“Plaintiffs have been denied equal protection where the Plaintiffs, predominately immigrant and minority owned grocery stores, are unable to offer similarly discounted products of the NYC-GP, and therefore, the former are being unduly denied the equal protection of the subsidized municipal grocery stores (i.e., NYC-GP), where the Defendants have failed to take corrective action, namely meaningfully study and analysis to avoid furthering historic discriminatory exclusion, and exclusion generally,” the first lawsuit , obtained by Fox Business Network, states.

“Therefore, the Plaintiffs are suffering undue harm,” attorneys for the plaintiffs add.

Grocers, represented by Mark Jaffe, the president of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, said the municipal stores offered to “sell food items 30 percent below the market-rate, a rate that rivals or exceeds Walmart discounts,” the second filing obtained by the New York Post states.

For years, grocers within the boundaries of New York City have fought to keep large retailers like Walmart outside the city’s market, afraid an “untold amount of opportunity for minority businesses and small business at large” would be eliminated, the lawsuit states.

Plaintiffs argue the five planned city-run grocery stores set to open next year with $70 million supported by taxpayers would have the same chilling effect.

Once a month the municipal grocery stores will evaluate prices and set the cost for food at 30 percent below retailers.

Mamdani has said he believes the measure will help crush inflation, cut overhead costs and stabilize prices across the city while giving residents more affordable grocery options.

The city will own the land and cover overhead costs like rent and construction while a private operator, selected through a request for proposals, will manage daily operations under a contract, according to Mamdani’s office.

“We are talking about a reflection of a cost-of-living crisis that has seen grocery prices increase by about 30 percent over the last few years, and we’re also talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than a thousand grocery stores,” Mamdani said Monday at a press conference.

“And we’ve seen, in fact, with Essex Street Market in Manhattan, as well as Moore Street Market in Brooklyn, a model where the city has subsidized groceries and it has not had a negative effect on bodegas around them or on grocery stores around them,” he added.

His office and Jaffe did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The second lawsuit alleges Mamdani’s administration didn’t engage in a proper analysis of the impact municipal grocery stores with reduced prices will have on current grocers.

“Plaintiffs have been denied equal protection where the Plaintiffs, predominately immigrant and minority owned grocery stores, are unable to offer similarly discounted products of the NYC-GP, and therefore, the former are being unduly denied the equal protection of the subsidized municipal grocery stores (i.e., NYC-GP), where the Defendants have failed to take corrective action, namely meaningfully study and analysis to avoid furthering historic discriminatory exclusion, and exclusion generally,” the first lawsuit , obtained by Fox Business Network, states.
“Therefore, the Plaintiffs are suffering undue harm,” attorneys for the plaintiffs add.

Grocers, represented by Mark Jaffe, the president of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, said the municipal stores offered to “sell food items 30 percent below the market-rate, a rate that rivals or exceeds Walmart discounts,” the second filing obtained by the New York Post states.

For years, grocers within the boundaries of New York City have fought to keep large retailers like Walmart outside the city’s market, afraid an “untold amount of opportunity for minority businesses and small business at large” would be eliminated, the lawsuit states.
Plaintiffs argue the five planned city-run grocery stores set to open next year with $70 million supported by taxpayers would have the same chilling effect.
Once a month the municipal grocery stores will evaluate prices and set the cost for food at 30 percent below retailers.
Mamdani has said he believes the measure will help crush inflation, cut overhead costs and stabilize prices across the city while giving residents more affordable grocery options.

The city will own the land and cover overhead costs like rent and construction while a private operator, selected through a request for proposals, will manage daily operations under a contract, according to Mamdani’s office.

“We are talking about a reflection of a cost-of-living crisis that has seen grocery prices increase by about 30 percent over the last few years, and we’re also talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than a thousand grocery stores,” Mamdani said Monday at a press conference.

“And we’ve seen, in fact, with Essex Street Market in Manhattan, as well as Moore Street Market in Brooklyn, a model where the city has subsidized groceries and it has not had a negative effect on bodegas around them or on grocery stores around them,” he added.
His office and Jaffe did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.body:
It’s Monday. We might technically still have about a month left of summer, but it’s feeling a bit like fall here in the D.C. area — just in time for the triumphant return tomorrow of the🧋Starbucks Pumpkin Spice Latte.

(One of your authors … *cough* Elliott *cough* … may or may not be excited about this.)

Awaiting details on “economic D-Day” for Iran

Runoffs on deck in South Carolina, Georgia

Measles outbreak collides with new school year

Programming note: Hello! We are Elliott Davis and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to edavis@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Mark Schiefelbein

The day President Trump first teased last week has arrived: The administration is set to unveil details about its economic offensive against Iran, which Trump and his allies have referred to as “economic D-Day.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at 1 p.m. EDT is scheduled to announce sanctions against Iran and any country, business or banking institution supporting it. Bessent in a Sunday night social media post described the to-be-announced moves as marking the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

How has Tehran responded?: A top Iranian official over the weekend warned the country’s Middle East neighbors against joining the U.S.’s “economic war.” Iranian Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei also told state media that if Trump “wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” according to The Associated Press .

In advance of the operation, Iran’s rial currency dipped to a record-low 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar early Monday morning, the AP also reported .

Where does China come into this?: Because China is Iran’s largest trading partner and primary purchaser of its oil exports, the Trump administration’s “economic D-Day” offensive will also put Beijing in the crosshairs, The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports .

After Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced tariffs in response to the U.S.-imposed 50 percent duties that went into effect at 12:01 a.m. Saturday, Trump took aim at Canada in several Truth Social posts.

The president on Monday morning threatened to hit imported Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel with new 50 percent tariffs that would go into effect on Jan. 1. (Happy New Year, Canada?)

The news came after Trump on Sunday claimed that Canada desires the “benefits of being a state, without being one,” in a reference to his previous talk of wanting to make the U.S.’s northern neighbor the 51st state.

Some pushback at home: A few notable Republicans have criticized the Trump administration’s moves. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) over the weekend urged the White House to “consider the negative impact” the tariffs would have on Americans, while former Vice President Mike Pence said on Sunday that the “last thing we need” is a trade war with Canada.

The midterms are kicking into a higher gear this week, with lawmakers fanning out for fundraisers and campaign stops — and two big runoffs on deck Tuesday.

South Carolina gets top billing, where Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman are duking it out for the GOP Senate nod. Trump gave Graham a final-week boost on Friday, hitting the trail for her in Myrtle Beach as she looks to turn her temporary appointment into a six-year job.

Georgia keeps the runoff theme going: Democratic candidate Marcye Scott is hoping to keep the House seat of her late father, former Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.), in the family. But first, she’ll have to get past former Gwinnett County Board of Education Chair Everton Blair Jr . in Tuesday’s all-Democratic faceoff.

Beyond the ballot: The campaign trail is only getting busier as August recess wraps up. Lawmakers are spending the week back home shaking hands, raising cash and making their case to voters, while party leaders are increasingly jumping into the races they think could tip control of Congress.

The calendar is quickly shrinking, too: Labor Day is just around the corner, marking the unofficial start of the fall sprint — and leaving candidates with little time to make their pitch before voters have the final say in November.

Iowa’s surprisingly tight Senate race is putting another statewide fight front and center: cancer. The Hawkeye State has the second-highest rate in the country.

Democrat state Rep. Josh Turek and Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson are making the issue part of their pitches as they battle to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa).

With the contest tightening, how each candidate tackles the state’s cancer crisis could prove to be a major X factor. The Hill’s Helen Huiskes explains more here .

Republicans and Democrats have found some rare common ground heading into the fall: Both think the other side is “radical.”

The label is quickly becoming a favorite midterm weapon, with Republicans tying the left to the Democratic Socialists of America, while Democrats are using it against Trump and his MAGA base.

In Florida, GOP gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds is calling Democrat David Jolly “radically liberal,” while the label is also flying in Sen. Jon Ossoff ’s (D-Ga.) reelection fight.

📖 The Hill’s Amie Parnes lays it all out .

Alaska’s Senate race has a Dan Sullivan problem — there are three of them , and two are now weighing in on the ballot.

Former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan is backing incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) over challenger Dan J. Sullivan , whom Republicans accuse of trying to confuse voters.

Students are heading back to class with an unwanted classmate: measles. The U.S. is closing in on 3,000 cases this year — a 35-year high — and health officials expect crowded classrooms to only add to the spread.

The timing isn’t great. Nonmedical vaccine exemptions among kindergartners hit a record 4.2 percent last school year, with 24 states reporting rates above 5 percent. 👓 Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Joseph Choi .

Enter the MMR debate: President Trump wants the three-in-one measles, mumps and rubella vaccine split into separate shots . Medical groups and others say there’s no scientific reason for the change — and warn it could turn two doses into as many as six doctor visits.

That could mean more copays, more scheduling headaches and more chances for kids to miss a dose. And it comes as officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, have endorsed the measles vaccine amid the surge.

The tension: The administration is urging Americans to get vaccinated while simultaneously pushing to make the vaccination process more complicated.

— 🏀 Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday’s Fever-Sky WNBA game after a courtside shouting match with Chicago’s Natasha Cloud . Security escorted Freedom out before Indiana cruised to a 113-90 win.

— 📰 An arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire columnist Karen Attiah , ruling she was wrongfully fired over social media posts following conservative activist Charlie Kirk ’s assassination. The outlet was also ordered to give her back pay.

— 🗽Trump is blaming New York Attorney General Letitia James and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg for pressuring his former fixer Michael Cohen to testify against him in his 2024 hush money trial. A federal judge on Friday will determine whether the president can move his appeal of the conviction in the case out of state courts.

— 🏁 IndyCar driver Kyle Kirkwood won the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, capping a history-making weekend of racing in the nation’s capital. Tens of thousands packed downtown for the America 250 event. 📷 Check out The Hill’s photo gallery .

The Wall Street Journal: U.S. Says Oil Is Pouring Through Hormuz. Trackers Can’t Find It.

The New York Times : Farmers Struggle to Get Basic Services From Depleted Agriculture Dept.

Axios: Anthropic candidates face blunt money question

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Washington. (All times EDT)

12:30 p.m.: Trump participates in a policy meeting.

1 p.m.: Bessent holds press conference on Iran sanctions.

2:30 p.m.: Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon hold a school choice event in the Rose Garden

TONIGHT: The president participates in tele-rallies.

🧇 Celebrate : Today is National Waffle Day . The New York Times recently tested the best frozen waffles. Check out its ruling here .

⛳ Tee time: Trump is heading to Ireland next month for the Irish Open — conveniently being played at his golf course in Doonbeg.

articles.title: Watch live: Bessent unveils ‘economic D-day’ sanctions on Iran
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday afternoon will unveil new sanctions on Iran, escalating the Trump administration’s pressure on the Islamic Republic to negotiate a deal to end the conflict and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump warned last week that Iran would face an “economic D-day” if it does not agree to…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday afternoon will unveil new sanctions on Iran, escalating the Trump administration’s pressure on the Islamic Republic to negotiate a deal to end the conflict and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

President Trump warned last week that Iran would face an “ economic D-day ” if it does not agree to a deal. Bessent said the goal is to sever Tehran’s remaining economic lifelines and hit potential allies of the regime as the war nears the six-month mark.

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi has dismissed the effort , arguing it would bring “further defeat” for the U.S.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Oklahoma GOP gubernatorial candidate: Trump’s ‘wrong’ on tariffs, beef imports
articles.summary: Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, a candidate in Tuesday’s GOP runoff for the Sooner State’s governor, said on Sunday that President Trump is “wrong” on tariffs and his beef import plan. “I think Oklahoma and I are supportive of President Trump and many of his policies. I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree…
articles.body:
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, a candidate in Tuesday’s GOP runoff for the Sooner State’s governor, said on Sunday that President Trump is “wrong” on tariffs and his beef import plan.

“I think Oklahoma and I are supportive of President Trump and many of his policies. I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree that the tariffs are too far. That importing cheap beef only injures Oklahoma’s cattlemen, ranchers and farmers,” Drummond told NewsNation , which is owned by The Hill’s parent company, Nexstar.

“I’m unafraid to disagree with the president when he’s wrong, and he’s wrong on tariffs. He’s wrong on importing cheap beef,” said Drummond.

The comments come after Trump’s decision last week to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports in an effort to mitigate the cost for American consumers — a plan that’s prompted swift blowback from GOP lawmakers and cattle ranchers. Critics say that lowering costs for Americans shouldn’t come at the expense of American ranchers.

The U.S. is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada starting next month, in response to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent tariffs on certain Canadian goods.

Drummond, a rancher, is battling in a tough runoff for Oklahoma governor against rival Mike Mazzei, a former state senator and state budget secretary backed by Trump.

Trump’s decision to back Mazzei for the governor’s mansion came as a surprise to some in the red state, after signs that Drummond and other Republicans were poised to be front-runners for the seat being vacated by term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt (R).

Drummond finished a hair ahead of Mazzei in the initial June primary, even as Trump called on Republicans to reject the state’s top prosecutor.

Trump looms large in Oklahoma, which sided with him by double digits in each of his presidential elections. But some of Trump’s recent moves could push some Republicans to reject his gubernatorial endorsee.

Drummond, as the state’s attorney general, has also resisted a planned aluminum smelter in Oklahoma, a Trump-backed project that would be the largest facility of its kind in the country. Opponents argue it would give too much control to the Dubai-based Emirates Global Aluminum.

Mazzei once criticized the plan , according to Oklahoma Watch, but has since championed it.

In his own appearance over the weekend on NewsNation, Mazzei touted his Trump alignment.

“President Donald Trump won all 77 counties three times in a row, and true conservative Republicans understand that my opponent is a liberal RINO,” he said, using the acronym for Republicans in name only.

But Drummond shrugged off the criticisms.

“I sued, successfully, President Biden’s administration 17 times and won. I have stood with President Trump in every issue. As a matter of fact, he’s had me into the White House twice in the last four months,” Drummond told NewsNation.

Trump’s approval numbers in Oklahoma, while still indicative of a Republican stronghold, have also appeared to tick down amid broader frustrations with his handling of the economy and foreign policy.

A recent survey from the firm of longtime Oklahoma pollster Pat McFerron found just 38 percent of Oklahoma Republicans identify themselves as “Trump Republicans,” while a 56 percent majority prefer the label of “Traditional Republican.”

articles.title: Vance defends Canada trade war in visit to Maine; Collins skips rally
articles.summary: BREWER, Maine — Vice President Vance rallied Republicans in Maine on Monday, defending the escalating trade war with Canada that has drawn criticism from Sen. Susan Collins (R), who skipped the event. Collins previously said she was already “scheduled” Monday, but she has been the loudest voice in the Republican Party so far against the…
articles.body:
BREWER, Maine — Vice President Vance rallied Republicans in Maine on Monday, defending the escalating trade war with Canada that has drawn criticism from Sen. Susan Collins (R), who skipped the event.

Collins previously said she was already “scheduled” Monday, but she has been the loudest voice in the Republican Party so far against the tit-for-tat tariffs with Canada, warning they will hurt Maine industries and consumers.

Vance forcefully defended the U.S. trade war with its northern neighbor during his remarks Monday, arguing that Maine was getting a raw deal from Canada under the status quo.

“I think that we need to send a message loud and clear to the prime minister of Canada: Stop taking advantage of the people of Maine. Stop taking advantage of America. It’s over, we expect fairness in our trade policy,” Vance said.

At one point, Vance referred to Canada as a state, an apparently accidental allusion to President Trump’s frequent suggestion that Canada should cede its independence and become America’s 51st state.

“Canada is a state … Freudian slip. That was actually an accident, an accident,” Vance said.

The vice president was responding to questions from reporters just hours after Trump threatened another wave of tariffs in January on Canadian automobiles and steel.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ended talks Friday just hours before 50 percent U.S. tariffs took effect on a range of products. He has since promised tit-for-tat retaliatory tariffs in a defiant stance with broad backing across the country’s political spectrum.

Collins on Saturday encouraged both sides to return to the negotiating table.

“The Administration must consider the negative impact tariffs would have on Maine businesses, communities, and families and work to reach a fair agreement with our Canadian neighbors,” she wrote on social platform X , reiterating her concerns to reporters Monday .

Vance took a friendly jab at Collins, but he mostly heaped praise on the senator, whose race against Democrat Troy Jackson is seen as key to the GOP maintaining control of the Senate.

“Whenever I’m in Maine, I’ve got to give Susan a little bit of crap because, as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” noting that in his role as president of the Senate “she sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder.”

However, Vance said Collins has been over to his home at the vice president’s residence at least half a dozen times during the second Trump administration.

“I have never seen a person who is more attuned to the details of every single thing,” Vance said. “She does an amazing job, so please give it up to our very independent friend, Susan Collins.”

Vance also forcefully voiced his support for former Gov. Paul LePage (R), who is running for the state’s 2nd Congressional District, a seat being vacated by Rep. Jared Golden (D).

“If we’re going to fight for Maine, we’ve got to fight for Paul LePage,” Vance said.

The district is considered a potential pickup opportunity for Republicans in their battle to maintain their hold on the House.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Republican.” LePage, who was in attendance at the event, will face off against Maine State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) in November.

The event marks the second time Vance has been to Maine in recent months. In May, Vance visited Bangor to discuss the administration’s efforts to combat fraud.

On Friday, Vance campaigned in his hometown of Middletown in battleground Ohio, which is also home to a high-stakes Senate and House races.

“Canada is a state … Freudian slip. That was actually an accident, an accident,” Vance said.
The vice president was responding to questions from reporters just hours after Trump threatened another wave of tariffs in January on Canadian automobiles and steel.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ended talks Friday just hours before 50 percent U.S. tariffs took effect on a range of products. He has since promised tit-for-tat retaliatory tariffs in a defiant stance with broad backing across the country’s political spectrum.
Collins on Saturday encouraged both sides to return to the negotiating table.

“The Administration must consider the negative impact tariffs would have on Maine businesses, communities, and families and work to reach a fair agreement with our Canadian neighbors,” she wrote on social platform X , reiterating her concerns to reporters Monday .
Vance took a friendly jab at Collins, but he mostly heaped praise on the senator, whose race against Democrat Troy Jackson is seen as key to the GOP maintaining control of the Senate.

“Whenever I’m in Maine, I’ve got to give Susan a little bit of crap because, as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” noting that in his role as president of the Senate “she sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder.”
However, Vance said Collins has been over to his home at the vice president’s residence at least half a dozen times during the second Trump administration.
“I have never seen a person who is more attuned to the details of every single thing,” Vance said. “She does an amazing job, so please give it up to our very independent friend, Susan Collins.”
Vance also forcefully voiced his support for former Gov. Paul LePage (R), who is running for the state’s 2nd Congressional District, a seat being vacated by Rep. Jared Golden (D).
“If we’re going to fight for Maine, we’ve got to fight for Paul LePage,” Vance said.
The district is considered a potential pickup opportunity for Republicans in their battle to maintain their hold on the House.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Republican.” LePage, who was in attendance at the event, will face off against Maine State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) in November.
The event marks the second time Vance has been to Maine in recent months. In May, Vance visited Bangor to discuss the administration’s efforts to combat fraud.
On Friday, Vance campaigned in his hometown of Middletown in battleground Ohio, which is also home to a high-stakes Senate and House races.

articles.title: Clarence Thomas thanks Cruz for defending him against ethics complaints
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas praised Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) during a podcast appearance for publicly defending him against ethics complaints in recent years. “You’re one of the people who actually stands up, particularly at times when others seem to wither, and I appreciate it,” Thomas said in the opening minutes of Monday’s episode of…
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas praised Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) during a podcast appearance for publicly defending him against ethics complaints in recent years.

“You’re one of the people who actually stands up, particularly at times when others seem to wither, and I appreciate it,” Thomas said in the opening minutes of Monday’s episode of “Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

“And more personally, when we, my wife and I, were under attack for obvious reasons, you and Mike Lee and some of the other friends would stand up,” he continued, referring to the Republican senator from Utah. “So I really appreciate that.”

Cruz responded, “That is very kind of you, and especially for you to observe that I stand up in the face of criticism and attacks, that is, that is powerful coming from you because you’re someone who knows what that’s like and has done so in a way that has been been world-changing.”

Thomas, the second-longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history, came under renewed scrutiny in 2023 over allegations that he failed to disclose gifts, luxury travel and property transactions involving billionaire and GOP mega-donor Harlan Crow.

The conservative justice later disclosed he had accepted several private jet trips but denied any wrongdoing. His justification centered around security concerns following the leak of the draft opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to abortion.

Thomas has also faced heavy pushback for perceived conflicts of interest related to his wife Ginni’s involvement in conservative political activity, including her reported efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election.

Amid the controversies, the Supreme Court adopted its first code of conduct for the justices, which directed them to “avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities,” among other rules.

Cruz decried the criticism over Thomas’s financial disclosures as a “political smear job” at the time.

“They’re not looking at any other judges,” Cruz said in April 2023 on Fox News. “This is a political smear job directed at Clarence Thomas, because he is an extraordinary constitutionalist.”

The Texas Republican, a Harvard Law School graduate who clerked for former Chief Justice William Rehnquist, has written a biography of the conservative justice titled “Going Further: The Incomparable Clarence Thomas.”

The book, which traces Thomas’s upbringing in poverty in segregated Georgia to his three decades on the Supreme Court bench, will be available on Tuesday.

articles.title: Collins blasts Trump’s Canada tariffs as a ‘mistake’
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough reelection race this November, blasted President Trump’s latest tariff threats against Canada as a “mistake,” arguing that the United States and especially her home state have a “beneficial” trade relationship with Canada. “I still think imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake,” Collins told News Center…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough reelection race this November, blasted President Trump’s latest tariff threats against Canada as a “mistake,” arguing that the United States and especially her home state have a “beneficial” trade relationship with Canada.

“I still think imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake,” Collins told News Center Maine in an interview.

Collins said she recently met with Canada’s ambassador to the United States and urged him to address what she called a trade barrier against U.S. dairy imports.

“I really want us to go back to the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship that we have with our Canadian neighbors. We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products,” Collins said.

The Maine senator said she thought the Trump administration was close to a deal with Canada.

“This has been really up and down,” she said. “Who knows what tomorrow will bring, but I hope it brings an agreement.”

Trump on Monday then threatened to enact a 50 percent tariff on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel. It would go into effect Jan. 1, 2027.

That followed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian imports such as hockey sticks, whiskey, goose-down jackets, ice skates, furniture, lumber and other products going into effect over the weekend.

“The on-again/off-again trade talks between the U.S. and Canada lead to higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses. If the Administration proceeds with these tariffs, they will increase costs for Maine families, as most businesses will have no choice but to pass on the tariffs to their customers through higher prices,” Collins wrote Saturday on social platform X.

She noted that Maine imports approximately $2 billion in nonpetroleum products from Canada each year.

Collins has urged U.S. and Canadian negotiators to resume talks until they reach a deal.

articles.title: Watch live: Trump, McMahon spotlight school choice at Rose Garden event
articles.summary: President Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon will host students and parents at the White House on Monday for a Rose Garden event highlighting the administration’s school choice push as a new academic year begins. Trump is expected to tout the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which expanded school choice by creating a federal tax…
articles.body:
President Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon will host students and parents at the White House on Monday for a Rose Garden event highlighting the administration’s school choice push as a new academic year begins.

Trump is expected to tout the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which expanded school choice by creating a federal tax credit for contributions to nonprofits that provide scholarships for learning-related expenses.

Education advocates and other stakeholders are also expected to attend.

The event is scheduled to begin at 2:30 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Firefighters make progress against a Nevada wildfire that’s destroyed more than 30 homes
articles.summary: Containment reached 27% and there was no new growth of the Hawk Fire, which has held steady at about 23 square miles since it burned out of control on Sunday, authorities said at an afternoon news briefing.
articles.body:
RENO, Nevada (AP) — Crews have started to contain a wildfire in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Reno, Nevada, that destroyed more than 30 homes as it spread perilously close to dense neighborhoods, officials said Monday.

Containment reached 27% and there was no new growth of the Hawk Fire , which has held steady at about 23 square miles since it burned out of control on Sunday, authorities said at an afternoon news briefing.

“We are making progress,” said U.S. Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein.

The number of residents under evacuation orders and warnings was reduced to about 63,000, down from more than 90,000 people when the blaze mushroomed over the weekend. While winds have eased, there’s still concern that gusts could push the flames through dry brush into newly developed neighborhoods in Nevada’s largest city outside of metro Las Vegas.

Firefighters are also contending with hot temperatures and low humidity. At least 32 homes have burned and six are damaged, but authorities said those numbers are sure to rise as assessment teams begin to survey the charred areas.

Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said the way the fire spread so quickly at its height had her fearing for the worst.

“It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said Monday. “It took your breath away, in the worst way.”

Hawk Fire triggers evacuations and school closures

Schools across Washoe County were closed Monday because of the evacuations and to keep roads clear for emergency crews. Nevada’s governor declared a state of emergency in the county and mobilized the National Guard to help with aerial firefighting and protecting evacuated neighborhoods northwest of downtown Reno.

At one roadblock, residents expressed frustration Monday that they could not get back into their homes.

“There’s no fire here! Why are the National Guard here?” a driver yelled.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said he understands that some residents are frustrated that they can’t get home but the danger isn’t over yet. “It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said.

Wildfires near Reno are blamed on human activity

The fire near the California state line began Saturday and exploded in size on Sunday. At least seven people — three first responders and four civilians — have been injured.

This is the third large wildfire in the rugged terrain north of Reno in the past two weeks — all caused by human activity, according to fire officials. They haven’t said whether the Hawk Fire was intentionally set or accidental. Much of the area that burned was sagebrush and grass.

Reno, home to about 280,000 people, is known for its casinos and as a gateway to nearby Lake Tahoe, North America’s largest alpine lake and a popular vacation destination. It’s also southwest of Nevada’s Black Rock Desert, site of the annual Burning Man festival, which begins next Sunday.

Many who travel to Burning Man make Reno a regular stop. But some are saying on social media they should avoid the city so they don’t take hotel rooms and other resources away from evacuees.

Fire claims a Reno woman’s home for a second time

Videos posted on social media showed the smoldering ruins of homes and cars, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.

Crystal Hallock, 53, lost her home to fire for a second time in less than a decade. She moved into the rebuilt house in 2019, a year after an electrical fire burned it down.

On Saturday, with a giant plume of smoke and flames visible on the nearby mountaintop, she fled with her children, grandchildren and pets. Her ex-husband tried to save the property and her vintage Cadillac, grabbing a garden hose as flames melted children’s toys and burned bushes.

She urged him over the phone to get out and feared the worst when the line went dead. “He was saying he can’t breathe, it’s so dark I can’t see, and I’m screaming at him, ‘Leave the car, just leave it,’” she said Monday.

Thirty minutes later, he called to say he had gotten out with the car. “I’m truly blessed because I have a place to stay with my animals and my grandkids. We were all able to get out safely,” she said from a niece’s apartment in Reno.

Many residents had little time to evacuate after the fire exploded in size.

“Honestly, I thought it was like in a movie,” said Ruby Delatorre, who got back from a concert only to find her home in the evacuation zone. She returned Sunday to walk to her house and get a few more possessions.

“I literally want to cry and go back for all my stuff. I just got what I thought I needed,” Delatorre said.

Some who spotted the smoke on Saturday thought it was from another wildfire that has been burning the past two weeks.

“The flames were pretty close to my house, and the smoke was really thick, but we have no idea if our house survived or not,” Jon Hanbury said Monday at Reno’s convention center, which is now a shelter.

Wildfire threat remains high in the West

Much of Nevada’s western edge is under an increased risk of wildfires this week because of high winds and low relative humidity, the National Interagency Fire Center said. The National Weather Service says the region will see warm, dry and breezy conditions, and that critical fire weather conditions are possible in the week’s later half. Reno sits at an elevation of 4,500 feet.

Extremely dry conditions across the American West have sparked a rash of wildfires this summer. Fires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area in early August.

Nationwide, there have been more than 50,000 wildfires — the most over the past 10 years covering the same time period, according to the national fire center.

articles.title: President Trump is right about data centers
articles.summary: Why are people so furious about buildings?
articles.body:
These buildings — which, to be clear, are a vital part of the modern tech-based economy and will only grow in importance as the AI boom continues — have suffered a complete collapse in overall public support. Falling approval for data centers has been rapid and sudden. A poll from Heatmap News found significant erosion over the course of the last year.

“It’s a swift, massive shift in U.S. public opinion on a scale that I wouldn’t have once thought possible,” writes Robinson Meyer of Heatmap.

This shift is happening in spite of the fact that data centers are economic boons to their neighbors. They generate so much money for Loudoun County, Virginia, for example, that the local government was able to cut everybody else’s property taxes. Yet people all over the country are saying they don’t want to live next to them — and political figures are listening.

Both Republican and Democratic state officials have announced efforts to slow down the approval processes for new construction, even over the objections of President Trump, who remains extremely supportive of data centers and frequently touts their benefits.

And Trump’s absolutely right. But a lot of folks disagree, and for once, it’s actually Trump who seems out of step with a growing left-right populist backlash against some economic consensus.

But the question remains: Why? Why are people so furious about buildings?

One idea I’m hearing over and over again is that people are not really mad about data centers per se : Instead, the data centers are a convenient scapegoat for the greater evil of Big Tech itself. And that’s something we’ve all been arguing about for years now. I even wrote a whole book about it a few years ago: “ Tech Panic: Why We Shouldn’t Fear Facebook and Future.”

In that book, I mostly covered elite media and policymakers’ sudden opposition to social media, rather than the internet specifically. I don’t think the proposition the internet itself is bad is actually up for debate: Is it really possible to argue that human beings were better off without it? The slightly more sophisticated version of this argument is that the internet has created forms of communication that are addictive and polarizing and brain-rotting, and these make people unhappy.

Still, it’s a curious argument for people who are themselves internet commentators to adopt.

Consider Saagar Enjeti , the co-host of the YouTube news show “Breaking Points” and a former host of Rising, who writes on X: “Data centers are the physical manifestation of all that makes us miserable. It is a monument to our existing misery and a gateway to a future where we’re told we’re not needed.”

OK, but Enjeti owes his entire career to Big Tech. Presumably he does not believe that “Breaking Points’s” 2 million subscribers would be better off without it. Data centers are just the physical infrastructure that make Big Tech possible.

Now, to be clear, I don’t really think that this is why people don’t like data centers. The opposition frequently cites misguided but tangible criticisms like electricity costs, water usage and noise. I suppose it’s possible that these criticisms are manifestations of some deeper existential dread, but is that likely?

It seems more likely — to me, anyway — that people are irritated about new construction and are falling for popular but incorrect talking points about how data centers are gobbling up resources . Advocates for building new data centers need to do a better job explaining to the public that they create huge amounts of value, for the country overall as well as the communities where they’re built. They don’t have to convince people that fancy new technology is good for their lives — most people who aren’t terminally online commentators already like new technology.

One thing Big Tech should do is invest in local communities. Conservative commentator Mike Cernovich points out on X: “Go to a small town. The baseball field is named after some local business owner. New track and field house at the high school. Same. Should be no different with data centers. Put a couple of million into small towns across America and watch this drama end overnight.”

That’s an idea that’s well worth pursuing, because Trump is right: These things are going to be hugely beneficial for their communities there in, as well as massively important for the future of this country and the conflict with our adversary, foreign authoritarian regimes.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: San Francisco 49ers owner arrested in Ohio
articles.summary: San Francisco 49ers owner John “Jed” York was arrested in the Valley over the weekend and found guilty of two misdemeanor charges.
articles.body:
EAST PALESTINE, Ohio ( WKBN ) — John “Jed” York, the principal owner and CEO of the San Francisco 49ers , was arrested in Ohio over the weekend.

York pleaded no contest Monday to misdemeanor charges of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools. He was arrested Sunday at a mobile home park in East Palestine, located near the Pennsylvania border.

According to an affidavit, York responded to an ad on a known prostitution website that, unbeknownst to him, was posted by an agent with a human trafficking task force. The document alleges that York arranged to have sexual activity with a woman in exchange for $140.

When he arrived at the agreed upon location, York was taken into custody.

York was originally charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. The “criminal tool” referred to in the second charge was the cell phone used to facilitate the other offense, a prosecutor told Nexstar’s WKBN.

York, who graduated from the local high school, Cardinal Mooney, posted a $5,000 bond, according to authorities.

Details of the case are limited, but an East Palestine Police report obtained by WKBN shows officers assisted the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force in arresting York on Sunday.

Court records show York was sentenced to two days in the Columbiana County Jail, served concurrently, with credit for a day served. He was also ordered to pay $1,150 in fines. Authorities seized $160, which was to be forfeited to the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force as part of the agreement, documents showed. A cell phone was returned to York.

Columbiana County Prosecutor Vito Abruzzino said cases like this typically end in plea agreements.

“Each case is looked at individually and for specific facts of the conduct, what evidence the police provide, and input from the arresting officer,” he said in an email to the Associated Pres. “You also have to factor in criminal history of the defendant, and whether or not they have committed these types of offenses in the past, and importantly, what the judges will allow.”

York has filed an expungement request to have the incident removed from his records, according to court records.

The Ohio native became team president of the 49ers back in 2008, taking over day-to-day control of the team from his parents.

“We are aware of the matter, which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy,” the NFL told Nexstar’s WKBN.

The 49ers said, “As this was a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: House Democrat: Party ‘does not stand for what Hasan Piker stands for’
articles.summary: Democratic Rep. Jake Auchincloss (Mass.) on Sunday said the party does not stand for what Hasan Piker does and criticized his rhetoric as it relates to political violence. “Piker’s ideology, whether it was seeming to celebrate or at least excuse 9/11, whether it is seeming to excuse the assassination of Charlie Kirk, which I condemned…
articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Jake Auchincloss (Mass.) on Sunday said the party does not stand for what Hasan Piker does and criticized his rhetoric as it relates to political violence.

“Piker’s ideology, whether it was seeming to celebrate or at least excuse 9/11, whether it is seeming to excuse the assassination of Charlie Kirk, which I condemned immediately, the Democratic Party does not stand for what Hasan Piker stands for,” Auchincloss said during an appearance on Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday.”

Piker is a left-wing Twitch streamer who has made appearances alongside several democratic socialists and other progressive candidates in congressional races as Democrats try to spur a blue wave in November.

He’s received blowback for alleging the U.S. “totally brought” the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attack “on ourselves,” and videos from last week show him dancing while singing an AI-generated song entitled “We Are Charlie Kirk,” in reference to the right-wing influencer who was assassinated last year.

Piker walked back the remarks about the 9/11 terror attacks two days after sharing them in a separate interview on “ The Young Turks .”

However, his views, which some see as antisemitic, have continued to gain traction.

In a recent interview , Piker said he frequently uses “pejoratives” when describing Israeli settlers and racial supremacist groups, including “inbred” and “pigs.”

Earlier this month, Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) and other lawmakers condemned Piker after he stated during a livestream that American Jews who support Israel are inviting action against themselves, specifically showing a picture of Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss.

Auchincloss, who is Jewish, said the Democratic Party should be doing more to engage young voters but disavowed Piker’s approach.

“The Democratic Party also needs to be able to reach young voters from all walks of life who are angry at a status quo in which they cannot afford to buy a home, in which they do not believe Social Security will be there for them in their retirement, and in which they see corruption run rampant in Washington, D.C.,” Auchincloss said.

“And we need to go out there and communicate with this younger generation on the basis of a new American dream, in which, with hard work and with fair play, you get an excellent education by 18, you get a home of your own by 30, and you have a dignified retirement by 65,” he added.

articles.title: El-Sayed weighs in on Piker controversy: ‘Nobody speaks for this campaign besides me’
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed weighed in on the blowback from far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker’s comments about a House candidate in the Great Lakes State, stating “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.” “My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my…
articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed weighed in on the blowback from far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker’s comments about a House candidate in the Great Lakes State, stating “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”

“My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters,” El-Sayed said in a statement on social media. “Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk.”

“But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople,” he added.

Piker, who campaigned alongside El-Sayed, stated in a recent Twitch stream that U.S. support for Israel is unpopular, suggesting that if “Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action.”

“Not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” he added.

The remarks were spurred by “manipulated and unsourced” audio of Michigan House candidate Jeremy Moss, who is Jewish, purportedly saying, “I would say that the entire purpose of my campaign is to make sure America continues to support Israel.”

Moss denounced the audio clip circulating over social media last week.

“There is a manipulated and unsourced audio, with things I never did and never would say, that is nothing more than political disinformation intended to portray me as anti-American,” Moss wrote in a lengthy post on the social platform X. “It peddles in offensive tropes and lies — especially the lie of dual loyalty suggesting that Jews are never fully citizens of or loyal to their home countries.”

Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) condemned Piker’s comments, seeking to tie them to El-Sayed.

“More calls for violence coming out of the El-Sayed campaign … Here is his running mate, Hasan Piker, saying that if AMERICAN JEWS support Israel, they will be violently targeted because of it,” Rogers wrote on X .

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.), who backed El-Sayed’s primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), also condemned Piker’s remarks, calling the streamer a “hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance.”

El-Sayed’s Monday statement did not explicitly condemn Piker’s remarks. The candidate has previously defended campaigning with Piker despite his past controversial statements, including saying that America “deserved” the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Piker defended himself on X , saying that “this isn’t a call for violence” and that “falsely tying israel to jewish people IS increasing antisemitism.”

“And while politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare,” El-Sayed said in his statement. “Because that’s what Michiganders keep asking about. It’s why I’m fighting to get money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All.”

The Michigan Senate seat of retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D) is seen as one of Republicans’ best pickup opportunities in the fall. The controversies stacking up around Piker could hurt Democrats’ chances of keeping the seat in November.

articles.title: Trump administration lays out new $103K fee proposal for H-1B visas
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new proposed rule for H-1B visas on Monday that would charge a $103,265 fee for all workers seeking to gain employment in the U.S. who are subject to the annual statutory cap. Notice of the proposed rule says the fee would be used for the federal government’s…
articles.body:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new proposed rule for H-1B visas on Monday that would charge a $103,265 fee for all workers seeking to gain employment in the U.S. who are subject to the annual statutory cap.

Notice of the proposed rule says the fee would be used for the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system, including activities carried out by the DHS and the departments of Justice, State and Labor.

“The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a release.

The move follows a federal judge’s decision in June to strike down the Trump administration’s previously proposed $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin ruled that it was unlawful to implement a tax on visa applications, as Congress is the only legislative body with the authority to set immigration policy and taxes.

The original proposal applied to universities, hospitals and research-based institutions; however, those employers won’t be impacted by the new fee under the DHS’s newly proposed rule.

“The administration claims the new fee will be a ‘cost recovery mechanism,’ even though the first fee led to a nearly 90 percent reduction in filings and a $28 million loss in revenue. The government itself told the court that the $100,000 fee was ‘arguably prohibitive’ and ‘does not raise revenue,'” David Bier of the Cato Institute said in a statement sent to The Hill.

“Even if it did raise revenue, that would not make it legal because immigration fees can only be imposed to recover the costs of adjudication and naturalization services. And because this is a filing fee, employers would have to pay it with no guarantee that USCIS [U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services] will approve the petition. Almost no one will risk more than $100,000 with no guarantee of approval,” Bier added.

The standard annual statutory limit for new H-1B visas is 85,000, which comprises the regular cap of 65,000 visas and 20,000 visas granted to applicants who hold a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. college or university. Out of the 65,000, a total of 6,800 are set aside exclusively for Chilean and Singaporean nationals.

The tech industry has been at the center of discussions surrounding H-1B visas, which allow U.S. companies to hire foreign workers in specialized, high-skill occupations.

Computer-related positions make up nearly two-thirds of all H-1B approvals, focusing heavily on software engineering, data science and IT support, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center .

Companies and tech workers will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule once it’s published on the Federal Register, which officials say will happen Tuesday.

articles.title: Abbott tells judge Minnesota’s ICE officer extradition lawsuit ‘doomed to fail’
articles.summary: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he’s not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Minnesota authorities with shooting a Venezuelan man earlier this year during “Operation Metro Surge.” Minnesota is pushing in court to force the extradition of ICE officer Christian Castro, with…
articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he’s not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Minnesota authorities with shooting a Venezuelan man earlier this year during “Operation Metro Surge.”

Minnesota is pushing in court to force the extradition of ICE officer Christian Castro, with a key hearing slated for Tuesday. The state insists Abbott has no discretion to avoid signing the warrant.

“In the end, Minnesota’s zeal to see Mr. Castro prosecuted on its home turf cannot justify pretermitting Governor Abbott’s ongoing deliberations pursuant to the Constitution and state statutes, which are designed to protect against abusive and baseless deprivations of individual liberty,” Abbott’s lawyers wrote in their formal written response to the court.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr., an appointee of President Trump who oversees the case, will consider Minnesota’s bid at a Tuesday afternoon hearing in his Brownsville, Texas, courtroom.

It has become a major legal clash between Abbott and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D), who requested Castro’s extradition as state authorities charged the ICE officer with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.

The officer stands accused of injuring a Venezuelan man in the leg by firing a gun at the front door of an occupied Minneapolis home on Jan. 14 amid an immigration enforcement surge in the Twin Cities. Castro had allegedly told investigators he opened fire in self-defense after being hit with a shovel and a broom, only for video footage to undercut the officer’s claim.

Abbott has refused to sign a rendition warrant that would pave the way for the officer to return to Minnesota for trial.

In the new filing, the governor’s lawyers raised doubts that Castro qualifies for the Constitution’s extradition requirement. It demands a state return defendants facing criminal charges who “flee from Justice” when they are “found in another State.” Abbott has suggested Castro didn’t flee because ICE had ordered him to return to Texas.

“The ordinary meaning of a fugitive entails a volitional act of fleeing, not mere involuntary movement across state lines,” his lawyers wrote.

Minnesota insists that Abbott’s role is ministerial, and the state wants a judge to immediately pave the way for the officer to be returned.

“The Framers of the Constitution and Congress intended the interstate extradition process to be a swift, summary one in which the state into which a defendant travels promptly returns a fugitive as soon as the requesting state demands it,” the state wrote in court filings last week.

Abbott cautioned he hasn’t yet made a final decision on the extradition request. But his new filing said that any notion Minnesota could unilaterally enforce the extradition power was “doomed to fail.” His filing also took shots at Walz for pardoning a man charged with sexually assaulting a minor.

“Equity favors those with clean hands,” Abbott’s lawyers wrote.

articles.title: US envoy clarifies Golan Heights comments after contradicting Trump
articles.summary: Tom Barrack, President Trump’s U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, on Sunday walked back comments he made last week suggesting that Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of United Nations resolutions, which contradict the president’s position. Barrack made the remark Friday in an interview with Lebanese Australian entrepreneur Mario Nawfal.…
articles.body:
Tom Barrack, President Trump’s U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, on Sunday walked back comments he made last week suggesting that Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of United Nations resolutions, which contradict the president’s position.

Barrack made the remark Friday in an interview with Lebanese Australian entrepreneur Mario Nawfal. He later told The Associated Press he was describing the territory’s historical status and that it was “not an endorsement of the United Nations’ position.”

“United States policy on the Golan was set by President Trump in 2019 and is unchanged,” Barrack told the AP, saying he intended to explain why he does not expect Israel to annex Lebanon.

The special envoy referred to negotiated agreements, like the end of the latest Israel-Hezbollah war, as more long-lasting, having used the Golan as an example of “territory taken by force remains contested for generations.”

Barrack said Hezbollah and Iran are the “two people missing from” those negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, emphasizing that the U.S. does not negotiate with Hezbollah. He said the U.S.-designated foreign terrorist organization’s “weapons in question are supplied and financed by Iran.”

“I was describing the difficulty of the problem, not proposing a new [negotiating] table,” he told the AP. “Hezbollah is a designated foreign terrorist organization. We do not negotiate with it, and nothing I said suggests otherwise.”

Israel claimed the Golan Heights after the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. The U.N. does not consider the occupied territory as belonging to Israel and does not recognize the annexation.

Trump reversed decades of U.S. policy and recognized Israel’s sovereignty over the Golan Heights in 2019.

Barrack, in the same interview with Nawfal, criticized Israel’s strikes on Abu Duhur air base in Syria last week. He called the strikes an “unnecessary escalation” and said the U.S. will host diplomatic talks to produce “de-escalation agreements” between Syria and Israel.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz defended the strikes Sunday on the social platform X , saying that critics who first called the attack “unnecessary and politically motivated” changed their position after the Israeli military released “clear intelligence” that clarified its actions.

“The statements by the Prime Minister and the Defense Minister to Erdoğan and the warnings that we will not allow Turkey to establish itself in Syria and endanger Israel’s security –– are unnecessary and dangerous,” Katz wrote, referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

The United Kingdom-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said Turkey has been working to rehabilitate the base and bring it back into service.

Turkey and Syria have denied that Turkish forces were deployed to the air base. The base has been out of service since 2013, after Syrian rebels clashed with former Syrian President Bashar Assad’s military.

Israel claimed the Golan Heights after the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. The U.N. does not consider the occupied territory as belonging to Israel and does not recognize the annexation.
Trump reversed decades of U.S. policy and recognized Israel’s sovereignty over the Golan Heights in 2019.

Barrack, in the same interview with Nawfal, criticized Israel’s strikes on Abu Duhur air base in Syria last week. He called the strikes an “unnecessary escalation” and said the U.S. will host diplomatic talks to produce “de-escalation agreements” between Syria and Israel.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz defended the strikes Sunday on the social platform X , saying that critics who first called the attack “unnecessary and politically motivated” changed their position after the Israeli military released “clear intelligence” that clarified its actions.

“The statements by the Prime Minister and the Defense Minister to Erdoğan and the warnings that we will not allow Turkey to establish itself in Syria and endanger Israel’s security –– are unnecessary and dangerous,” Katz wrote, referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
The United Kingdom-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said Turkey has been working to rehabilitate the base and bring it back into service.

Turkey and Syria have denied that Turkish forces were deployed to the air base. The base has been out of service since 2013, after Syrian rebels clashed with former Syrian President Bashar Assad’s military.

articles.title: Supreme Court rules blue states sued too early over Trump’s mail voting order
articles.summary: The Supreme Court lifted a judge’s block on President Trump’s executive order adding to mail voting requirements, removing a key roadblock that prevented the policy from going into effect for the midterms. Over the public dissents of the three liberal justices, the high court said Monday that the judge had no authority to block Trump’s…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court lifted a judge’s block on President Trump’s executive order adding to mail voting requirements, removing a key roadblock that prevented the policy from going into effect for the midterms.

Over the public dissents of the three liberal justices, the high court said Monday that the judge had no authority to block Trump’s directive, at least ahead of the U.S. Postal Service implementing the new ballot standards.

“Federal courts review final rules, not proposed rules—and certainly not antecedent internal directives to propose a rule. If the Postal Service’s final rule harms the States, they may challenge that rule,” the court wrote.

It allows Trump to move closer to implementing his mail ballot restrictions for November’s contests. But now that the Postal Service announced its final regulation late last week, the states had already begun their new push to block it.

In dissent, the court’s liberal justices said they would’ve kept the block in place.

“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with States’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful,” wrote Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Elena Kagan. “Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives.

“Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, the court’s junior liberal justice, said her colleagues had a “lack of situational awareness” and were injecting chaos into the election cycle. “Rather than swallow the Government’s gamesmanship whole, the Court should have given this empty, strategic, and bad-faith stay bid the swift rejection it deserves,” Jackson wrote in her separate dissent.

California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington co-led the suit, which involves 23 states and the District of Columbia in total.

In March, Trump signed an executive order directing his administration to create a list of verified citizens who are eligible to vote and ordered the Postal Service to implement new standards for mail ballots.

It’s part of Trump’s years-long targeting of mail ballots over his claims they drive mass election fraud . States have found some instances of fraud and noncitizens voting, but not nearly at the massive scale Trump has purported.

The Trump administration turned to the Supreme Court after U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani blocked Trump’s order in a group of the Democratic-controlled states that are suing. Talwani is an appointee of former President Obama.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the judge got involved too early. The Postal Service hadn’t yet implemented Trump’s policy and only announced the final regulation last week.

“The issuance of a final rule underscores the need for relief from the district court’s improper, unripe injunction,” Sauer wrote to the Supreme Court.

The case now returns to the lower courts, where Talwani has already set a speedy schedule to consider the legality of the Postal Service’s new announcement. The judge is an appointee of former President Obama.

She had also blocked Trump’s executive order in response to a separate lawsuit brought by private groups. But unlike the states’ case, that block applied nationwide.

“A majority of the U.S. Supreme Court does not seem to recognize the grave threat the president’s actions pose for our democracy. There is nothing hypothetical about his intent to illegally suppress legitimate votes,” Washington Attorney General Nick Brown (D) said in a statement.

“Fortunately, today’s decision does not bless the substance of the president’s actions, it simply says states must wait slightly longer to challenge them,” he continued. “We stand ready to take action to protect the integrity of our elections and prevent this clearly unconstitutional overreach from taking effect. States control elections, not the president.”

The ruling marks the president’s latest win on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket, where the justices intervene immediately on time-sensitive matters, usually on a compressed timeline without oral arguments.

The Democratic-controlled states told the Supreme Court it “would not be sensible” to force them to wait to sue. They say the policies will ultimately be unlawful and they won’t have enough time to convince the courts to block it before November’s contests.

“Because of the high risk of errors and the limited window for correcting mistakes, many of the millions of voters who rely on mail voting—especially voters with disabilities and those in rural areas—would likely be denied mail ballots and, as a result, disenfranchised. Many more voters would be confused,” the states wrote.

articles.title: DOJ signals it will appeal ruling requiring removal of some redactions in Epstein files
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Monday signaled its plans to appeal a ruling requiring the department to unredact various documents from the Epstein files in a suit brought by attorney and independent journalist Katie Phang. The preliminary injunction, entered in June, orders redactions be removed in key documents of interest in the files, including “at…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Monday signaled its plans to appeal a ruling requiring the department to unredact various documents from the Epstein files in a suit brought by attorney and independent journalist Katie Phang.

The preliminary injunction , entered in June, orders redactions be removed in key documents of interest in the files, including “at least eight email exchanges with Mr. Epstein regarding a ‘torture video’ and sexual activity with young women, including minors,” as well as interviews with a woman who said she was abused by President Trump as a minor.

Under the June order, the Justice Department must either produce the documents or “show cause” as to why they cannot comply.

The notice of appeal does not get into any of the DOJ’s legal arguments and narrowly complies with a 60-day ruling to appeal U.S. District Judge Emmit Sullivan’s order.

But it also raises that the Justice Department is unsure about its ability to appeal the order, calling the matter “inconclusive” and describing its filing as a “protective notice of appeal.”

The Justice Department has argued it has a number of reasons as to why it has not fully unredacted the documents, including that the redactions cover victim identities and contact information for some who were communicating with Epstein.

Some of the details sought by Phang have since been unveiled — including that Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem was the one who had been emailing the now-deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein about the torture video.

“Given this and widespread media attention as to the purported identity of the sender of this email—information Plaintiff could have readily obtained with a simple internet search—unredacting the email address would not only be inconsistent with how other private email addresses have been treated; it would serve no purpose beyond sharing that private email address,” the DOJ wrote in responding to Phang.

But Phang’s suit also sought further information about a tranche of documents that detailed the FBI’s interviews with a woman who claimed Trump violently attacked her as a minor.

Sullivan chastised the DOJ during a recent hearing for failing to comply with his initial order and warned prosecutors that he has held attorneys in contempt before.

“You want me to issue another order and say, ‘I really mean it this time’?” Sullivan said during a hearing earlier this month, according to NBC News .
