articles.title: David Hogg: Media focus on Hasan Piker ‘kind of weird’
articles.summary: Activist David Hogg on Sunday said he finds recent media focus on left-wing streamer Hasan Piker “kind of weird.” “To be honest with you, I find it kind of weird. Like he’s a streamer. This guy is not an elected official, and there’s a lot of elected officials out there that are saying incredibly horrible…
articles.body:
Activist David Hogg on Sunday said he finds recent media focus on left-wing streamer Hasan Piker “kind of weird.”

“To be honest with you, I find it kind of weird. Like he’s a streamer. This guy is not an elected official, and there’s a lot of elected officials out there that are saying incredibly horrible thing[s],” Hogg told left-wing media personality Jack Cocchiarella, discussing the recent national spotlight on Piker.

Hogg added later that he believed “that it’s fascinating that people are so obsessed with a streamer that the median voter knows nothing about.”

“You know, that’s not to diss Hasan, I think he would probably agree with me, generally, that like they don’t — they don’t know who he is,” Hogg continued.

“And I think it speaks to the fact that a lot of moderates in our party don’t have an actual vision that they are fighting for other than the center, because they’re constantly repositioning themselves on the political spectrum to say, ‘You know, I’m going to be in the middle,’ but the middle is always changing,” he said. “And instead, what people are looking for is somebody that actually offers a new vision.”

Hogg’s comments come in the wake of Piker’s dramatic rise in the last few months, as the streamer has had on his stream multiple left-leaning candidates who have taken down more establishment or long-term figures in Democratic primaries.

The streamer campaigned with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who won his race against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) earlier this month.

In response to Piker’s recent comments about Michigan House candidate Jeremy Moss, El-Sayed on Monday issued a statement on the social platform X that “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”

Piker has a history of controversial statements , including saying in 2019 that “America deserved 9/11” as blowback against the U.S. because of its military campaigns worldwide. However, the streamer recently said he could’ve better phrased his comments about the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

More moderate Democrats, like Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) and Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), have gone after Piker in recent weeks.

articles.title: Politicians aim to distance themselves from data centers
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Politicians aim to distance themselves from data centers As public pushback to data centers boils over, politicians on both sides of the aisle are racing to distance themselves from the controversial facilities. © Adobe Stock Key swing state candidates are scrambling to endorse stricter…
articles.body:
Politicians aim to distance themselves from data centers

As public pushback to data centers boils over, politicians on both sides of the aisle are racing to distance themselves from the controversial facilities.

Key swing state candidates are scrambling to endorse stricter data center policies — and accusing their opponents of being too cozy with the industry — as Americans become increasingly hostile to the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), who once touted data center investments in the Keystone State, signed an order Tuesday implementing new requirements for developers to cover electricity costs and secure local approval for projects.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the GOP candidate in Michigan’s Senate race, announced Thursday that he is backing a one-year state moratorium on new data centers.

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), the Democratic candidate in Ohio’s Senate race, is going after Sen. Jon Husted (R) over the incumbent’s record on data centers in the Buckeye State. The National Republican Senatorial Committee recently issued an internal memo warning that “data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the progressive Sunrise Movement, told The Hill that during her canvassing in Michigan and Wisconsin, she has talked to voters who “are flipping their party affiliation because of the importance of data centers.”

Tech companies are pushing to build scores of new centers to fuel the development of artificial intelligence, which requires vast amounts of computing power.

But in the face of growing concerns about electricity costs, water usage and other environmental impacts, public opinion has soured.

A Fox News poll released in late July found that 70 percent of voters oppose the building of a data center in their area to support AI, with 78 percent in support of slowing construction to address environmental and community concerns.

Voter concerns appear to have shifted the political calculus for officials from both parties who previously embraced data centers.

articles.title: Trump administration proposes new H-1B visa fee
articles.summary: {beacon} Technology Technology The Big Story Trump administration lays out new $103K fee proposal for H-1B visas The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new proposed rule for H-1B visas on Monday that would charge a $103,265 fee for all workers seeking to gain employment in the U.S. who are subject to the…
articles.body:
Trump administration lays out new $103K fee proposal for H-1B visas

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new proposed rule for H-1B visas on Monday that would charge a $103,265 fee for all workers seeking to gain employment in the U.S. who are subject to the annual statutory cap.

The tech industry has been at the center of discussions surrounding H-1B visas, which allow U.S. companies to hire foreign workers in specialized, high-skill occupations.

Computer-related positions make up nearly two-thirds of all H-1B approvals, focusing heavily on software engineering, data science and IT support, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center .

Notice of the proposed rule says the fee would be used for the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system, including activities carried out by the DHS and the departments of Justice, State and Labor.

“The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a release.

The move follows a federal judge’s decision in June to strike down the Trump administration’s previously proposed $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin ruled that it was unlawful to implement a tax on visa applications, as Congress is the only legislative body with the authority to set immigration policy and taxes.

The original proposal applied to universities, hospitals and research-based institutions; however, those employers won’t be impacted by the new fee under the DHS’s newly proposed rule.

Companies and tech workers will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule once it’s published on the Federal Register, which officials say will happen Tuesday.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin ruled that it was unlawful to implement a tax on visa applications, as Congress is the only legislative body with the authority to set immigration policy and taxes.
The original proposal applied to universities, hospitals and research-based institutions; however, those employers won’t be impacted by the new fee under the DHS’s newly proposed rule.
Companies and tech workers will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule once it’s published on the Federal Register, which officials say will happen Tuesday.

articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter {beacon} Defense &National Security Defense &National Security The Big Story Trump bets on economic chokehold on Iran over military strikes, for now Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday that the Trump administration’s economic pressure on Iran is hurting the regime “the most right now,” but did not…
articles.body:
Trump bets on economic chokehold on Iran over military strikes, for now

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday that the Trump administration’s economic pressure on Iran is hurting the regime “the most right now,” but did not rule out the U.S. military resuming airstrikes if necessary.

“If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them. If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the with the American military, we’ll do what we need to do ,” Hegseth told reporters in Oshkosh, Wis. as part of the Pentagon’s “Arsenal of Freedom” tour. “But economic pressure, hurts them the most right now.”

The Pentagon chief’s remarks came hours after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previewed the U.S. new economic pressure campaign against Tehran as the conflict has reached a stalemate after six months of hostilities.

Bessent warned countries to cut off any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, discussing the new “Operation Economic Outcast,” but offering few specifics.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior , why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent told a reporter when asked about specifics.

The Treasury secretary said that President Trump is dialing world leaders and that officials at the State Department, the Pentagon and Treasury are connecting with their counterparts, asking them to cut ties with Iran.

“I would expect that very quickly, if they do not respond, then you will see the ramifications of their actions ,” Bessent said.

Iran’s Parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, fired back Monday at the U.S. over the rollout of the economic pressure campaign.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” Qalibaf said on social platform X.

“More economic pressure only ensures that Iran really has – the only choice they have is to come to the table and actually talk about their nuclear program, which is what the president has demanded,” Hegseth said.

articles.title: Trump’s super PAC drops more than $800K on Graham in South Carolina
articles.summary: President Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc. spent more than $827,000 to support Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) ahead of the state’s Republican Senate primary runoff on Tuesday, marking the group’s most significant spending in months. The filing with the Federal Election Commission, which was made public on Monday, marks the group’s first independent expenditure since March…
articles.body:
President Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc. spent more than $827,000 to support Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) ahead of the state’s Republican Senate primary runoff on Tuesday, marking the group’s most significant spending in months.

The filing with the Federal Election Commission, which was made public on Monday, marks the group’s first independent expenditure since March when it threw $18,000 behind now-Rep. Clay Fuller (R-Ga.) in the special election race to fill former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene’s (R-Ga.) seat.

MAGA Inc. spent more than $1 million to support now-Rep. Matt Van Epps (R-Tenn.) late last year in the race to replace former Rep. Mark Green (R-Tenn.).

The group’s haul supporting Graham comes as Trump signaled he will start spending money to help elect Republicans in the midterms.

“Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump told reporters ahead of a campaign rally for Graham last week. “I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money — but I’ll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates.”

According to invitations obtained by CBS News on Monday, MAGA Inc. is slated to hold two $1 million-per-person fundraisers this fall at Trump National Golf Club in Virginia and at Mar-a-Lago.

Republicans are facing an uphill battle in their bids to defend their majorities in the House and the Senate.

articles.title: Byron Donalds: Kushner ‘just keepings lines of communication open’ with Jeffries meeting
articles.summary: Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) on Monday said President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) in recent weeks to create an opportunity for future discussions. “I think knowing Jared Kushner, I think he’s used to keeping lines of communication open. These are some of the things that he does repeatedly,…
articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) on Monday said President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) in recent weeks to create an opportunity for future discussions.

“I think knowing Jared Kushner, I think he’s used to keeping lines of communication open. These are some of the things that he does repeatedly, even during his time as a top official in the Trump 45 White House,” Donalds, the Republican nominee for Florida’s governorship, said during an appearance on CNN’s “Situation Room.”

“Jared is probably just continuing conversations he had with Hakeem Jeffries,” he added.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) also chalked up the meeting first reported by The New York Times as a one-off.

Johnson said Kushner is “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House.”

Kushner operates his own private equity firm, Affinity Partners, and acts as an informal outside adviser to Trump on foreign policy and Middle East initiatives.

When Jeffries was asked to comment on his meeting with Kushner, he cited Democrats’ push for affordability, noting “that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition.”

“In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable. We are fighting for an affordable America,” Jeffries added in the statement.

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.) said the meeting was likely meant to mend relations in case Democrats gain the House majority in November.

“I think it signals that they know he’s going to be the Speaker. And they know that he’s going to be somebody that they can’t, you know, kind of continue to roll over,” Krishnamoorthi said during a Monday appearance on CNN’s “News Central.”

“They’re going to have to accord respect. And if they want any item on their legislative agenda to move forward, they’re going to have to work with him,” he added.

articles.title: Mamdani voices support for Jeffries amid Kushner meeting blowback
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday voiced his support for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) after the congressman received blowback for meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law. A reporter asked Mamdani if he supported Jeffries were he to become Speaker if Democrats reclaim the House following the fall midterm elections.…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday voiced his support for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) after the congressman received blowback for meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law.

A reporter asked Mamdani if he supported Jeffries were he to become Speaker if Democrats reclaim the House following the fall midterm elections.

“I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader,” Mamdani said.

Jeffries, who represents parts of Brooklyn, had declined to weigh in on the city’s mayoral race last year when Mamdani faced off against former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, who ran as a Democrat in the primary and as an independent in the general election. Jeffries endorsed Mamdani hours before New York’s early voting started and weeks before the election.

The New York Times reported Sunday that Kushner and Jeffries recently met in New York City to talk about areas of common ground — such as housing, immigration and the cost of living — as potential areas of collaboration between the Trump administration and a Democratic-led House.

Kushner, married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka Trump, has served as a foreign envoy for the White House. He has focused on the conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, as well as failed peace talks with Iranian officials.

Kushner told Jeffries he should meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, two people with knowledge of the meeting told the Times.

Rep. Beth Van Duyne (R-Texas) told NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” that Kushner and Jeffries “are trying to come up with compromises.”

“Congratulate them for that. It seems like they can’t win for losing,” she told host Chris Stirewalt. “If they talk to Democrats, they get criticized. If they don’t talk to Democrats, they get criticized.”

Jeffries has long been at odds with the White House and the president, having called the Medicaid cuts resulting from the GOP-backed One Big Beautiful Bill “ devastating ,” the Iran conflict “ Operation Epic Failure ” and Republicans “ phonies ” for adding to the national debt — which surpassed $40 trillion this week.

Some Democratic lawmakers have expressed support for the meeting.

“I’m in favor of people meeting with whoever they want to discuss ideas,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” Sunday. “But it’s one thing to have a meeting. It’s another thing to see something real come out of that.”

Tommy Vietor, who was once an aide to former President Obama and is now one of the co-hosts of the “Pod Save America” podcast, wrote on social media that Kushner “has no actual government job.”

Vietor added that Kushner “just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way @RepJeffries should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas.”

During an appearance on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing,” House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told host Peter Doocy that he does not “ know what that’s about .”

“I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on,” Johnson said Sunday. “He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House.”

articles.title: Trump administration preparing to revoke visas of up to 200K foreigners in largest mass visa revocation ever
articles.summary: The Trump administration is preparing to revoke business and tourism visas from up to 200,000 migrants who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the U.S. on a rolling basis — a move that would trigger the largest mass visa revocation ever, The Associated Press reported Monday. The State Department is expected to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke business and tourism visas from up to 200,000 migrants who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the U.S. on a rolling basis — a move that would trigger the largest mass visa revocation ever, The Associated Press reported Monday.

The State Department is expected to announce the revocation, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), of B1 and B2 visas issued since 2016, according to two U.S. officials and department documents obtained by the AP.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told The Hill.

Pigott declined to comment on the number of visa revocations and said that the “number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.”

The officials told the AP that revoking the visas will not result in immediate deportation, with pending asylum cases recategorized to no longer be for business or tourism travelers.

“People in the U.S. and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau wrote on social media Monday. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws; rather, it’s supposed to provide a narrow safe harbor for persons persecuted because of their ‘race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.'”

Landau added that the asylum system “has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims, meaning that it takes years to adjudicate whether applicants are actually entitled to asylum—during which time they can typically work, have children, and otherwise put down roots in our country.”

Current B1 and B2 visa applicants are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum and prove that they plan to return to their home countries.

President Trump has sought to ramp up restrictions on visas for asylum applicants since he returned to the White House last year. Since then, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people convicted or accused of various crimes, as well as for those who have spoken out against U.S. policies in the Middle East.

Last month, the Trump administration started to cut off asylum seekers’ access to interviews to weigh their claims, instead allowing officers to funnel migrants into immigration court for deportation proceedings. Migrants could be quickly funneled into the immigration court system without a chance to make their case to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
paragraphs: The Trump administration is preparing to revoke business and tourism visas from up to 200,000 migrants who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the U.S. on a rolling basis — a move that would trigger the largest mass visa revocation ever, The Associated Press reported Monday.

The State Department is expected to announce the revocation, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), of B1 and B2 visas issued since 2016, according to two U.S. officials and department documents obtained by the AP.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told The Hill.
Pigott declined to comment on the number of visa revocations and said that the “number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.”
The officials told the AP that revoking the visas will not result in immediate deportation, with pending asylum cases recategorized to no longer be for business or tourism travelers.

“People in the U.S. and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau wrote on social media Monday. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws; rather, it’s supposed to provide a narrow safe harbor for persons persecuted because of their ‘race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.'”

Landau added that the asylum system “has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims, meaning that it takes years to adjudicate whether applicants are actually entitled to asylum—during which time they can typically work, have children, and otherwise put down roots in our country.”
Current B1 and B2 visa applicants are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum and prove that they plan to return to their home countries.

President Trump has sought to ramp up restrictions on visas for asylum applicants since he returned to the White House last year. Since then, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people convicted or accused of various crimes, as well as for those who have spoken out against U.S. policies in the Middle East.

Last month, the Trump administration started to cut off asylum seekers’ access to interviews to weigh their claims, instead allowing officers to funnel migrants into immigration court for deportation proceedings. Migrants could be quickly funneled into the immigration court system without a chance to make their case to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

articles.title: Jackson calls Supreme Court’s mail-in voting ruling a ‘Kafkaesque nightmare’
articles.summary: Ketanji Brown Jackson, the Supreme Court’s junior liberal justice, excoriated her colleagues for lifting a block on President Trump’s mail-in voting executive order on Monday, saying it “needlessly injects chaos” into this year’s elections. “It also lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who…
articles.body:
Ketanji Brown Jackson, the Supreme Court’s junior liberal justice, excoriated her colleagues for lifting a block on President Trump’s mail-in voting executive order on Monday, saying it “needlessly injects chaos” into this year’s elections.

“It also lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges,” Jackson wrote .

She didn’t sign on to the dissent authored by Justice Sonia Sotomayor, which was joined by Elena Kagan, the third member of the court’s liberal wing. Instead, Jackson penned 23 pages of her own, saying the case wasn’t a “close call.”

Jackson said her colleagues lacked “situational awareness” in ruling that blue states needed to wait for the U.S. Postal Service to at least begin implementing Trump’s policy before challenging it. She called it a “catch-me-if-you-can” approach.

“When the Government’s obvious goal is to interfere with the Plaintiff States’ practices and prerogatives in a manner that the Constitution does not authorize, it is both a serious legal error and a grave misuse of our equitable emergency powers to let the Executive proceed even one step further,” Jackson wrote.

The Supreme Court’s emergency ruling enables Trump to move closer to implementing his March executive order targeting mail-in ballots in time for the midterms. But the decision is not a final ruling on the legality of the new requirements.

It follows a long series of cases in which Jackson has ruled against the administration on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket in forceful terms. In recent public appearances, she has accused her colleagues of having a “potentially corrosive” effect on the judiciary with their decisions.

articles.title: Back-to-school season fuels growing measles concerns
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Back-to-school season fuels growing measles concerns With back-to-school season underway, students are returning to class amid the worst year of measles in recent U.S. history, record-high vaccine exemptions reported among kindergarteners and continuously changing immunization guidance under the Trump administration. …
articles.body:
Back-to-school season fuels growing measles concerns

With back-to-school season underway, students are returning to class amid the worst year of measles in recent U.S. history, record-high vaccine exemptions reported among kindergarteners and continuously changing immunization guidance under the Trump administration.

Most U.S. public schools will have begun their 2026-27 academic years by the end of August and public health officials are wary of regions where vaccine coverage remains low .

“Because of the situation that we are finding ourselves in, we can definitely anticipate seeing more of what we’ve seen all year long,” Lori Freeman, CEO of the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO), told The Hill.

“There’s nothing that I can think of that’s going to stem the tide of what we’ve experienced; the only thing that’s going to turn it back is by addressing people’s fears about immunization, vaccination, and getting people vaccinated.”

As measles cases continue to rise, new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released this week found that nonmedical vaccine exemptions among kindergartners reached an all-time high during the 2025-26 school year — at 4.2 percent.

Further complicating matters is the Trump administration’s push to rewrite long-held vaccine policy.

Earlier this month, President Trump signed an executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split up by disease , which would in effect separate two vaccine appointments into six. Since he signed the order, one state after another has affirmed plans to keep the preexisting vaccine guidance, including California, New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania.

Acting on Trump’s executive order is also currently unfeasible as no manufacturers in the U.S. make monovalent vaccines individually targeting measles, mumps or rubella.

articles.title: El-Sayed and Watters clash in Fox News interview over culture war, gas prices
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Monday clashed with Fox News host Jesse Watters in a wide-ranging interview that was often full of cross talk and covered culture war topics, the candidate’s faith and gas prices, among other topics. El-Sayed, a progressive, appeared for roughly half an hour on “Jesse Watters Primetime,” where the…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Monday clashed with Fox News host Jesse Watters in a wide-ranging interview that was often full of cross talk and covered culture war topics, the candidate’s faith and gas prices, among other topics.

El-Sayed, a progressive, appeared for roughly half an hour on “Jesse Watters Primetime,” where the host played clips of past comments from El-Sayed and attempted to challenge him on those subjects, sometimes abruptly moving on to the next topic.

The two quarreled over gas prices, as El-Sayed accused Watters of not seeming “to be upset” about how they have soared as a result of the Iran war. He made a dig at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying he was the “sixth host” on Fox News’s “The Five” and that he “wanted to raise our military budget to $1.5 trillion.”

“You don’t seem to be upset about that,” El-Sayed continued. “What, so we can fight a war we don’t know how to get out of, to raise our gas prices to $5 a gallon? That doesn’t make sense to me.”

The two talked over each other about the $7 trillion federal budget, with El-Sayed emphasizing President Trump’s words about the conflict ending not long after it began in February.

“You go to war and you tell us that it’s going to be a special military operation. That was February,” he continued. “We’re now in September almost, and we’re still fighting the special military operation. I mean, it’s not working for us.”

“We’re not really fighting it, it’s a blockade,” Watters said.

Watters pressed El-Sayed on past comments he made about Sharia law, the official law of practicing Muslims. El-Sayed, who is Muslim, once said people seeking a ban on Sharia law are the “same exact forces that drove Native peoples from their land two centuries ago, destroyed Black Wall Street a century ago, bombed a building decades ago and tried to ban Sharia law not a decade ago, but those forces are alive and well today.”

“Do you know what canon law is, Jesse?” El-Sayed said, referring to the religious laws of Christianity. “I assume you’re Christian, right?”

“All right, so canon law is the name for Christian law,” El-Sayed said. “I don’t begrudge you your right to practice your faith as you choose. I don’t know why the idea that I could practice my faith as I choose is a problem. Nobody is trying to push Sharia law on anyone else, just like, I hope, nobody is trying to push canon law on anybody else, because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion.”

El-Sayed said lawmakers going after Sharia law “seems to me to be deliberately targeting the Muslim community.” Watters claimed that Sharia law in Michigan is “kinda scary” and said voters would not be for it.

“I don’t think that’s a good position,” Watters said.

“Nobody’s pushing it. No –– but Jesse, Jesse, nobody’s pushing it,” El-Sayed replied, before saying Michiganders “are worried about how they’re going to afford their gas.”

Watters later asked the candidate about his past comments referring to the NFL as racist and that activist and former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick “was a good guy.” El-Sayed said he thought Kaepernick was a “pretty damn good quarterback” who “should have had several more years in the NFL.”

“The bigger issue that we have for football right now is I looked at ticket prices to try and go and see a game with my family,” El-Sayed said. “It’s astronomical, through the roof.”

Watters then asked about gender-affirming care for children. El-Sayed, a physician, said decisions like that should be made between a child’s doctor and their parents, not by the federal government. Watters pushed back by asking if the candidate thought “it’s OK for a parent to slash his kid’s thing a little?”

“Do you really want to have this conversation?” El-Sayed asked. “Are you circumcised?”

“Yeah, but I mean, that’s a personal question, doctor,” Watters exclaimed. “A circumcision’s different than castration.”

“It’s a problem that you think that you get to decide what happens between a parent, a doctor and a patient,” El-Sayed replied back. “And I’m just saying that, yes, circumcision is surgery on a kid’s ding-a-ling. So if you really want to bring that up, you can. I just think you guys are really selective about how you want to go about these things.”

Asked about transgender athletes, El-Sayed pushed back on the question. Watters clapped back, claiming that it is “kind of a big thing if you’ve been following the news recently.”

“Please be serious,” El-Sayed replied. “I’m here with you, I want to talk about the issues that matter. Let’s talk about the things that people are actually talking about. … I know you guys are talking about that, but, like, most of the country’s not.”

El-Sayed won a narrow victory against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the Michigan Democratic primary for Senate earlier this month and will face off against Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in November.

articles.title: Jeffries responds to Kushner meeting backlash: ‘No one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass’
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Monday said “no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass” in a post on the social media platform X. The video comes after he faced backlash for meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law. The New York Times reported Sunday that the two met privately ahead…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Monday said “no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass” in a post on the social media platform X. The video comes after he faced backlash for meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law.

The New York Times reported Sunday that the two met privately ahead of November’s midterms to discuss common ground on issues like housing, immigration and the high cost of living.

Jeffries said Kushner reached out to him first, and he accepted so the pair could discuss affordability. His post emphasized, however, that House Democrats have pushed the Trump administration on issues including tariffs, the Affordable Care Act, nutritional assistance and more.

“I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass,” he said. “We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, and be guided by the Constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.”

Reactions to the meeting have been mixed. Tommy Vietor, a co-host of “Pod Save America” and former Obama aide, took to X on Sunday to criticize Kushner .

“Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals,” he said.

Kushner has served as a foreign envoy for Trump, working on conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the meeting to Fox News’s Peter Doocy on “The Sunday Briefing.”

“I don’t know what that’s about. I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on,” he said. “He’s not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day to day in the White House.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) backed Jeffries at a Monday press conference when asked whether he’d support the representative as House majority leader if Democrats take back the House in November. “I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader,” Mamdani said.

Jeffries said House Democrats have “delivered results” in battling corruption. “Pam Bondi is gone. Kristi Noem is gone, and we’re just getting started,” he said, referring to the former attorney general and secretary of Homeland Security, respectively.

He concluded the video by discussing affordability.

“People are drowning in this failed economy and are demanding action. We have a responsibility to deal with the fact that life is too expensive,” he said. “And that’s what we intend to do.”

articles.title: El-Sayed spars with Jesse Watters on Fox News on immigration, Iran war: ‘Let me just answer the question’
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Monday clashed with Fox News host Jesse Watters on a slew of topics, including immigration enforcement and the Iran war, along with culture war topics, prompting the host twice to let him “just answer the question.” The interview on “Jesse Watters Primetime” kicked off with a discussion on…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Monday clashed with Fox News host Jesse Watters on a slew of topics, including immigration enforcement and the Iran war, along with culture war topics , prompting the host twice to let him “just answer the question.”

The interview on “Jesse Watters Primetime” kicked off with a discussion on immigration and the duties carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Watters pressed El-Sayed on calling for ICE to be abolished, but the candidate stressed the Immigration and Naturalization Service’s (INS) handling of federal immigration cases before it was replaced by ICE in 2003.

“We were able to enforce our immigration policies without shooting people in the face and the back of the head,” El-Sayed said.

Watters dismissed this, saying INS “did the same thing as ICE back then” before cross talk erupted, with the host asking how many migrants without legal status were in the U.S.

articles.title: Graham hopes Trump propels her across finish line in South Carolina
articles.summary: The South Carolina Senate runoff on Tuesday is becoming a key test of President Trump’s endorsement power, as he throws all his weight behind a political newcomer seeking to fill shoes left by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The race has divided the party between those who back Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.),…
articles.body:
The South Carolina Senate runoff on Tuesday is becoming a key test of President Trump’s endorsement power, as he throws all his weight behind a political newcomer seeking to fill shoes left by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The race has divided the party between those who back Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who was tapped to serve out her brother’s term and whom Trump encouraged to run for another six years, and supporters of Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), a member of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus with a long history of representing the state.

Trump has leaned into the race in a way he has rarely done this midterm cycle, holding a campaign rally Friday night in Myrtle Beach, S.C., for Graham and attaching his own political clout to the outcome.

“What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump told supporters at a rally for Graham Friday night in Myrtle Beach.

“So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time,” the president added. “You got to say it, and you got to come out and vote.”

Trump’s MAGA Inc. also spent over $827,000 for Graham, marking the super PAC’s first independent expenditure since March.

Graham’s support has come from establishment Republicans , including the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the president himself , political action committees and business executives. The Palmetto State’s governor, who appointed Graham to her brother’s seat , is campaigning with the senator on Monday.

Norman, meanwhile, has self-funded much of his campaign and has leaned on his conservative policy chops, while accusing Graham of being “controlled by the Washington elite.”

But with such a short campaign window and a limited public record to run on, every move Graham has made matters.

So during last week’s debate, when Graham struggled to answer a rudimentary question on foreign policy — a subject matter that came to define much of her late brother’s legacy in public service — the moment came to dominate the news cycle.

“That’s the kind of thing that, if she does lose on Tuesday, I feel like we’ll be chalking entirely up to that,” Geoffrey Skelley, Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst, said of the debate flub.

“Of course that would be simplistic, but if you’re not familiar, and you find yourself as the front-runner … that really stands out as a defining moment for your candidacy,” he continued. “You can see how she might end up blowing this.”

Norman has pledged not to go negative on the campaign against Graham, saying last week, “She’s been through a lot. … She really has, losing a brother. I’m not going to do that,” referring to his decision not to run antagonistic ads.

But the congressman has still highlighted Graham’s lack of political experience, both on the debate stage and in the days that followed.

“By her choice, she’s running for the United States Senate. It’s a six-year term,” Norman said during the debate. “You need to get fully versed in what issues you’re going to be dealing with. This isn’t a get-training-on-the-job. You can’t do that.”

At last week’s debate, Graham responded that she was “not that informed on national security” when asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues.

Graham then touted her family’s service in the military, saying she’s “not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.”

In an interview with Fox News’s Sean Hannity the following evening, Graham acknowledged the fumble and leaned into attacks on her lack of experience, saying she’s since talked to voters and they appreciate her candor and that she’s not a “career politician.”

“I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan, but you know, I’ve said many times, I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” she said. “I was just honest, and I think that’s kind of a foreign concept.”

Trump echoed a similar defense when asked Friday about the gaffe, telling reporters that Graham “was being honest.”

“She’s surrounded by very good people, and she said that she’s totally for the military,” the president said.

As Graham has continued to brand herself as a political outsider, her opponent has repeatedly attacked her as the candidate backed by “the Washington elite,” pointing to her donors, which include Boeing’s political action committee, private equity firm Blackstone’s chief executive officer, social media platform TikTok’s head of public policy, and tech company Palantir’s head of defense chief of staff, according to South Carolina-based news outlet The State .

But Graham has pushed back on these efforts, saying earlier this month, according to The State, “When people give to me, that means they support me.”

“That doesn’t necessarily mean I support them,” she added.

The race has drawn millions of dollars from individual donors as well as from super PACs. In the last week of the race alone, Security is Strength PAC contributed more than $1.8 million and Palmetto Action gave nearly $1.2 million to boost Graham or oppose Norman, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records. Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a renewable energy-backed group, announced on Aug. 14 that it would spend $1 million to defeat Norman.

Norman’s funding from outside groups is dwarfed by Graham’s, but his campaign has benefited from his personal wealth. He donated $1.3 million to his own campaign on Aug. 17, four days after giving another $400,000, according to FEC reports.

Endorsements in the race have also swung more in Graham’s favor. On Monday alone, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) campaigned with the senator, and Trump joined a tele-rally with Graham at night for a last-ditch push to encourage South Carolinians to vote.

But last Friday, Norman got a boost when former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R), who came in fourth place during the special primary this month, backed Norman over Graham.

Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.), who came in a close third, backed Graham, who rallied in his district with Trump on Friday.

The results of the Aug. 11 primary were close, with Graham and Norman advancing with 32.75 percent and 24.62 percent, respectively, followed by Fry with 19.66 percent and Sanford with 14.94 percent.

Public polling has been limited in the couple of weeks since, and the dynamics have changed. As a result, many political observers are going in blind on Tuesday, waiting to see to what extent the debate, cash and Trump’s support will make a difference in the outcome.

“If you’re in the lead and … you have the support of the president, it’s a pretty good place to be,” Skelley said. “So I’m not necessarily saying that I think Graham is going to lose. I just think that this race really does feel up in the air.”

articles.title: Trump’s fight with GOP senators over trade intensifies
articles.summary: President Trump is headed for a clash with Senate Republicans over his decision to pause tariffs on beef imports while ratcheting up tariffs on key Canadian goods. Trump’s plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices while simultaneously threatening Canada with 50…
articles.body:
President Trump is headed for a clash with Senate Republicans over his decision to pause tariffs on beef imports while ratcheting up tariffs on key Canadian goods .

Trump’s plan to exempt 300,000 tons of product for ground beef from out-of-quota tariffs to address Americans’ concerns about high food prices while simultaneously threatening Canada with 50 percent tariffs on imports that could impact auto and housing prices has sparked a furious response from GOP senators across the party’s political spectrum.

“I think it’s a mistake. It’s what happens when he has advisers trying to micromanage things. They’re skating where the puck is versus where it needs to be. If you think that providing subsidized beef for some period of time is going to make farmers happy and prices go down on systemic basis, you’re wrong. It doesn’t happen,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said at the Capitol Monday.

“Every time the government micromanages the economy, consumers suffer,” Tillis warned.

Tillis is one of several Republicans from an agriculture-heavy state to warn against allowing cheap beef imports to flood the U.S. market over the next three months — something that Trump hopes will bring down the price of an American diet staple through the midterm election.

Senate Republican Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), the second-ranking member of the Senate Republican leadership, declared Monday that “Americans want US beef on the table — not foreign imports.”

“Wyoming ranchers produce the highest quality beef in the world. Our ranchers don’t ask for special treatment. They simply want a fair marketplace. It needs to be easier – not harder – for Wyoming ranchers to feed America,” he posted on X, the social media platform.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the third-ranking member of the Senate GOP leadership, warned that opening U.S. markets to cheaper imports is “ill-advised” and will hurt domestic producers.

“Beef prices are too high for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small. Imported beef below market prices will only put more pressure on our cattlemen,” Cotton argued on social media.

“I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider. We need to support our cattlemen, grow the herd, and let the market work,” Cotton wrote.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also took to social media to dismiss Trump’s move as a “quick fix” and argued it’s out of step with the president’s efforts to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity with tariffs, such as those he’s threatening against Canada.

“What our market really needs is a stable, America-First national policy that promotes American beef rather than continuing to import foreign beef as a quick ‘fix.’ This instability harms hardworking American ranchers and consumers who want American-made beef,” he wrote.

“This is the exact opposite approach we take compared to manufacturing, and it doesn’t make sense,” Rounds added.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), a member of the Agriculture Committee, shared that relatively strong beef prices were a “bright spot” for the nation’s “struggling agriculture industry.”

“Importing beef below market prices will only put further downward pressure on the livestock sector, endangering what has been a bright spot in a struggling agriculture industry,” the Kansas senator wrote on social media. “I urge President Trump to halt this action, listen to ranchers and let the free markets work.”

Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley (Iowa), Deb Fischer (Neb.) and Pete Ricketts (Neb.) also raised alarms over foreign beef showing up in American grocery stores.

Grassley said he was “concerned” while Fischer said she was “extremely disappointed by this decision” and Ricketts warned that “flooding the market with lower quality beef” would hurt Nebraska farmers and ranchers.

Yet Trump appears to be more sensitive to ground beef prices, which have risen by approximately 20 percent since he took office in January of 2025.

The average price of ground beef reached $6.89 per pound in July.

Trump pledged that imported beef will be sold at “25 percent below current market prices” over the next three months.

Some Democratic candidates, such as Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek who’s eyeing a Senate seat, are highlighting “skyrocketing” beef prices on the campaign trail.

But many Republicans don’t think that allowing cheap imports into the country is the best solution.

“Increasing beef imports would lead to more uncertainty and instability for our farmers,” said Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), the GOP candidate in Iowa’s Senate race.

“We should be focused on cutting red tape for cattle producers, lowering the cost of production and supporting market-based solutions to support Iowa producers and lower costs for consumers,” she wrote on social media.

The criticism from GOP senators of Trump’s decision to pause tariffs on beef imports comes as other Republican senators are pushing back against Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on an array of Canadian imports and his threat to impose equally high fees on even more.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who faces a tough reelection race in a state that voted for former President Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the last two presidential elections, called Trump’s threatened tariffs against Canada “a mistake.”

“We produce a lot in Maine — our blueberries, our potatoes, our lobster, our lumber — that is processed across the border. If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products,” Collins told News Center Maine in an interview Monday.

Collins was one of four Republicans who voted last year to revoke Trump’s tariffs against Canada. She and Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Rand Paul (Ky.) and Mitch McConnell (Ky.) voted with Democrats to pass a resolution blocking them.

Six House Republicans voted with Democrats to pass a similar measure in the House last year.

Former Trump economic adviser Stephen Moore warned that any gains that domestic businesses might get from higher tariffs on Canadian goods are likely outweighed by the “pain” felt by U.S. consumers and businesses that import Canadian products or sell to Canadian markets.

“Probably the pain is not worth the gain. And you know, I’ve been a bit of a skeptic on the tariff front with respect to the Trump strategy,” Moore told Fox Business in an interview Monday.

He warned that raising the cost of Canadian goods may come while Americans are still coping with higher energy prices because of Iran war’s impact on oil and gas prices.

“We’re in a sticky situation obviously in Iran with respect to those negotiations. Now … do I think now is a good time to fight a trade war with Canada? Probably not,” he said. “Commodity prices are rising right now in the U.S. That’s a bad sign. That’s an indication that inflation continues to tick up.”

Tillis on Monday warned that charging steep tariffs on Canadian goods threatens to disrupt the economies of border states — such as Maine — that are closely integrated with the Canadian economy.

“Let the economy do what the economy’s doing. Get the trade relationships with Canada done versus all this volatility. You’re going to address more price fluctuations by doing this than all these gimmicks,” Tillis said.

The North Carolina senator warned that Republicans are running out of time to help farmers before the midterm elections as both a farm bill, which includes relief programs for ranchers hurt by drought and fire, and a budget reconciliation package, which includes $12 billion in emergency assistance to farmers, is stalled in the Senate.

“We’ve got 71 days” until the election “and right now we don’t have a positive message to tell farm country,” he said. “And we haven’t since Liberation Day last year, which is why I was concerned.”

Trump announced sweeping global tariffs on April 2, 2025, which the president proclaimed “Liberation Day.”

If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products,” Collins told News Center Maine in an interview Monday.

Collins was one of four Republicans who voted last year to revoke Trump’s tariffs against Canada. She and Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Rand Paul (Ky.) and Mitch McConnell (Ky.) voted with Democrats to pass a resolution blocking them.
Six House Republicans voted with Democrats to pass a similar measure in the House last year.

Former Trump economic adviser Stephen Moore warned that any gains that domestic businesses might get from higher tariffs on Canadian goods are likely outweighed by the “pain” felt by U.S. consumers and businesses that import Canadian products or sell to Canadian markets.
“Probably the pain is not worth the gain. And you know, I’ve been a bit of a skeptic on the tariff front with respect to the Trump strategy,” Moore told Fox Business in an interview Monday.
He warned that raising the cost of Canadian goods may come while Americans are still coping with higher energy prices because of Iran war’s impact on oil and gas prices.

“We’re in a sticky situation obviously in Iran with respect to those negotiations. Now … do I think now is a good time to fight a trade war with Canada? Probably not,” he said. “Commodity prices are rising right now in the U.S. That’s a bad sign. That’s an indication that inflation continues to tick up.”
Tillis on Monday warned that charging steep tariffs on Canadian goods threatens to disrupt the economies of border states — such as Maine — that are closely integrated with the Canadian economy.

“Let the economy do what the economy’s doing. Get the trade relationships with Canada done versus all this volatility. You’re going to address more price fluctuations by doing this than all these gimmicks,” Tillis said.

The North Carolina senator warned that Republicans are running out of time to help farmers before the midterm elections as both a farm bill, which includes relief programs for ranchers hurt by drought and fire, and a budget reconciliation package, which includes $12 billion in emergency assistance to farmers, is stalled in the Senate.
“We’ve got 71 days” until the election “and right now we don’t have a positive message to tell farm country,” he said. “And we haven’t since Liberation Day last year, which is why I was concerned.”
Trump announced sweeping global tariffs on April 2, 2025, which the president proclaimed “Liberation Day.”

articles.title: The Memo: Trump and Bessent crank up economic pressure on Iran as other options fall short
articles.summary: Six months into the war on Iran — and with less than three months left before the midterms — the Trump administration has decided it’s time for Plan C. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out his ambitions for an “economic onslaught” against the Islamic Republic that would target its “financial connections around the…
articles.body:
Six months into the war on Iran — and with less than three months left before the midterms — the Trump administration has decided it’s time for Plan C.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out his ambitions for an “economic onslaught” against the Islamic Republic that would target its “financial connections around the globe.”

The hope within the administration seems to be that turning up the economic heat on Iran can produce tangible results without the baleful complications that could result from the two other broad options before the president.

If President Trump were to return to all-out war, he would risk a new spike in oil prices, Iranian reprisals aimed at U.S. allies in the Gulf, and a further diminution of American munition stockpiles. Even then, it is not clear that a definitive victory would be achieved without putting U.S. boots on Iranian soil — a scenario that has vanishingly thin support from the public.

If, on the other hand, Trump were to sue for peace right now, Iranian recalcitrance — and an apparent belief in Tehran that they retain plenty of leverage — would require him to make sizeable concessions.

The memorandum of understanding signed in June provided a preview of how such an approach would be received: Negatively.

The memorandum drew criticism from GOP hawks, who suggested it was too soft on Iran; from liberal opponents, who asked rhetorically what the war had been for in the first place; and from Israel, which jointly launched the war with the U.S. in late February.

So, on Monday it fell to Bessent to put some flesh on the bones of Trump’s earlier threats to up the economic pressure on Iran. The president, in a morning social media post, had insisted in his customary all-caps style that “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

The Treasury secretary communicates in a different register to his boss, but his language was aggressive all the same.

The administration’s objective, he said, was “to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Taking questions from reporters after his prepared remarks, Bessent characterized the U.S. as intent upon the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran.

When it came to the U.S. desire to see other nations comply with Washington’s demands to cut off Iran or face secondary sanctions, Bessent warned, “We do not have infinite patience here.”

There were some definite lines of economic attack — but also a lot of detail that was not filled in.

For example, Bessent asserted that five areas of activity by which Iran sustains itself would be targeted: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also insisted that branches of Iran’s Bank Melli “must be shuttered and dark.”

Bessent also contended, even as he spoke, that an office within the Treasury Department was “sanctioning over 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world that enable the Iranian regime to procure illicit nuclear and missile technology, conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.”

Yet, alongside the tough talk, there was also some vagueness.

Importantly, a sizeable question mark hangs over how aggressive the administration is prepared to be with China, which is by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil exports.

Asked about that topic, Bessent asserted both that “no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” and that “the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy.”

It is, of course, rather debatable how committed the Trump administration is to quiet diplomacy. A few hours before Bessent’s appearance before the cameras, Trump had delivered a new jab in an unrelated trade dispute with the U.S.’s northern neighbor, beginning a lengthy social media post by declaring, “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years.”

That being so, Bessent’s supposed commitment to a softer, more private approach could also function to provide cover for ambivalence about how hard to push Beijing.

The unignorable backdrop to all the machinations is the unpopularity of the war with the American public.

Trump’s approval on Iran in the RealClearPolitics polling average is deep underwater. Roughly 61 percent of Americans disapprove of his handling of the issue, while about 35 percent approve.

The war is intertwined with voters’ chief concern — rising prices and the cost of living. The average gas price nationally was roughly $4.10 per gallon on Monday, according to AAA , having been just below $3 before the war began.

Inflationary pressures, in part caused by the Iran war, are also part of the reason why there have been some jitters on the bond market recently. Bessent stepped in to try to calm the unease last week, with only partial success.

Put it all together, and it is an inhospitable landscape for Republicans seeking office in November’s midterms.

For now, the administration is clearly recalibrating its rhetoric.

Even the pugilistic Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters on Monday that, although he was not “foreclosing” using direct strikes on Iran, “economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now .”

Bessent, in a lesser-noted part of his Monday remarks, characterized the U.S. armed forces as having “laid the groundwork” for the achievement of American objectives.

This was a notably more circumspect assessment than those given by other senior administration officials in the early part of the war.

So, for now, the Iranian economy is the battlefield.

The big question is how fast, if at all, the U.S. can secure a meaningful victory.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: South Carolina runoff pits America First against MAGA
articles.summary: Voters, especially Republican primary voters, don’t tend to make their decisions based on what’s going on overseas. But with Uncle Sam’s place in the world looking a little unsteady and a doozy of a debate gaffe in a snap election, we suddenly have in today’s South Carolina Senate runoff the first big electoral test of…
articles.body:
Voters, especially Republican primary voters, don’t tend to make their decisions based on what’s going on overseas.

But with Uncle Sam’s place in the world looking a little unsteady and a doozy of a debate gaffe in a snap election, we suddenly have in today’s South Carolina Senate runoff the first big electoral test of President Trump’s Iran war strategy with Republican voters.

Sen. Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) already-legendary line — “I’m not that informed on national security” — is thought by many to have recast what had appeared to be a perfunctory runoff with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) into a competitive race. I say perfunctory because in the first round, the MAGA candidates got most of the vote, almost all of which presumably would filter down to Graham in today’s contest.

There were five candidates who got at least 5 percent of the vote in the first round of the snap primary on Aug. 11, held to replace Graham’s brother, Lindsey. The elder Graham died in July after winning renomination for a fifth Senate term, leaving the state GOP without a Senate candidate in a good Democratic year — one in which the blue team happens to have a nonterrible Senate nominee in Annie Andrews. It’s South Carolina, where no Democratic Senate candidate has come within even 10 points of winning in decades. But still, a bad enough Republican nominee in a bad enough year could have put the Palmetto State race on the map, at least notionally.

There’s plenty that’s weird and wild in South Carolina Republican politics, so Gov. Henry McMaster (R) took no chances and appointed Darline Graham to serve out the final months of her brother’s term. That appointment and her decision to seek a full, six-year term came at the behest of Trump, who has had his own troubles with South Carolina politics.

Before Lindsey Graham became Trump’s wingman and shadow secretary of State, he had been among Trump’s fiercest early critics. And then there’s former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R), who went the other direction, serving deferentially as Trump’s first-term ambassador to the United Nations before running a dogged if doomed race against Trump as he sought renomination in 2024. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) also opposed Trump that year, but only halfheartedly and not for very long.

Knowing that South Carolina can be problematic and looking for another member of the Senate MAGA caucus, Trump clearly judged that backing a sentimental favorite in the beloved sister of the late senator would be easy electoral politics and give him an easy vote in Washington, where things have only been getting harder for the lame-duck commander in chief.

In that way, Graham’s gaffe was proof of concept for Trump. Asked about her professed ignorance ahead of his trip to campaign for Graham, Trump told reporters , “She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants. She understands that national security is my thing.” That presumably applies when his “thing” is increasingly unpopular with voters.

Trump’s electoral assumption about Graham was proven right in Round 1 of the snap primary, when she got about a third of the vote, besting Norman by 8 points. Norman is not MAGA but rather a dissident from South Carolina’s underlying don’t-tread-on-me tradition. The House Freedom Caucus is pretty much a MAGA operation now, but back when Norman joined in 2017, there was still a little of the rebellious streak left. Norman has always had a little of Marjorie Taylor Greene energy about him — more about the movement than the man. But he’s also won friends among traditional conservatives for his hawkishness on spending and Reaganite foreign policy. It wasn’t just home-state sentiment that led Norman to back Haley in 2024 or Haley to back him now.

In third place on Aug. 11 was Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.), who is stone-cold MAGA to his core. Team Trump backed Fry in his 2022 primary bid against then-Rep. Tom Rice (R-S.C.), an old-school conservative who had voted to impeach Trump for trying to overturn the 2020 election. Fry beat Rice in a major show of strength for Trump early in his interregnum, making Fry a made man in MAGA. He got nearly 20 percent of the vote in Round 1 and then, to the surprise of no one, fell in behind Trump-endorsed Graham for the runoff.

Next in the running was Mark Sanford, the former governor and congressman who was a conservative heartthrob until the vivid unraveling of his marriage while still the state’s chief executive. Sanford is neither MAGA nor America First in any strict sense. He’s a traditional, small-government conservative with some areas of overlap with both groups but is clearly and stubbornly a dissident. He is also a hated figure in MAGA World for his frequent opposition to Trump during Sanford’s House tenure. No surprise, then, that he is backing Norman over Graham on Tuesday. It’s an echo of the onetime conservative dream team in the state that once included Sanford, Haley, Scott and former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.), now long eclipsed by Trump and McMaster’s very effective machine.

Rounding out the top five was Mark Lynch, who has a massive appliance store in South Carolina’s Upstate. Lynch proved that he is more America First than MAGA when he ran against Lindsey Graham in the original June primary. While Lynch is part of a movement that takes out-there stances on things like allegations of election corruption and vaccines , he is willing to publicly disagree with Trump. And given that his central charge against the elder Graham was that he was too much of an internationalist, one suspects Lynch isn’t a “forever war” kind of guy. He too has endorsed Norman .

All of which makes the Iran question particularly interesting. Darline Graham accidentally summed up the MAGA Iran position: Back the president and let him do his “thing.” The America First position tends to be that the war was a betrayal of Trump’s promises and a mistake from the start that is only getting worse. The conservative stance seems to be that bombing Iran could have been the right move but that Trump has subsequently blundered it away. The candidates in this race have been cagy about their own stances, but voters are going to make their own inferences.

Not everyone who voted in Round 1 will vote in Round 2, but we can use the results as a rough guide for where today’s electorate started. The MAGA candidates — Graham and Fry — combined for 52 percent of the vote. America Firsters and conservatives — Norman, Sanford and Lynch — combined for 46 percent, with 2 percent sprinkled across minor candidates.

The question today is whether Graham’s textbook Kinsley gaffe is worth at least 4 points for Norman with swing among voters who are having their own doubts about whether the president should be running foreign policy without supervision. Norman’s hope has got to be that he’s got enough cred with both America First and the conservatives to make it happen.

Stirewalt is the politics editor for The Hill, veteran campaign and elections journalist and best-selling author of books about American political history.

articles.title: Bessent slow rolls ‘Economic D-Day’ on Iran
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Voters head to polls in GOP runoffs ▪ Supreme Court upholds mail-in order for now ▪ Trump threatens another round of Canada tariffs ▪ Nevada sues over Colorado River use cuts Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of…
articles.body:
▪ Supreme Court upholds mail-in order for now

▪ Trump threatens another round of Canada tariffs

▪ Nevada sues over Colorado River use cuts

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of a threat than immediately bringing the hammer down, at least for now.

Bessent issued a warning during a press conference for all countries to cut off business and other financial ties with Iran or else face significant sanctions.

The plan has been named “Operation Economic Outcast” and promoted as comparable to the U.S. invasion of Normandy during World War II. But Bessent avoided naming specific countries that the U.S. is seeking to pressure and didn’t share many specific actions or a timeline that the federal government would take.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said, when asked at a press conference why sanctions wouldn’t take effect immediately.

Bessent said diplomacy is happening behind the scenes, as President Trump is calling world leaders to get them to cut off Iran. He said officials from the State, Treasury and Defense departments are also calling their counterparts around the world.

He expressed confidence about the plan, saying that the U.S. has “already seen some results” and emphasizing that Trump can be “quite persuasive.”

But the announcement fell short of quite the boisterous threats that the president has been making for days leading up to the move, as he seeks to force Iran back to the bargaining table and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!” Trump said in a Truth Social post Wednesday. “This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

Trump said any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide “any type of lifeline” to Iran will face “TREMENDOUS” economic consequences.

While the president hasn’t ruled out additional military action against Iran, he has shifted his focus to the economic realm amid growing warnings over depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles.

One complicating factor to the “outcast” plan is the role of China, which is Iran’s largest trading partner. Bessent said “no country is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” when asked plans for China.

Experts told NBC News that the success of Bessent’s announcement will depend on whether Iran’s most powerful trading partners — China, India and Russia — deem the U.S. threats credible.

Bessent also announced other actions designed to squeeze Iran economically, including placing sanctions on 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs, its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Treasury Department said it was expanding its authority to sanction any person, regardless of location, for operating specific sectors of the Iranian economy, including digital assets, technology, aviation and shipping.

Iran’s currency, the rial, continued to take a hit on Monday, falling to a record low of about 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. U.S. markets seemed to mostly shrug at the news, as the Dow Jones finished slightly up compared to the start of the day, while Nasdaq and the S&P 500 finished slightly lower.

Signs of Iran’s economic struggles amid the war continue to multiply. The International Monetary Fund said its economy will contract by 5.4 percent this year, while the government is signaling a coming hike to fuel prices in a bid to buoy the economy, a move that will compound rising prices.

What’s less certain is whether that pain is increasing pressure on the hardline regime to end the war.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , who has led negotiations with the U.S., have pointed to the economic anxiety in remarks about the country’s war posture in recent days.

However, leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps are seen as digging in, promoting a more assertive approach to the war focused on “offensive operations.”

An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the “strategy of shifting the war to an offensive posture if Iran’s conditions are not met will undoubtedly transform the balance of power in the world,” CNN reported.

How much Iran’s military is willing to test that theory, or whether the U.S. is willing to put the screws to global powers still supporting Iran, are key questions in a war that has now gone on for almost six months.

▪ The Hill : The Memo: Trump cranks up Iran economic pressure.

▪ The Hill : Democrats demand war cost details from Trump, Hegseth.

▪ Reuters : U.S. cancels joint Marine drills with South Korea over war constraints.

Republican California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton revealed to NewsNation his plan to try to stop parents and teachers from having to pick up the cost of school supplies. It’s another way to address the affordability issue . As we saw last week, Trump had his own idea regarding importing beef to lower prices for consumers. However, American ranchers have panned the plan. So did Hilton when I spoke with him on Monday.
