Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent rolled out the Trump administration’s much-anticipated “Economic D-Day” offensive against Iran on Monday but signaled the plan entails more of a threat than immediately bringing the hammer down, at least for now.
Bessent issued a warning during a press conference for all countries to cut off business and other financial ties with Iran or else face significant sanctions.

The plan has been named “Operation Economic Outcast” and promoted as comparable to the U.S. invasion of Normandy during World War II. But Bessent avoided naming specific countries that the U.S. is seeking to pressure and didn’t share many specific actions or a timeline that the federal government would take.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he said, when asked at a press conference why sanctions wouldn’t take effect immediately.

Bessent said diplomacy is happening behind the scenes, as President Trump is calling world leaders to get them to cut off Iran. He said officials from the State, Treasury and Defense departments are also calling their counterparts around the world.
He expressed confidence about the plan, saying that the U.S. has “already seen some results” and emphasizing that Trump can be “quite persuasive.”

But the announcement fell short of quite the boisterous threats that the president has been making for days leading up to the move, as he seeks to force Iran back to the bargaining table and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!” Trump said in a Truth Social post Wednesday. “This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”
Trump said any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide “any type of lifeline” to Iran will face “TREMENDOUS” economic consequences.
While the president hasn’t ruled out additional military action against Iran, he has shifted his focus to the economic realm amid growing warnings over depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles.
One complicating factor to the “outcast” plan is the role of China, which is Iran’s largest trading partner. Bessent said “no country is above the reach of U.S. sanctions” when asked plans for China.
Experts told NBC News that the success of Bessent’s announcement will depend on whether Iran’s most powerful trading partners — China, India and Russia — deem the U.S. threats credible.

Bessent also announced other actions designed to squeeze Iran economically, including placing sanctions on 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs, its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Treasury Department said it was expanding its authority to sanction any person, regardless of location, for operating specific sectors of the Iranian economy, including digital assets, technology, aviation and shipping.

Iran’s currency, the rial, continued to take a hit on Monday, falling to a record low of about 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. U.S. markets seemed to mostly shrug at the news, as the Dow Jones finished slightly up compared to the start of the day, while Nasdaq and the S&P 500 finished slightly lower.

Signs of Iran’s economic struggles amid the war continue to multiply. The International Monetary Fund said its economy will contract by 5.4 percent this year, while the government is signaling a coming hike to fuel prices in a bid to buoy the economy, a move that will compound rising prices.
What’s less certain is whether that pain is increasing pressure on the hardline regime to end the war.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf , who has led negotiations with the U.S., have pointed to the economic anxiety in remarks about the country’s war posture in recent days.
However, leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps are seen as digging in, promoting a more assertive approach to the war focused on “offensive operations.”

An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the “strategy of shifting the war to an offensive posture if Iran’s conditions are not met will undoubtedly transform the balance of power in the world,” CNN reported.

How much Iran’s military is willing to test that theory, or whether the U.S. is willing to put the screws to global powers still supporting Iran, are key questions in a war that has now gone on for almost six months.

articles.title: The victory lap on Trump’s nuclear campus plan is premature
articles.summary: Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan should clear five tests.
articles.body:
In late July, the Department of Energy announced that five states — Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho — had agreed to explore hosting Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses .

Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the campuses “massive generators of economic growth” that would be “crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance.” The American Nuclear Society echoed him, its president promising “multigenerational job creation, sustained economic growth, and new investment in education and workforce development.”

By folding nuclear waste into a sweeping economic development package, the department has invited states to compete for campuses that could co-locate multiple stages of the nuclear fuel cycle — such as uranium enrichment, fuel fabrication, spent fuel reprocessing, waste disposition and, in some states, advanced reactors. This is all while using the appeal of nuclear power investment to soften the politics of hosting long-term waste facilities.

It is an appealing vision. But five signed memoranda are not five host communities. No final host agreement has been signed, no construction funds awarded and the states have agreed only to continue negotiations. That is a real beginning, but it is not a victory. Treating it as one risks repeating the cycle of overpromising and disappointment that has paralyzed American nuclear waste policy for four decades.

I say this as a former Energy Department official who served as federal manager for the Consent-Based Siting Consortia — a $24 million 12-team initiative supporting public engagement around the siting of spent-fuel storage facilities. Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan must clear five tests.

First, the department must explain the scale of its projections. Its January solicitation offered an illustrative scenario in which one campus employed 50,000 direct workers, generated another 100,000 to 150,000 indirect jobs, and required 10,000 to 20,000 housing units. The same document put the entire existing U.S. nuclear workforce at roughly 80,000. By July, the Energy Department was projecting 25,000 jobs per campus .

Those figures may rest on different assumptions, but the Energy Department has not explained the methodology or reconciled the difference. Numbers that swing this far before a single site is chosen are aspirations, not plans.

Second, the department needs a technically credible schedule. Its solicitation says it wants initial facilities online “in the 2027 timeframe” and promises preference to the states with “more ambitious timelines” — remarkably soon for infrastructure of this kind.

States, meanwhile, had just nine weeks to assemble sweeping proposals. Any serious schedule for the waste disposition component must separately account for geological screening, independent site characterization, groundwater and seismic studies, environmental review, Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing, transportation planning and host-agreement negotiation. A facility built to isolate waste for decades, centuries, or millennia cannot be validated on a ribbon-cutting schedule.

Third, Washington must put up real money and enforceable commitments. A repository would, in principle, draw on the federal Nuclear Waste Fund . But for nearly everything else, the department told states to look to private capital — industry, technology firms, private equity, venture funds. It floats possible federal cost-sharing, loan guarantees and grants, but it commits to none and says states and private investors are expected to lead and finance the effort.

Communities asked to keep nuclear waste for generations need money that is committed and obligations that are enforceable against future administrations.

Fourth, Congress must authorize the plan’s spent-fuel storage and disposal components. The Nuclear Waste Policy Act still directs the federal repository program toward Yucca Mountain, whose development Congress has not funded since fiscal 2010 . The act also prevents construction of a centralized federal spent fuel storage facility until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has authorized construction of a repository. The department cannot designate one of the five states as a spent fuel site by press release.

Fifth, host communities must consent. States applied and governors signed, and some local governments in Utah, Idaho and Tennessee have expressed preliminary support. But it is far from clear that any specific community has agreed to live beside nuclear waste facilities.

Genuine consent requires a named candidate community, early involvement rather than after-the-fact persuasion, meaningful say over benefits, the participation of affected Tribal Nations and a real chance to walk away before commitments are final. The Energy Department’s process ran the other way: It gave states nine weeks to name sites and gauge local sentiment and rewarded those promising to streamline permitting and move fast.

After decades in which states treated nuclear waste as politically untouchable, the willingness of five governors to enter the negotiating room is a real achievement. But no spent-fuel repository in any of the five states is authorized under current law, no community has completed a voluntary siting process, no binding host agreement has been signed and no durable financing package or credible schedule has been demonstrated.

When a willing community stays at the table through investigation, negotiation, licensing and construction, the Energy Department will have earned its victory lap. For now, it has earned only the right to begin the hard work of getting there.

Vincent Ialenti is a former U.S. Department of Energy official and a senior research fellow at Tampere University in Finland. He is the author of “Deep Time Reckoning” and “Longstorming,” both from MIT Press.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the campuses “massive generators of economic growth” that would be “crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance.” The American Nuclear Society echoed him, its president promising “multigenerational job creation, sustained economic growth, and new investment in education and workforce development.”

By folding nuclear waste into a sweeping economic development package, the department has invited states to compete for campuses that could co-locate multiple stages of the nuclear fuel cycle — such as uranium enrichment, fuel fabrication, spent fuel reprocessing, waste disposition and, in some states, advanced reactors. This is all while using the appeal of nuclear power investment to soften the politics of hosting long-term waste facilities.

It is an appealing vision. But five signed memoranda are not five host communities. No final host agreement has been signed, no construction funds awarded and the states have agreed only to continue negotiations. That is a real beginning, but it is not a victory. Treating it as one risks repeating the cycle of overpromising and disappointment that has paralyzed American nuclear waste policy for four decades.

I say this as a former Energy Department official who served as federal manager for the Consent-Based Siting Consortia — a $24 million 12-team initiative supporting public engagement around the siting of spent-fuel storage facilities. Before anyone declares the gridlock is broken, the plan must clear five tests.

First, the department must explain the scale of its projections. Its January solicitation offered an illustrative scenario in which one campus employed 50,000 direct workers, generated another 100,000 to 150,000 indirect jobs, and required 10,000 to 20,000 housing units. The same document put the entire existing U.S. nuclear workforce at roughly 80,000. By July, the Energy Department was projecting 25,000 jobs per campus .

Those figures may rest on different assumptions, but the Energy Department has not explained the methodology or reconciled the difference. Numbers that swing this far before a single site is chosen are aspirations, not plans.

Second, the department needs a technically credible schedule. Its solicitation says it wants initial facilities online “in the 2027 timeframe” and promises preference to the states with “more ambitious timelines” — remarkably soon for infrastructure of this kind.

States, meanwhile, had just nine weeks to assemble sweeping proposals. Any serious schedule for the waste disposition component must separately account for geological screening, independent site characterization, groundwater and seismic studies, environmental review, Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing, transportation planning and host-agreement negotiation. A facility built to isolate waste for decades, centuries, or millennia cannot be validated on a ribbon-cutting schedule.

Third, Washington must put up real money and enforceable commitments. A repository would, in principle, draw on the federal Nuclear Waste Fund . But for nearly everything else, the department told states to look to private capital — industry, technology firms, private equity, venture funds. It floats possible federal cost-sharing, loan guarantees and grants, but it commits to none and says states and private investors are expected to lead and finance the effort.
Communities asked to keep nuclear waste for generations need money that is committed and obligations that are enforceable against future administrations.

Fourth, Congress must authorize the plan’s spent-fuel storage and disposal components. The Nuclear Waste Policy Act still directs the federal repository program toward Yucca Mountain, whose development Congress has not funded since fiscal 2010 . The act also prevents construction of a centralized federal spent fuel storage facility until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has authorized construction of a repository. The department cannot designate one of the five states as a spent fuel site by press release.

Fifth, host communities must consent. States applied and governors signed, and some local governments in Utah, Idaho and Tennessee have expressed preliminary support. But it is far from clear that any specific community has agreed to live beside nuclear waste facilities.

Genuine consent requires a named candidate community, early involvement rather than after-the-fact persuasion, meaningful say over benefits, the participation of affected Tribal Nations and a real chance to walk away before commitments are final. The Energy Department’s process ran the other way: It gave states nine weeks to name sites and gauge local sentiment and rewarded those promising to streamline permitting and move fast.

After decades in which states treated nuclear waste as politically untouchable, the willingness of five governors to enter the negotiating room is a real achievement. But no spent-fuel repository in any of the five states is authorized under current law, no community has completed a voluntary siting process, no binding host agreement has been signed and no durable financing package or credible schedule has been demonstrated.

When a willing community stays at the table through investigation, negotiation, licensing and construction, the Energy Department will have earned its victory lap. For now, it has earned only the right to begin the hard work of getting there.

Vincent Ialenti is a former U.S. Department of Energy official and a senior research fellow at Tampere University in Finland. He is the author of “Deep Time Reckoning” and “Longstorming,” both from MIT Press.

articles.title: Bakery owner addresses encounter with Bovino
articles.summary: CHARLOTTE, N.C. (QUEEN CITY NEWS) — Manolo Bentancur is talking about the conversation he had with the former commander of U.S. Border Patrol, Greg Bovino, when Bentancur saw Bovino at his popular east Charlotte bakery Sunday afternoon. “He said, ‘Well, I can be wherever I want; it’s free,” said Bentancur. “I said, ‘This is private…
articles.body:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (QUEEN CITY NEWS) — Manolo Bentancur is talking about the conversation he had with the former commander of U.S. Border Patrol, Greg Bovino , when Bentancur saw Bovino at his popular east Charlotte bakery Sunday afternoon.

“He said, ‘Well, I can be wherever I want; it’s free,” said Bentancur. “I said, ‘This is private property; you are not allowed on this property. There’s a lot of fear of you, a lot of fear of ICE, and a lot of fear over what is going on in our nation.'”

Bovino and a cameraman were spotted in the parking lot of the bakery when Bentancur arrived to pick up his wife from work.

Last November, Bovino led Operation Charlotte’s Web , a federal immigration enforcement sweep that resulted in over 1,300 arrests, with much of the activity starting in the parking lot of Manolo’s bakery.

“‘Ah, you’re Manolo, you are the owner,'” Bentancur says Bovino told him. “‘You are the one who shut the business down in November so you can protect all the illegals that are here.'”

Queen City News reached out to Gregory Bovino, and he tells us that’s not what happened in the parking lot. In a written statement, Bovino says he never tried to enter the bakery. Bovino went on to say he was recording video of businesses from Operation Charlotte’s Web when his videographer asked to buy something in the bakery, and Bentancur declined.

“It’s not like he came to walk inside the bakery; ‘No,’ I told him if you are thinking about going inside the bakery, you are not going to go inside,” added Bentancur.

Bovino says he asked Bentancur, “Why he would choose an illegal alien over an American citizen and he was unable to answer.”

Bentancur says this interaction shows how his community and businesses in east Charlotte remain under attack. From bad reviews of his bakery to someone recently throwing eggs at the business, the hate speech keeps increasing.

“I have been prepared since November about what I am going to be reacting, what I am going to be saying the day I had to face these people, but I never thought it would be Bovino man,” said Bentancur.

Gregory Bovino says he plans to post the entire video of the interaction online later this week.

Action NC, a non-profit advocacy group, shared a statement following Bovino’s visit calling his actions “reprehensible” and an “attempt at intimidation tactics.”

“ They can only be described as an attempt by a man who perceives himself to be strong attempting to intimidate a business in a community that he perceives to be weaker. What he encountered showed the opposite. He was immediately told he was not welcome and made to leave ,” the group said.

Action NC Immigrant Justice Director, Héctor Vaca, added, “ We applaud Manolo and support his business. He is the type of leader that our community needs more of. He not only talks the talk, he walks it and strongly defends those that feel disempowered in the current climate created by people like Bovino. We call on all of Charlotte to show its love and support a business that supports its community. ”

The group praises Bentancur, who is an Action NC member, calling him “a community leader that builds and supports his community” and “a model of what a good leader should be–kind, generous, empowering others, advocate, hardworking.”

articles.title: ‘Medicare for All’ means Medicare for none
articles.summary: Merrill Matthews argues that Sen. Bernie Sanders’ “Medicare for All” proposal deceptively seeks to replace the highly-rated existing Medicare program with a centralized, government-run system modeled after the United Kingdom’s less efficient National Health Service.
articles.body:
It may be one of the most deceptive public policy marketing schemes in modern history. First, pick the most popular health insurance program in the country, which is Medicare. Then call your health insurance reform proposal “ Medicare for All ,” even though the intent is to eliminate the Medicare program as we know it, so that no one would have that coverage anymore.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has long pushed to end the nation’s current mix of private health insurance (that is, employer-based and individually purchased) and government-provided health insurance (Medicare and Medicaid) and replace it with a new government-run program. Taxpayers would pay higher taxes — though no one would pay premiums — and the government would pay all medical bills.

Under most government-run health care systems, as in the United Kingdom , the government determines what services and medicines are available, who can have them and when. Bureaucrats rather than doctors decide whether patients are allowed to have access to those services and medicines.

That is what Sanders and 71 percent of Democrats mean by Medicare for All. But that’s not Medicare.

Sanders knows he’s being deceptive. His Senate website says , “Medicare is the most popular health care program in America.” Then he claims that under Medicare for All, “every resident of the U.S. will receive health insurance through an expanded Medicare program.” That is a blatantly false statement.

Medicare has multiple parts. Part A covers hospital bills, Part B covers doctors’ bills, Part C is now Medicare Advantage and Part D covers prescription drugs. Medicare for All has none of that.

Importantly, Medicare Advantage relies on private sector health insurance similar to employer plans. Seniors have a choice between traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage . Currently, 55 percent of eligible seniors choose Medicare Advantage. Medicare for All excludes private sector coverage, including Medicare Advantage.

Remember President Obama’s promise for the Affordable Care Act? “If you like your health plan, you can keep it,” is what he said. That won him Politifact’s 2013 “Lie of the Year.” But Sanders won’t make that claim, because he intends to ensure no one has their current health plan, including people currently on Medicare.

A recent NBC News poll found that 82 percent are “satisfied with their health care coverage” and 90 percent of seniors on Medicare are satisfied with their plan, with 42 percent reporting they are “very satisfied.” But under Medicare for All, seniors can kiss their Medicare plan goodbye.

Medicare for All is more like the British National Health Service’s government-run health care system. Are the Brits as satisfied with their coverage as U.S. seniors are with Medicare? The 40-year running British Social Attitudes survey found last year that only 26 percent of British subjects are satisfied with the National Health Service, with 51 percent dissatisfied.

So, to recap, we’re going to take a system that has 90 percent satisfaction and abolish it in favor of one that has 26 percent satisfaction.

To be sure, Medicare is also a government-run program. It has many of the same problems as Great Britian’s system, including the very low rates it pays health care providers. When the government takes over the health care system, it must balance what it spends on health care with other claims on government funds, such as education, defense and welfare. There is never enough money to go around. That is why bureaucrats decide what medical services and products are available, usually based on political pressure.

Anyone who tracks the National Health Service’s problems knows this. It was a typical occurrence when officials warned last October about coming layoffs within the service unless funding was increased by £3bn “to cover unexpected costs.”

There are often long waiting lines to see a doctor — and very long lines to see a specialist. The NHS currently states on its website that it tries to cap waits for “non-urgent” treatment at “18 weeks from the day your appointment is booked” — so if you get a referral today, you might be treated in January. Also, many of the newest treatments and prescription drugs available in the U.S. are not available in Great Britain.

The Medicare program survives because most Americans are in private insurance plans, which essentially cross-subsidize Medicare. Health care providers make more from private-sector health insurers, allowing most of them to continue providing care for seniors on Medicare. That is far from ideal, but it is better than putting everyone into government-run health care.

Remember that when health care becomes political, the politically powerful — like members of Congress, including Sanders — and the well-connected will still get the care they want or need. Sanders won’t have to wait for care; you will.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.

articles.title: A MAGA plot to keep power in Congress if they lose the election?
articles.summary: He will scare them away from the polls by posting federal agents at their voting places or discouraging them by disparaging mail-in ballots.
articles.body:
Democrats are widely expected to win control of the House in November’s election. The Senate remains a tossup. But there is a nagging suspicion that Trump will somehow pervert the will of the people to ensure that Republicans retain their majority in the House and somehow steal the election.

Here’s his playbook: For starters, MAGAs will demonize the Democrats. Evoking Senator Joseph McCarthy, President Trump has already referred to Democrats as “hard core, godless Communists.”

Republican House majority leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) said , “The Bolshevik takeover of the Democratic Party is in full swing, and communism is on the ballot this November.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) posted , “The question before Congress is whether we will preserve our constitutional republic OR chart a fundamentally different course that leads us down the ROAD TO COMMUNISM.”

Trump will delegitimize eligible voters. He will scare them away from the polls by posting federal agents at their voting places or discouraging them by disparaging mail-in ballots.

But here’s the crusher: If the outcome is close, his minions can refuse to seat elected Democrats by reason of a yawning loophole in how congressional elections are administered. But beware! If Republicans try this one on the Democrats, and the Democrats at some point reverse positions, you can count on them to return the compliment next election. The bottom-line of such an action will be constitutional chaos.

The Constitution provides : “Each house shall be the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members.” Those decisions are not reviewable by the courts . This leaves an opportunity for presumptive Speaker-in-waiting Johnson to deny Democratic members-elect their seats in the 120th Congress.

A losing House candidate may contest his or her election. The issue is decided by a simple majority vote. The new House can refuse to seat the winner while the challenge is pending. If things are close, Republicans may even temporarily hold a majority. Thus, even if Democrats only narrowly win a House majority, one or more defeated Republican candidates might try to deny office to their Democratic opponents. The Senate has its own rules for dealing with contested elections and normally seats the certified winner without prejudice.

We are accustomed to voters having final say, but this has not always been the case. Jeffrey Jenkins , a Professor of Law at USC Price determined there have been 601 election contests in the House between 1789 and 2002 — an average of around 5.6 per Congress.

In 2021 Mike Pence followed the advice of his courageous lawyer, retired Judge J. Michael Luttig, who persuaded him that our constitutional traditions required an orderly transfer of power and the election result must be respected. The same quandary may be unfolding now. And Johnson is no Mike Pence. A card-carrying election-denier, Johnson once filed a brief in the Supreme Court claiming there were “unconstitutional irregularities” in 2020 election outcomes.

That is exactly why I fear that Republicans have a legal loophole to subvert the will of the people. The 2026 midterms could thus be a decisive test of U.S. democratic norms, with the potential for a constitutional crisis if elected members are denied seats.

As the 2020 election conspiracies illustrate, the challenges could be based on virtually anything. Defeated contestants could claim that their state’s refusal to turn over voter rolls to the Trump administration meant the election was corrupt. They could argue that the Senate’s refusal to pass the SAVE Act allowed illegal immigrants to vote for their opponents in large numbers. They could try to cast doubt on mail-in ballots.

The brooding omnipresence in the midterms is Trump, whose endorsements have already proved to be the kiss of death. One thing is clear about Trump — most Americans don’t like him. His job approval rating stands at 33 percent in a new Reuters-Ipsos poll of adults , with 63 percent disapproving.

Trump has a big stake in the outcome aside from just his hatred of losing. He does not want to face congressional investigations, much less potential impeachment for corruption.

So, what’s the answer? Only an unambiguous election landslide will scotch Trump and his movement. That’s what dethroned Viktor Orban in Hungary. But there is no prospect that such a landslide is imminent. The influential Cook Political Report lists 18 tossup races in the House out of 435. A further 19 races lean Democratic or Republican. Even taken together, it means less than 10 percent of House races that will prove decisive.

So, it is entirely possible that we will run a reprise of 2020, when the outcome of a narrow election beclouded with accusations of fraud, and MAGA determined to retain control. The hope is only fleeting that men like Johnson have enough honesty and integrity to keep the nation from a constitutional crisis.

Whatever you learned in school, it is ultimately the House and the Senate deciding who sits in Congress — not the American people.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Location isn’t everything: The science of flexible work
articles.summary: Researchers studying nearly 165,000 employees across more than 73,000 U.S. firms found that the satisfaction advantage linked to remote work largely faded after accounting for workplace culture, trust in management, communication, professional development and compensation.
articles.body:
A new scientific finding lands like a warning shot in the return-to-office wars: Remote work may not be what makes employees happy, according to a recent study in Science.

Researchers studying nearly 165,000 employees across more than 73,000 U.S. firms found that the satisfaction advantage linked to remote work largely faded after accounting for workplace culture, trust in management, communication, professional development and compensation.

But that finding should not comfort executives eager to drag everyone back to the office — it should unsettle them. The study does not prove that location is irrelevant. Rather, it proves that location alone is just one factor. The broader issue is whether people experience work as trusted, fair, well-managed and compatible with the way they do their best.

The strongest lesson from the new workplace flexibility research is that flexibility cannot be reduced to a remote-work checkbox. Employees are happier when they feel appreciated, trust management, have effective communication, see fair compensation practices, and have access to development. Those are not perks. They are the architecture of a workplace people want to stay in.

This is where many leaders misread the evidence. They hear “remote work alone is not enough” and conclude that the office must be the answer. But a bad culture does not become healthy because people commute to it. A confusing manager does not become clear because a team sits nearby. A lack of trust does not disappear under fluorescent office lights.

The better conclusion is that flexible work works when it gives employees meaningful agency inside a healthy operating system. People need clarity about goals, norms, meetings, responsiveness and performance. Then they need room to choose the path that lets them deliver.

A major randomized controlled trial in Nature found that hybrid work improved job satisfaction, reduced quit rates by one-third, and did not harm performance reviews over the next two years. That evidence matters, because it shows that hybrid work can benefit both employees and employers when it is designed deliberately.

Yet even that finding does not mean every employee needs the same two days at home. Some jobs need more face-to-face collaboration. Some workers need more quiet focus. Some employees value office energy, while others lose hours and patience to long commutes. A blanket policy pretends these differences do not exist.

That is why employee autonomy is the missing ingredient. Managers should define outcomes, service standards, collaboration moments and team rhythms. Employees should have real input into where and when they work within those boundaries. That is not chaos. It is disciplined trust.

Rigid return-to-office mandates often promise culture while delivering compliance. They may increase attendance without improving communication, belonging, mentoring or performance. articles.title: Federal judge declines Maxwell bid to toss conviction
articles.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday declined a petition from Ghislaine Maxwell to set aside her conviction, a long-shot bid that would have allowed for a new trial. Maxwell represented herself in the habeas petition challenging her detention that she filed last December. New York-based U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer noted Maxwell had previously been “represented…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday declined a petition from Ghislaine Maxwell to set aside her conviction, a long-shot bid that would have allowed for a new trial.

Maxwell represented herself in the habeas petition challenging her detention that she filed last December.

New York-based U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer noted Maxwell had previously been “represented by able counsel” but did not use her attorney to file what the jurist described as “a lengthy and rambling petition” that did little to open new avenues for her defense.

The judge also said the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), the law passed by Congress mandating the release of millions of files collected by the Justice Department on Maxwell’s late associate, Jeffrey Epstein, did not support her claims of innocence.

“Maxwell’s claims are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous. The vast majority are procedurally barred — either because Maxwell made and lost the same arguments on direct appeal, or because she could have made such arguments on appeal but elected not to do so.” Engelmayer wrote.

“And the purported ‘new’ evidence to which Maxwell points, principally materials released under the EFTA, is largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell and does not support her claims of error. On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges.”

Maxwell is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence after she was found guilty of conspiring with and aiding Epstein in his sexual abuse of underage girls.

When she filed the December petition, Maxwell said the new evidence was derived from litigation against the FBI, financial institutions and Epstein’s estate, in addition to sworn depositions, released records and other “verified sources” that show evidence suggesting her innocence was “withheld,” “false testimony” was presented and “material facts” were “misrepresented” to her jury and the court.

Her claims included alleged juror misconduct, mischaracterizations of evidence, private attorneys functioning as de facto prosecutors and the decades-long delay between her alleged conduct and indictment.

“The cumulative effect of these constitutional violations constitutes a complete miscarriage of justice, rendering Petitioner’s conviction invalid, unsafe and infirm,” Maxwell wrote at the time.

Maxwell has exhausted all of her direct appeals, something Engelmayer nodded to in the ruling, noting that an appeals court upheld her conviction and that the Supreme Court declined to review her case.

articles.title: Darline Graham dodges when asked if she would’ve certified 2020 election
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Monday refused to say whether she would have voted to certify the 2020 presidential election, as the Republican looks to secure a win in South Carolina’s GOP Senate runoff this week. The senator was asked by MS NOW’s Mychael Schnell about whether she would have affirmed former President Biden’s victory…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Monday refused to say whether she would have voted to certify the 2020 presidential election, as the Republican looks to secure a win in South Carolina’s GOP Senate runoff this week.

The senator was asked by MS NOW’s Mychael Schnell about whether she would have affirmed former President Biden’s victory — a result President Trump has consistently denied without evidence.

“I think our election system is broken,” Graham responded. “That’s why I think it’s so important that we get the SAVE America Act passed. That’s why I wanted to stay through recess to get that done.”

Graham was tapped to replace her late brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), and serve out the remainder of his term after he died last month from a “brief and sudden illness.”

Trump urged the late lawmaker’s sister to run for a full term shortly after their July meeting in the Oval Office, calling her a “spectacular person” and a “true American Patriot” in a Truth Social post.

“Lindsey was one of the greatest people and Senators I have ever known, and his sister shares his deep love of our Country, and the State of South Carolina,” Trump wrote.

Darline Graham will face Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) in the Tuesday runoff, after both candidates failed to obtain a majority of the vote in the state’s Republican primary earlier this month.

Norman criticized Graham after she fumbled a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea during a debate last week and admitted that she was “not that informed on national security.”

“Contrary to my opponent, foreign policy and national security is a top concern,” Norman told Fox Business on Monday.

Graham later defended her response in an interview with Fox News, saying she has “said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician.”

The winner of the Republican runoff will face pediatrician Annie Andrews (D) in November. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates this race as “solidly Republican.”

Join The Hill’s Amie Parnes and Caroline Vakil for a live discussion of tonight’s GOP faceoff in the South Carolina Senate runoff between Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who is backed by President Trump, and Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

Finally, the show will discuss Sen. Jon Ossoff’s (D-Ga.) recent attacks and the backlash from the White House as well as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and her current standing with Democrats amid her egg-freezing journey .

articles.title: DOJ asks judge to lift nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) asked a federal judge in Massachusetts late Monday to lift a nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions ahead of the November midterms. The DOJ wrote in a late-night filing that the Supreme Court’s ruling in a separate challenge to President Trump’s executive order “leaves no room for further dispute” in…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) asked a federal judge in Massachusetts late Monday to lift a nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions ahead of the November midterms.

The DOJ wrote in a late-night filing that the Supreme Court’s ruling in a separate challenge to President Trump’s executive order “leaves no room for further dispute” in the case brought by several voting rights groups.

“This is a textbook case for reconsideration,” Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s Civil Division, and others wrote in the 6-page motion to Judge Indira Talwani.

The high court said earlier Monday, over the dissent of its three liberal justices, that the judge had no authority to block Trump’s directive because the new U.S. Postal Service regulations had not yet been finalized when a group of Democratic-led states initially sued .

“Federal courts review final rules, not proposed rules—and certainly not antecedent internal directives to propose a rule. If the Postal Service’s final rule harms the States, they may challenge that rule,” the court wrote.

The Justice Department argues that specific language “plainly bars” the nationwide injunction from remaining in place.

“Because it is now clear that this Court lacked jurisdiction to issue the preliminary injunction in this case, it must be vacated immediately,” officials wrote.

The lawsuits target the president’s March executive order, which directed his administration to compile a list of verified U.S. citizens who are eligible to vote and ordered the Postal Service to implement new standards for mailing ballots.

The order quickly drew challenges from nearly two dozen states, the District of Columbia and a coalition of voting rights groups, which argued the order was unlawful and threatened to disenfranchise thousands of voters.

The Postal Service has since unveiled new requirements for mail ballots. The rule is set to be published Wednesday, but the agency has said it will not implement the regulation before the November midterms unless both injunctions are lifted.

Absentee and overseas ballots are set to go out in a matter of days in some states, and voting rights groups have argued that the “fast-approaching deadline” creates complications for state election officials and voters.

“The issuance of the Final Rule with immediate effect will also sow widespread confusion among election officials and the public, thereby undermining voter confidence and disrupting the administration of elections,” the groups wrote in an emergency motion to Talwani on Saturday.

articles.title: Fetterman viewed more favorably than GOP senator by Pennsylvania Republicans: Poll
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.), a centrist Democrat who frequently criticizes his party for catering to its left-wing base, is more popular among Republicans in Pennsylvania than the state’s GOP senator, Dave McCormick, according to a new poll. A New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll of registered voters in Pennsylvania found that 73…
articles.body:
Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.), a centrist Democrat who frequently criticizes his party for catering to its left-wing base, is more popular among Republicans in Pennsylvania than the state’s GOP senator, Dave McCormick, according to a new poll.

A New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University poll of registered voters in Pennsylvania found that 73 percent of Republicans in the state have a favorable opinion of Fetterman while only 63 percent of Republicans view McCormick, a former hedge fund CEO, favorably.

The survey, which was conducted from April 28 to May 7 and from Aug. 17 to Aug. 21, found that 49 percent of independents in Pennsylvania have a favorable view of Fetterman while 36 percent have an unfavorable view.

Democrats’ opinions of Fetterman, however, are more negative than positive.

Sixty-three percent of registered Democrats in the state say they view Fetterman unfavorably while 22 percent view him favorably.

That’s a significant decline in support compared with 2024, when 74 percent of Pennsylvania Democrats said they had a favorable view of Fetterman while 20 percent said they viewed him unfavorably.

At the same time, Republicans who have a favorable view of Fetterman increased from 25 percent in 2024 to more than 7 in 10 this month.

Interviewers for the poll spoke with 760 voters between Aug. 17 and Aug. 21 and placed more than 100,000 calls to nearly 47,000 voters picked from a demographically balanced survey group.

Fetterman’s growing popularity with Republicans in Pennsylvania and around the country has fueled speculation that he could leave the Democratic Party before facing reelection and a likely Democratic primary challenge in 2028.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and other Senate GOP colleagues have approached Fetterman about a potential party switch and have pledged to welcome him to their conference with open arms.

“I have had conversations with him in the past, as have many of my colleagues about the challenges he faces in his caucus. And there are many of us who, I think, would welcome the opportunity to have him join the Republican conference, but ultimately that’s a decision that’s up to him,” Thune told reporters last month.

Fetterman, however, says he has no plans to leave the Democratic Party, but he warned last month that could change if Democrats ever turn their backs as a party against Israel.

“If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave because that’s been a moral clarity for me,” he said during an interview at the Hill Nation Summit in Washington.

Fetterman said he “can’t understand why the Democratic Party” would turn against a long-standing ally.

He voiced major “concern” over the views of Democrats who have become increasingly critical of U.S. aid for Israel amid growing pressure from the party’s progressive base.

“My long-term concern has been with the Democratic Party, as I am a member of that, is that our party is going to back away and turn their back to Israel,” he said.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has urged Fetterman not to leave the party.

Asked last month if he wants Fetterman to remain a Democrat, Schumer responded: “Yes, and he is a very good member of Congress.”

“People in our caucus very much like him and respect him and we’re a big-tent party. We can have a lot of different views in that party,” Schumer said.

articles.title: Cruz says GOP hasn’t coalesced behind Vance for 2028 nomination: ‘Oh, no’
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who ran for president in 2016 and is considered a possible future contender for the White House, says the Republican Party has not coalesced around Vice President Vance as its 2028 nominee and needs to have a broader discussion about its direction after President Trump leaves office. Asked by MS NOW’s…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who ran for president in 2016 and is considered a possible future contender for the White House, says the Republican Party has not coalesced around Vice President Vance as its 2028 nominee and needs to have a broader discussion about its direction after President Trump leaves office.

Asked by MS NOW’s Ali Vitali whether Republicans have settled on Vance as their standard-bearer in 2028, Cruz replied: “Oh, no.”

“There’s going to be a full discussion about who we are and what we believe,” he said, noting earlier in the interview that he was Trump’s strongest rival in 2016 and beat him in primary contests in 12 states that year. He added that Trump has been an “extraordinary president.”

Cruz said there “is no Never Trump lane” in the Republican Party anymore and praised Trump’s willingness to fight for his views.

“Love him or hate him, you’ve got to acknowledge this guy has a backbone — he is fearless. And there are a lot of Republicans that were so tired of lily-livered Republicans who were afraid of their own shadow,” he said. “Trump doesn’t hide in the corner. He is ferocious. I like that.”

But Cruz said he wished Trump showed more “message discipline and focus” and noted that he speaks with Trump on a weekly or daily basis.

“He doesn’t always listen to me but he frequently listens to me, and I’m grateful because he’s got courage,” he said.

Cruz said there needs to be soul-searching over the future of the Republican Party once Trump, who is 80, leaves office in two and a half years.

“Going forward, we’re in the midst of a debate about who our party is and what we believe, and I think economically we’ve got to debate, ‘Are we a small-government, free-market conservative party, are we a big-government, nanny-state party?'” he said.

Asked if he will be part of the discussion, possibly as a future presidential candidate, about what the Republican Party stands for, Cruz said: “There’ll be time to figure that out.”

“I’ll certainly be part of the discussion because I care deeply about — economically, I think we should be a conservative party. And on foreign policy, we’ve got to debate, ‘Are we an isolationist party that withdraws from the world or do we believe in American leadership?’”

“I care about both of those issues and who the party is,” he said.

Cruz called Trump’s rise to power and his reshaping of the Republican Party to embrace his “America First” and MAGA agenda a “Black Swan event,” a term used to describe highly improbable events that have major consequences.

“He is a unique historical figure. There’s never been anyone like him, I don’t think there will be anyone like him going forward,” he said. “And we’re going to have over the next several years a conversation among Republicans” about what comes next.

“He doesn’t always listen to me but he frequently listens to me, and I’m grateful because he’s got courage,” he said.
Cruz said there needs to be soul-searching over the future of the Republican Party once Trump, who is 80, leaves office in two and a half years.

“Going forward, we’re in the midst of a debate about who our party is and what we believe, and I think economically we’ve got to debate, ‘Are we a small-government, free-market conservative party, are we a big-government, nanny-state party?'” he said.
Asked if he will be part of the discussion, possibly as a future presidential candidate, about what the Republican Party stands for, Cruz said: “There’ll be time to figure that out.”

“I’ll certainly be part of the discussion because I care deeply about — economically, I think we should be a conservative party. And on foreign policy, we’ve got to debate, ‘Are we an isolationist party that withdraws from the world or do we believe in American leadership?’”
“I care about both of those issues and who the party is,” he said.

Cruz called Trump’s rise to power and his reshaping of the Republican Party to embrace his “America First” and MAGA agenda a “Black Swan event,” a term used to describe highly improbable events that have major consequences.

“He is a unique historical figure. There’s never been anyone like him, I don’t think there will be anyone like him going forward,” he said. “And we’re going to have over the next several years a conversation among Republicans” about what comes next.

articles.title: States can build America’s affordable energy future
articles.summary: Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee argues that state governments must leverage their regulatory authority to advance affordable clean energy initiatives to counter the Trump administration’s federal opposition.
articles.body:
Americans are facing rising energy bills while witnessing a presidential administration with a vendetta against the cheapest, fastest-to-install form of energy. It’s a bizarre mix: President Trump tried to shut down an 80 percent complete wind energy project that would have powered 350,000 homes, while forcing American ratepayers to pay $180 million to keep a zombie coal plant alive.

I’ve heard the question repeatedly in recent months: With an administration so hostile to affordable clean energy, where can Americans turn for hope? The answer is in the states, the “laboratories of democracy” that are continuing to lead on clean affordability energy today, despite what’s happening in Washington, D.C. Try as he might, President Trump cannot stop state progress on clean energy.

States have long been at the forefront in America’s energy policy innovation, and amidst skyrocketing utility bills their leadership is now more important than ever. Iowa in the 1980s passed the first renewable energy standard. Texas in the 2000s enacted policies that have made it the national leader in low-cost clean energy deployment. And nine years ago, I joined the governors of California and New York to launch the U.S. Climate Alliance — a bipartisan alliance of over 20 states advancing a shared clean energy agenda, regardless of what happens in Washington, D.C.

In recent years, when federal policy has lurched from the neglect of Trump’s first term, to the historic investments of the Biden years, to an even more hostile second Trump administration, states have continued making progress building a more affordable, reliable, and cleaner energy system.

Today, states have a larger responsibility than ever. Energy costs have become one of the top financial concerns for American families, with Gallup polling showing worry about energy prices at its highest level in 18 years. At the same time, electricity demand is projected to rise 55 percent over the next 25 years, driven largely by the growth of data centers. And rather than helping states meet that demand affordably, with clean energy the Trump administration is doing all it can to block new energy projects — driving costs up for consumers. All the while, the climate crisis continues to raise costs for Americans and cause increasing harm to our communities — just look at the wildfires that have raged throughout North America this summer.

This is precisely why state leadership matters right now. States control major levers over their own energy systems — from utility regulation and permitting, to infrastructure development and finance. And clean energy is the tool best suited to the moment. A July report from the advisory firm Lazard shows that solar and wind are now the cheapest forms of new electricity generation by far, cheaper than new gas power plants. Clean energy is also faster to build, which matters enormously given how quickly demand is growing. Clean energy made up 91 percent of new grid capacity added in the first quarter of 2026, and solar outpaced coal generation for the first time in American history this past May . States that embrace that reality can deliver real relief to their residents. States that don’t will be left paying more for less.

This year also presents an inflection point, in which American voters will elect the governors, legislators and public utility commissioners that will help determine our nation’s energy future. Thirty-six states hold gubernatorial elections this November, and at least 21 brand new governors will take office next year. Voters will decide on new members and majorities in state legislatures and utility commissions in places like Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Georgia. One way or the other, 2027 will bring a new crop of state leaders, and with it the opportunity to build a more affordable and prosperous American economy — powered with clean energy.

We’re already seeing what this leadership looks like in practice, with two new governors elected just last year, both of whom ran with affordable energy at the center of their campaign platforms. In New Jersey, Gov. Mikie Sherrill has taken on out-of-control utility rate increases, signed legislation to modernize the grid, and approved 18 new clean energy projects. In Virginia, Gov. Abigail Spanberger has signed legislation to expand solar deployment — helping families save an average of 23 percent on their utility bills with in-home energy installations. From the plains of Illinois to the coast of New England to the deserts of New Mexico, states are moving the ball forward with more affordable and reliable clean power.

State leaders must of course be clear-eyed about the obstacles the federal government is putting in their path. The Trump administration has admitted in court that it has cancelled energy grants to states that did not vote for him, while preserving them for red states — a sign of how Republican governors wanted to keep their clean energy money.

Trump’s cuts to clean energy programs are projected to add $11.6 billion to American household energy bills over the next decade; the predictable result of a federal approach that favors the profits of incumbent energy interests over the interests of ratepayers. But states have their own power — they can accelerate interconnection of new clean generation, control how utilities recover costs, hold data center developers accountable, and ensure that as energy demand grows the costs of meeting it aren’t dumped onto American households.

The market has already shifted. Clean energy is cheaper and faster to build than the alternatives, and demand for electricity is only going to keep climbing. The only question left is whether current and future state leaders, and the voters who elect them, will use the tools they have to turn that shift into lower bills and more reliable power for the people they serve. That is the opportunity in front of states right now — this year. And it cannot and must not wait for Washington, D.C.

Jay Inslee served as governor of Washington from 2013-2025. He previously served in Congress from 1993-1995 and 1999-2012. Inslee is currently working with state leaders to advance a more affordable and prosperous clean energy economy, through the State Power Project.

articles.title: Graham, Norman tied in South Carolina Senate poll
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman are neck and neck in a new survey, as voting concludes Tuesday to determine which Republican will be on the ballot in South Carolina’s Senate race. The poll, which the Trafalgar Group conducted from Saturday through Monday, found that 47.9 percent of 1,031 respondents backed Graham, whom South…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman are neck and neck in a new survey, as voting concludes Tuesday to determine which Republican will be on the ballot in South Carolina’s Senate race.

The poll, which the Trafalgar Group conducted from Saturday through Monday, found that 47.9 percent of 1,031 respondents backed Graham, whom South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) appointed to complete the term of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Norman received support from 47.8 percent of respondents, while 4.4 percent of respondents were undecided. The survey had a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points.

Voters in the Palmetto State will determine Tuesday whether Darline Graham or Norman will face off against Democrat Annie Andrews, a physician, in November. The two Republicans advanced to Tuesday’s runoff via their top-two finish in the GOP primary Aug. 11.

Graham has the backing of President Trump, who ventured to South Carolina last week to stump for the incumbent senator . Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC has also spent more than $827,000 in support of Graham ahead of the runoff.

Norman has pointed to Graham’s relative inexperience in public office on the campaign trail, highlighting that fact after the senator said she was “not that informed on national security” in response to a question on Taiwan and the South China Sea during last Tuesday’s debate .

“Contrary to my opponent, foreign policy and national security is a top concern,” Norman told host Brian Brenberg on Monday’s edition of Fox Business’s “The Bottom Line.”

Graham has defended her lack of focus on foreign affairs, contrasting herself with her interventionist brother by saying she is focused on kitchen-table issues.

“I think people in South Carolina are more worried about making ends meet,” she said last Wednesday on Fox News’s “Hannity.” “So, they are concerned about a lot of other things other than Taiwan.”

Trump also said Graham was being “honest” by noting her lack of expertise on national security, saying the South Carolina senator is “into the price of groceries.”

articles.title: Man charged with forging Chief Justice John Roberts’s signature, impersonating NSA agent
articles.summary: A man is facing federal charges over allegations that he impersonated a federal officer on several occasions and forged Chief Justice John Roberts’s signature on fabricated Indiana court documents. Joshua Culver was indicted last week in the Northern District of Indiana on four counts of falsely impersonating an officer of the United States and one…
articles.body:
A man is facing federal charges over allegations that he impersonated a federal officer on several occasions and forged Chief Justice John Roberts’s signature on fabricated Indiana court documents.

Joshua Culver was indicted last week in the Northern District of Indiana on four counts of falsely impersonating an officer of the United States and one count of forging the signature of a judge and court seal.

He was taken into custody in Colorado and is expected to appear before a judge on Tuesday morning for a detention hearing, according to court records.

Culver’s arrest was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

The indictment alleges Culver falsely identified himself as an agent with the National Security Agency on at least two occasions last September, including in attempts to gain information about a family member.

Authorities said that on another occasion in January, he claimed to be a “Special Master enforcing orders of the United States Supreme Court” to pressure a Lake County, Ind., judge into dismissing criminal cases and judgments against him.

He is also accused of forging the chief justice’s signature and using a counterfeited seal on an order last September that purportedly directed a Grant County, Ind., court to drop separate theft charges against him.

Culver is being represented by a court-appointed attorney with the federal public defender’s office in Denver.

articles.title: Trump approval reaches record low in new survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating for his second term has reached a new low, according to a new poll. In the Reuters/Ipsos poll, the president’s approval rating hit 33 percent, a 14-point slide from the start of his second term, when it was at 47 percent, and a 4-point slide from about a month ago, when…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating for his second term has reached a new low, according to a new poll.

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll , the president’s approval rating hit 33 percent, a 14-point slide from the start of his second term, when it was at 47 percent, and a 4-point slide from about a month ago, when it was at 37 percent.

The president’s disapproval rating hit 65 percent in the same poll, up 24 points from the beginning of his second term, when it was at 41 percent, and up 4 points from last month, when it was at 61 percent.

The poll comes amid challenging political territory for the president and Republicans as the midterms approach, with the unpopular war in Iran nearing its six-month mark and Americans expressing economic concerns in recent polling.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.7 percent on Tuesday morning, and his disapproval rating was at 57.9 percent.

On Sunday, Trump touted his endorsements were “stronger than ever,” in spite of notable losses in recent primaries.

“My Endorsements are stronger than ever — Not to mention the fact that good people are getting elected that never had the chance,” Trump said Sunday on Truth Social, boasting that 254 candidates he supported won their races this election season.

In recent weeks, however, candidates backed by Trump lost congressional races in Florida, Tennessee and Michigan.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll took place from Aug. 21 to 24, featuring 1,215 people and a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

articles.title: Democratic governors react to Supreme Court ruling on mail-in voting: ‘States run elections, not Donald Trump’
articles.summary: Democratic governors are expressing their dissatisfaction with the Supreme Court’s Monday decision to lift a lower court’s block on the Trump administration’s executive order restricting mail-in ballot voting. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill criticized the move as a “terrible decision” in a social media post. “States run elections, not Donald Trump,” she wrote. “I will…
articles.body:
Democratic governors are expressing their dissatisfaction with the Supreme Court’s Monday decision to lift a lower court’s block on the Trump administration’s executive order restricting mail-in ballot voting.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill criticized the move as a “terrible decision” in a social media post .

“States run elections, not Donald Trump,” she wrote. “I will do everything I can to protect New Jerseyans’ right to vote — by mail and in person.”

Twenty-three Democrat-led states and the District of Columbia sued the administration shortly after President Trump directed federal agencies to create “state citizenship lists” of eligible voters and instructed the U.S. Postal Service not to mail ballots on behalf of anyone who did not appear on the list.

The court’s conservative justices found in an emergency opinion that the states sued too early and that the administration could proceed with planning for restrictions on mail-in ballot voting while a lower court weighs the legality of these new guidelines.

The three justices in the court’s liberal minority said they would have kept the lower court’s hold in place, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson calling the majority’s ruling a “ Kafkaesque nightmare .”

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), whose state attorney general’s office led the lawsuit against the Trump administration’s executive order, slammed the high court’s decision.

“WOW. The Supreme Court just let the Trump Admin move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country,” Newsom wrote on social media . “California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented.”

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) wrote in a statement shared on social media that his state would also “see the Trump Administration in court.”

“In the meantime, I’ll keep defending Pennsylvanians’ right to free, fair, and secure elections,” he added.

Connecticut’s own Democratic governor, Ned Lamont, called the high court’s decision “disappointing,” but he stressed that it was “not the end of the story.”

“SCOTUS allowed the Trump Administration to begin planning for the executive order, but it did not rule on whether carrying it out would be lawful,” he wrote in a social media post .

“While the court defers that decision for another day, Connecticut will continue to defend the safe, secure, and accessible elections we hold in this state — including mail-in ballots,” he continued. “We are not handing over control of our elections to the Trump Administration, and Donald Trump’s ongoing campaign of spreading misinformation to undermine public trust in our elections will not succeed.”

articles.title: Shapiro holds 16-point lead in reelection bid polling
articles.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is cruising toward reelection, according to a new poll of likely voters in the Keystone State. The latest survey from The New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena University showed 55 percent of respondents supported Shapiro in the gubernatorial race. Another 39 percent backed GOP state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, and 6 percent did…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is cruising toward reelection, according to a new poll of likely voters in the Keystone State.

The latest survey from The New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena University showed 55 percent of respondents supported Shapiro in the gubernatorial race. Another 39 percent backed GOP state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, and 6 percent did not choose either candidate or refused to answer.

Shapiro’s edge over Garrity among Pennsylvanians of multiple backgrounds is apparent based on the data.

The incumbent governor leads among men, women, likely white voters, likely Black voters and the four age groups the survey split respondents into: ages 18-29, 30-44, 45-64 and 65-plus. He also holds a 34-point lead over Garrity among voters with a college degree and a 4-point edge among those without one, according to the poll.

That includes a whopping 72-point lead among nonwhite respondents without a college degree — while Garrity leads by 5 points among white respondents without a degree.

In 2022, Shapiro won his first election to the governor’s mansion by nearly 15 points over GOP state Sen. Doug Mastriano.

Less than two years after that race, the Pennsylvania governor was a finalist in former Vice President Kamala Harris’s search for a running mate in the 2024 presidential election. Harris ultimately selected Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, with the Democratic duo losing to President Trump and Vice President Vance that year.

Shapiro has indicated he is considering a bid for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

At the annual National Action Network convention in April, the governor said the Democratic Party is undertaking a “debate” that it “hasn’t had for a good long while,” an internal battle he deemed “healthy” for the country.

“What I can tell you for sure is that I want to be a part of that debate,” he told the Rev. Al Sharpton.

Forty-seven percent of 296 respondents, a smaller group, in the survey said they would be “very likely” to back Shapiro for the Democratic nomination in 2028 . About 39 percent said they were somewhat likely to do so, while 9 percent said they were not too likely and 4 percent said they were not at all likely, the numbers show.

The Times/Inquirer/Siena University survey was conducted from Aug.17-21 among 760 respondents. It has a margin of error of 4.6 percentage points.

At the annual National Action Network convention in April, the governor said the Democratic Party is undertaking a “debate” that it “hasn’t had for a good long while,” an internal battle he deemed “healthy” for the country.
“What I can tell you for sure is that I want to be a part of that debate,” he told the Rev. Al Sharpton.

Forty-seven percent of 296 respondents, a smaller group, in the survey said they would be “very likely” to back Shapiro for the Democratic nomination in 2028 . About 39 percent said they were somewhat likely to do so, while 9 percent said they were not too likely and 4 percent said they were not at all likely, the numbers show.
The Times/Inquirer/Siena University survey was conducted from Aug.17-21 among 760 respondents. It has a margin of error of 4.6 percentage points.

articles.title: Maxwell’s attempt at freedom ‘deeply troubling’: Survivor
articles.summary: Maxwell is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence for her part in the sex trafficking of minor females.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Ghislaine Maxwell, who was charged as a co-conspirator of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, was recently denied a bid to overturn her sexual abuse crimes conviction on Tuesday.

Maxwell, who is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence for her part in the alleged sex trafficking scheme, which involved minors, attempted to have her conviction thrown out earlier this year.

In a motion made public Tuesday, Judge Paul A. Engelmayer ruled Maxwell was unauthorized to file any more requests to toss out her conviction.

The summary read in part, “Maxwell, however, is not to submit any further filings. Any such filings will not be considered.”

Epstein survivor calls Maxwell’s post-conviction activity ‘troubling’

Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell attend de Grisogono Sponsors The 2005 Wall Street Concert Series Benefitting Wall Street Rising, with a Performance by Rod Stewart at Cipriani Wall Street on March 15, 2005 in New York City. (Photo by Joe Schildhorn/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)

After the judge’s decision was made public, former Playboy Playmate Audra Christiansen called Maxwell’s motion to try to overturn her conviction “deeply troubling.”

“For decades, survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s network fought to be taken seriously. Many were children or very young women like me when they were exploited,” she told NewsNation. “They lived with the consequences while powerful people had access to money, attorneys, influence and institutions that repeatedly failed to protect victims.” “Maxwell now argues that attorneys representing Epstein’s accusers somehow acted as ‘de facto prosecutors’ and that newly released documents prove her due process rights were violated,” Christiansen continued. “A federal judge has rejected those claims, finding that the supposed new evidence was largely irrelevant to her case.”

She accused Epstein of sexual abuse in 2004, and asked Playboy founder Hugh Hefner to report him to the FBI.

Christiansen told NewsNation that after the abuse, Maxwell allegedly threatened her and her family .

On Tuesday, the former playmate said, “The focus cannot continually shift away from the people who were harmed and toward portraying those convicted in this network as its victims.”

“Survivors deserved due process, too. We deserved investigations when we came forward. We deserved institutions that acted when warning signs were raised,” she added. “We deserved transparency, accountability, and protection from people who used wealth and power to avoid consequences.”

Epstein survivors’ attorney calls Maxwell’s motion ‘frivolous’

A document that was included in the U.S. Department of Justice release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, photographed Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026, shows a U.S. passport renewal in 2012 for Ghislaine Maxwell. (AP Photo/Jon Elswick)

Arick Fudali, who represents 11 Epstein survivors , told NewsNation that Maxwell’s attempts are “frivolous.”

“It was apparently not enough for Ms. Maxwell that she was moved to a minimum-security resort style prison, and she has once again attempted to get her sentence and conviction overturned,” Fudali continued. “I am very pleased to see that those frivolous efforts were rejected, and I agree that her arguments were meritless.”

He added, “Ghislaine Maxwell is a convicted child sex trafficker, and she belongs behind bars for the remainder of her sentence.”

Ghislaine Maxwell’s legal maneuvers behind bars

This is not the first time the convicted sex trafficker has tried to overturn her prison sentence.

In October 2025, the Supreme Court dismissed her bid to overturn the conviction. Epstein’s former girlfriend was convicted in 2021 and arrested in 2019.

In April 2025, her attorney, David Oscar Markus, wrote in their petition to the Supreme Court, “In this case, the government made a written promise that Epstein’s co-conspirators would not be prosecuted by the United States, and Maxwell was in fact prosecuted as a co-conspirator of Epstein by the United States.

He continued, “The only question is whether the government’s promise that the ‘United States’ would not prosecute her was enforceable against the U.S. Attorney’s office in New York, or only against the Southern District of Florida.”

This undated photo released by the U.S. Department of Justice shows Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. (U.S. Department of Justice via AP)

In August 2025, the Department of Justice released 16 audio recordings and four transcripts from then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche’s meetings with the imprisoned Maxwell on July 24 and 25.

Shortly after Maxwell’s meeting with Blanche, she was moved to a minimum- security prison , Federal Prison Camp Bryan, in Texas.

Diana Falzone is the senior national investigations reporter at NewsNation Digital, covering the federal government, warzones and top-level criminal investigations.
