articles.title: How Trump can fix Puerto Rico’s broken infrastructure
articles.summary: Former Gov. Luis Fortuño argues that the Federal Oversight and Management Board must replace its current mainland members with local leaders to resolve PREPA’s decade-long bankruptcy and address Puerto Rico’s critical infrastructure failures.
articles.body:
Puerto Rico is facing its worst drought in nearly 100 years this summer. The majority of San Juan, Puerto Rico’s capital, is now under severe water rationing due to aging and poorly maintained water infrastructure that is incapable of handling the severe drought conditions. The current water crisis is only the latest manifestation of Puerto Rico’s infrastructure deficiencies. Unfortunately, Puerto Rico has been dealing with an electricity infrastructure failure for decades. Examining why electricity reliability hasn’t improved over the past 10 years despite immense federal supervision from the Federal Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico holds the key to solving Puerto Rico’s infrastructure challenges.

In 2016, Congress created the oversight panel to oversee Puerto Rico’s economic recovery. For the last 10 years, it has kept the territory’s sole provider of electricity, with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Company, known as PREPA, in a perpetual state of bankruptcy. This decision impairs both reliable power for Puerto Rico’s residents and the island’s future economic growth.

How could this happen? The short answer is that the current members of the federal oversight board charged with getting PREPA out of bankruptcy do not live in Puerto Rico. They do not experience firsthand the consequences of decisions that delay much-needed investment in the power grid to improve reliability upon PREPA’s exit from bankruptcy. Last August, President Trump dismissed six of the seven oversight board members for being ineffective at resolving the PREPA bankruptcy. Three of those dismissed members are prolonging the inevitable by challenging these dismissals in court .

The people of Puerto Rico deserve better. The solution seems obvious. PREPA needs capital to improve electric service for customers. Electric utilities depend on assets with long useful lives, such as power plants. Standard practice is to finance long-term assets with long-term debt, which spreads the cost to ratepayers over an extended period. Otherwise, today’s customers pay in full for assets today that will benefit future generations of ratepayers. PREPA’s existing bondholder investors, who comprise most of the municipal finance market, have already offered billions to PREPA to this end. The governor of Puerto Rico has also indicated that over $13 billion in Puerto Rico’s cash balance account could be part of a broad solution.

The result is a worst-case scenario for the people of Puerto Rico. Critical modernization efforts to the electric grid are delayed, all while current customers bear the cost of capital improvements that should be financed and pay high electric rates for unreliable and inadequate service.

Rather than resolve PREPA’s bankruptcy, the board has wasted over half a billion dollars of Puerto Rican taxpayers’ money on high-priced New York attorneys and consultants who haven’t advanced the bankruptcy case in nearly 10 years.

The current and the previous board chairs are both professors who specialize in teaching corporate bankruptcy law. Neither has real-world expertise in understanding how U.S. public utilities operate or finance themselves. The current board chair has also gone out of his way to reject two previously signed consensual PREPA debt restructuring agreements.

The board wasn’t always like this. When it convened in the summer of 2016, it had strong on-island representation and leadership for the first four years, led by local Puerto Rican businessman Jose Carrion serving as board chair. Through his efforts and those of other on-island board members, Puerto Rico reached largely consensual debt restructuring deals that led to the reduction of Puerto Rico’s government debt by more than $40 billion.

We need on-island business leaders, who have a much better understanding of the island’s needs than mainland bankruptcy professors and academics, to run the board once again.

Both the recent Trump v. Cook and Trump v. Slaughter U.S. Supreme Court rulings support the president’s right to hold the FOMB accountable for its failures, including through exercising the right to fire these officials.

I urge local elected officials to support the Trump administration in first filling the three vacant board seats with qualified individuals capable of solving PREPA’s crisis. Once those seats are filled, and consistent with the Supreme Court’s recent rulings affirming the president’s authority to hold the the board accountable, I urge the administration to terminate the three remaining board members who challenged the president’s decision, none of whom will take the steps needed to free PREPA from bankruptcy.

Luis Fortuño served as governor of Puerto Rico from 2009-2013.

articles.title: Donalds picks state senator as running mate for Florida governor
articles.summary: Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) announced Tuesday that Florida state Sen. Bryan Avila (R) will be his running mate in the Sunshine State’s gubernatorial race. Donalds, who won the GOP primary last week, praised Avila as a “proven warrior” and “conservative fighter.” Avila, the former speaker pro tempore of the Florida House, has represented the state’s…
articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) announced Tuesday that Florida state Sen. Bryan Avila (R) will be his running mate in the Sunshine State’s gubernatorial race.

Donalds, who won the GOP primary last week, praised Avila as a “proven warrior” and “conservative fighter.” Avila, the former speaker pro tempore of the Florida House, has represented the state’s 39th Senate District since November 2022.

“He has fought woke ideology, he’s fought higher taxes, he’s fought higher costs every single day, and I could not be more prouder to have him stand by my side,” Donalds said at an event at the Freedom Tower in downtown Miami.

Avila, the son of Cuban immigrants, resides in the heavily Cuban-influenced city of Hialeah, located in north Miami-Dade County. Miami-Dade is the largest county in Florida, and 29.2 percent of Floridians are Hispanic or Latino, according to 2025 estimates by the U.S. Census Bureau .

The Florida state lawmaker, a captain in the Florida Army National Guard, said it was an “incredible honor” to be the running mate of Donalds.

“Byron, thank you for your trust, thank you for your friendship and thank you for your leadership,” Avila said, with Donalds standing behind him.

The Donalds-Avila pairing will face off against former GOP Rep. David Jolly (Fla.), a converted Democrat who won the party’s gubernatorial nomination last week.

Jolly’s running mate is former Rep. Gwen Graham (D-Fla.), an assistant Education secretary during the Biden administration and the daughter of former Florida Gov. and Sen. Bob Graham (D).

While Jolly has campaigned as a moderate Democrat, Donalds on Tuesday tied him to state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), the party’s Senate nominee . Nixon is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Donalds also called the Jolly-Graham ticket “boring,” a quip that elicited cheers from the crowd.

“They’ve joined forces to create the most boring and uninspiring ticket Florida Democrats could have ever put together,” the Republican nominee remarked.

A Democrat has not won a governor’s race in Florida since 1994, with the state morphing from the largest purple state in the country to a conservative stronghold under Gov. Ron DeSantis (R). DeSantis defeated former Gov. Charlie Crist (D) by nearly 20 points in 2022.

In the statewide primary that concluded last week, more than 1.7 million Republicans and nearly 1.3 million Democrats cast a ballot, according to data from Fresh Take Florida .

Overall, nearly 51 percent of registered Republicans and nearly 38 percent of registered Democrats voted in the primary.

articles.title: Carville rips Jeffries for meeting with Kushner: ‘We don’t want to f‑‑‑ with them’
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville went after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) over his recent meeting with President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. “One thing that I know and you know, these are a pack of crooks, and they’re a pack of people that don’t give a s‑‑‑ about the United States of America, and we…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville went after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) over his recent meeting with President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“One thing that I know and you know, these are a pack of crooks, and they’re a pack of people that don’t give a s‑‑‑ about the United States of America, and we don’t want to f‑‑‑ with them unless we absolutely have to. No more meetings, no more bulls‑‑‑,” Carville said in a Monday clip of the “Politics War Room” podcast.

The New York Times reported Sunday that Kushner and Jeffries met privately before the upcoming midterm elections to find common ground on issues such as housing, immigration and the cost of living.

According to Jeffries, Kushner reached out to him first, and he accepted the invitation in order to talk about affordability. Jeffries also said that the Trump administration has received pressure from House Democrats on issues like tariffs, the Affordable Care Act, and nutritional assistance.

On Monday, Jeffries, following backlash for his meeting with Kushner, wrote “no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass” in a post on the social platform X.

“I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass,” he said. “We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, and be guided by the Constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.”

Former Obama aide and co-host of “Pod Save America” Tommy Vietor on Sunday criticized Kushner in reaction to the meeting.

“Jared Kushner has no actual government job; he just uses his family connections to get money from Gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals,” Vietor said.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Supreme Court throws election curveball
articles.summary: Plus:🍁 Canada fires back ‘dollar-for-dollar’ {beacon} It’s Tuesday, the last one in the month of August. 🎵 Queue Noah Kahan’s “End of August”🎵 In today’s issue: Supreme Court’s mail-in voting ruling South Carolina, Oklahoma runoffs USS Lincoln finally heads to port Lake America? Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz, filling in…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday, the last one in the month of August. 🎵 Queue Noah Kahan’s “End of August”🎵

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com .

The Supreme Court on Monday lifted a block that was preventing President Trump’s mail voting executive order from going into effect ahead of November’s midterms.

That doesn’t mean the order – which would direct the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to only send ballots to verified citizens – is moving ahead.

First of all, there’s a second injunction on the directive in a related case before the U.S. district court in Boston. Secondly, the Supreme Court did not decide on the constitutional merits of the order, it just said the lawsuit was premature because the order had not been finalized.

That’s about to change: The USPS is set to publish a finalized rule tomorrow and states are already moving to block it — again.

All eyes are now on U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani , an appointee of former President Obama , who imposed both injunctions.

The administration says it will ask the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to pause Talwani’s other injunction if she doesn’t lift it by 5:30 p.m. EDT on Tuesday.

She has previously found the administration overstepped its constitutional authority with the order, as states have the express power to oversee elections.

Sound like a “Kafkaesque nightmare”? Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson thinks so.

The Supreme Court’s junior liberal justice wrote 23 pages of her own, saying the lift “lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”

She wrote that it “needlessly injects chaos” into upcoming elections and that her conservative colleagues had a “lack of situational awareness.”

GOP runoff elections for senator in South Carolina and governor in Oklahoma Tuesday night will test the power of Trump’s endorsement.

And it’s honestly not looking great for his candidates.

According to Al Weaver at NOTUS , multiple Republican sources have said that a Graham win over Norman is looking increasingly unlikely, especially following her mistakes in last week’s debate.

And a new poll has the race in a dead heat. The Trafalgar Group survey shows Graham with 47.9 percent of the vote, Norman with 47.8 percent and 4.4 percent undecided.

If Graham goes down, much of the blame will likely point toward her debate flub last week, when she admitted she didn’t know much about national security in response to a question about Taiwan.

“That’s the kind of thing that, if she does lose on Tuesday, I feel like we’ll be chalking entirely up to that,” Geoffrey Skelley, Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst, told The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky.

In the Sooner State, Trump-endorsed candidate Mike Mazzei , a former state senator and state budget secretary, finished just ahead of Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the primary.

Trump surprised some by doubling down on his support for Mazzei, who is seen as an underdog in the race.

“Oklahoma marks one of the final midterm primary gauges of the president’s political power amid his lackluster approval numbers — and it comes after five of his gubernatorial picks in open primaries lost so far this cycle,” The Hill’s Julia Mueller writes .

Mazzei’s campaign paid almost $70,000 to Trump confidant Roger Stone for consulting services, Mueller reported, which prompted critics to ask if money factored into the president’s endorsement. The candidate has pushed back against these claims.

Whoever crosses the finish line tonight is likely assured to win the November election in the red state.

After 250 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln has finally started making its way to land.

Read the receipts : Texts shared with USA Today said the USS Abraham Lincoln planned to stop in Thailand after its lengthy deployment in the Middle East for the continued conflict with Iran.

One sailor aboard the ship told their relative to send them hotel options in Thailand, while another told her family member that she was excited to visit the country.

Family members of those aboard the ship said that they have received messages about food and water shortages and mental health issues on the ship, which have been serious enough to where multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard.

The Supreme Court on Monday lifted a block that was preventing President Trump’s mail voting executive order from going into effect ahead of November’s midterms.
That doesn’t mean the order – which would direct the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to only send ballots to verified citizens – is moving ahead.

First of all, there’s a second injunction on the directive in a related case before the U.S. district court in Boston. Secondly, the Supreme Court did not decide on the constitutional merits of the order, it just said the lawsuit was premature because the order had not been finalized.
That’s about to change: The USPS is set to publish a finalized rule tomorrow and states are already moving to block it — again.
All eyes are now on U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani , an appointee of former President Obama , who imposed both injunctions.
The administration says it will ask the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to pause Talwani’s other injunction if she doesn’t lift it by 5:30 p.m. EDT on Tuesday.
She has previously found the administration overstepped its constitutional authority with the order, as states have the express power to oversee elections.
Sound like a “Kafkaesque nightmare”? Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson thinks so.

The Supreme Court’s junior liberal justice wrote 23 pages of her own, saying the lift “lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”

articles.title: Democrat jabs Trump over Lake Ontario threat: ‘Let’s just call it Lake Natalie’
articles.summary: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Tuesday took a jab at President Trump over his threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America amid his trade war with Canada, saying the U.S. should “just call it Lake Natalie” after White House executive assistant Natalie Harp. Dingell shared on the social platform X a screenshot of Trump’s…
articles.body:
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Tuesday took a jab at President Trump over his threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America amid his trade war with Canada , saying the U.S. should “just call it Lake Natalie” after White House executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Dingell shared on the social platform X a screenshot of Trump’s threat written on Truth Social . The president said that the U.S. was “giving serious consideration” to changing the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“Let’s just call it Lake Natalie so we know you’ll start protecting our Great Lakes,” she wrote.

The president’s threat mirrors his executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America . Other locations in the U.S. share the Canadian province’s name, including Washington, D.C.’s own Ontario Road in the Reed-Cooke neighborhood and the Southern California city and transportation hub located in San Bernardino County.

Democrats, beginning with Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), have taken digs at Harp after she boarded an Air Force jet with Trump upon leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month.

The president said he was boarding the older Air Force One instead of his Qatari-gifted jet, leaving some Cabinet members aboard the old plane while he, Harp and other White House staffers flew off on the third plane.

Ossoff mocked the president and Harp during a rally with supporters earlier this month. He said that as president, Trump only “wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Republican lawmakers clapped back at Ossoff, with Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) calling the discourse around Trump and Harp “ super misogynistic .” The president’s son, Eric Trump, defended Harp as a “ genuinely good person ” and called the discourse around their relationship “absolute trash.”

“It’s been amazing to watch this White House melt down over this all week,” Ossoff later said in response to the backlash during an interview with MS NOW.

Ossoff also told MS NOW’s Lawrence O’Donnell that as a White House employee in a government position, Harp and other officials working for Trump should be permissible targets of political criticism.

Harp frequently travels with Trump on golfing trips and at Mar-a-Lago, occasionally bringing along a printer to pass him information in hard copy and drafting his social media posts.

She fought bone cancer in 2019 and sent letters to Trump that described him as her “guardian and protector in this life,” while he wrote back praising her battle with the disease, The New York Times reported. Harp said that the Right to Try Act, legislation the president passed in 2018, provided her with access to experimental treatments.

Harp’s brother, Preston Harp, told CNN that his sister’s devotion to Trump was an “unhealthy obsession.”

articles.title: Mike Lindell misses deadline for recount payment, seeks restraining order
articles.summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the state’s gubernatorial primaries. His campaign said in a statement that Simon’s office had put Lindell “in an untenable position” by placing restrictions on…
articles.body:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the state’s gubernatorial primaries.

His campaign said in a statement that Simon’s office had put Lindell “in an untenable position” by placing restrictions on his proposed audit — limiting the recount to just the two leading Republican candidates.

Lindell lost the election to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) by roughly 11 percentage points, according to Decision Desk HQ. But the MyPillow founder refused to concede, later claiming there were irregularities in vote totals .

“The rest of the candidates’ vote would not be counted under their contingent plan. Nor would the Democrat ballots be recounted,” Lindell’s campaign wrote Monday.

“Why is this important?” it continued. “In addition to being a violation of Minnesota state law, the anomalies on election night reporting identified by Mike Lindell’s team show an algorithm that applies to ALL of the candidates not simply Lindell and Demuth.”

Cassondra Knudson, a spokesperson for Simon, told The Hill that the office did not receive a payment or a discretionary request by the Aug. 24 deadline. She added that, at this time, the state does not plan to conduct a recount for the Aug. 11 primary.

In its statement, Lindell’s campaign attached an authorization form appearing to show an $825,000 transaction in progress as proof of “wire transfer readiness” for the potential audit, dated Monday morning.

The campaign is now asking the state officials to waive the Monday deadline until a court can rule on the alleged Minnesota law violations.

Knudson said that “next steps” for Lindell’s legal action against Simon and the Minnesota State Canvassing Board for their handling of the recount processes “will be decided by the court.”

“Our office provided the contingent recount plan to Mr. Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on August 18. The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans,” she said.

The MyPillow founder currently owes the electronic voting system company Smartmatic $56,369 in sanctions following a defamation lawsuit — which his attorneys say he cannot afford. Lindell accused the company in several media appearances of rigging the 2020 presidential election, echoing President Trump’s similar false claims .

On Aug. 19, Lindell’s lawyers sent a letter to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan to file a motion to reconsider the ruling holding him liable for defamation.

articles.title: Places that have been renamed during Trump’s second term
articles.summary: President Trump said renaming Lake Ontario is under “serious consideration.” It wouldn’t be the first place renamed during his second term.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Amid the ongoing trade war with Canada , President Trump said Tuesday that renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” is under “serious consideration.”

Trump didn’t give many details in a Truth Social post , but explained that the U.S. doesn’t “expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

While Ontario Premier Doug Ford dismissed the idea , calling it “a lot of rhetoric” while speaking to CNN, the Great Lake would not be the first site to be renamed since Trump took office for a second time.

After taking office in January 2025, Trump signed orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, and Mount Denali as Mount McKinley .

In February, North Carolina military base Fort Liberty was reverted back to Fort Bragg . The base had been known as Fort Liberty since 2023, when Congress, as part of a congressionally mandated rule to rename installations honoring Confederate generals, changed it.

Back in December, the Trump administration changed the name of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory to the National Laboratory of the Rockies .

Trump has also called for other things outside his purview to be renamed, like reverting the name of the Washington Commanders back to a dictionary definition of a slur against Native Americans.

Trump’s name, signature, and likeness have also found their way onto several other places during his second term. That includes “limited edition” passports , National Park Service passes , and currency .

His name has also been added to the Kennedy Center and the U.S. Institute of Peace building, and Florida’s Palm Beach International Airport has adopted the name “President Donald J. Trump International Airport.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Hochul predicts Mamdani will ‘be helpful’ in her reelection bid
articles.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said she believes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will give a boost to her reelection campaign. “I think he’ll be helpful,” Hochul said Monday after Politico asked about the chance of the New York City mayor stumping for her. In a recent poll, Hochul led Republican Bruce…
articles.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said she believes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will give a boost to her reelection campaign.

“I think he’ll be helpful,” Hochul said Monday after Politico asked about the chance of the New York City mayor stumping for her.

In a recent poll , Hochul led Republican Bruce Blakeman by 10 points in her race for a second term. The poll from Siena University found 49 percent of 811 likely voters backing Hochul, with 39 percent supporting Blakeman.

Last September, Hochul formally endorsed Mamdani in his own bid for Big Apple mayor, announcing her endorsement in a New York Times op-ed. Her endorsement of Mamdani was notable, considering Mamdani’s background as a democratic socialist and then-relative political outsider.

“The question of who will be the next mayor is one I take extremely seriously and to which I have devoted a great deal of thought,” Hochul said in her opinion piece.

In February, Mamdani endorsed Hochul for reelection , possibly helping to shore up the governor’s support among progressives.

“At its best, the Democratic Party has been a big tent not because it avoids conflict, but because it channels conflict toward progress. A party united not by conformity, but by a commitment to structural change — and to the work required to achieve it,” Mamdani wrote in an op-ed published in The Nation.

“I’ve seen a model of what that can look like in my collaboration with Governor Hochul: a relationship built on candor, a shared commitment to government that is equal parts competent and trustworthy, and results that working people can feel in their day-to-day lives,” he added.

The two New York politicians recently teamed up in proposing a new tax on property owners who have second homes in New York City worth more than $5 million. But a judge in Staten Island, N.Y., earlier this month temporarily blocked the rollout of the second-home tax.

articles.body:
Dolly Parton — a country music songwriting legend and philanthropist who captured and united fans across the generational and political spectrum — has died. The “9 to 5” star “died peacefully” at 80 on Tuesday in Nashville, Tenn., her publicity team announced.

“A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family,” the statement from True Public Relations said.

In a video posted on Parton’s X account, Bryan Seaver, her nephew who served as the entertainer’s head of security, praised his aunt.

“Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible. Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent,” Seaver said.

“By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history,” he added

Raised with her 11 siblings in a one-room cabin in rural Tennessee, Parton often reflected on her impoverished childhood in a “dirt poor” family.

“Mama used to sew all of our quilts and curtains for the windows, remake our clothes, and make clothes out of feed sacks or scraps,” she said .

Gifted a guitar by her uncle, Parton landed an appearance in 1967 on “The Porter Wagner Show.”

Hit after musical hit saw Parton’s career explode in the 1970’s, with chart-toppers including 1974’s “Jolene,” “Love is Like a Butterfly” and “I Will Always Love You.”

Parton married husband Carl Dean in 1966 and later translated her music fame into big screen success, starring in 1980’s “9 to 5” and penning the film’s ear-worm title song. Dean died last year.

In 1995, inspired by her father’s illiteracy, Parton launched Imagination Library. The organization mails free books to children from birth until they start school.

Parton marked a philanthropic milestone in 2018 in Washington, presenting the 100 millionth book donation from her Imagination Library to the Library of Congress’s collection.

But the visit to the nation’s capital was about the closest Parton would get to politics during her life. She repeatedly said in interviews over the years, “I don’t do politics.”

“My mother was a Democrat and my daddy was a Republican, so I’m a hypocrite,” Parton, leaning on her trademark wit, quipped in 2017.

In a 2023 song she wrote called “World on Fire,” Parton sung of “greedy politicians, present and past.”

“They wouldn’t know the truth if it bit ‘em in the ass,” she sang in her tune.

“I don’t think any of them are trying hard enough,” Parton said of lawmakers in an interview when asked about the song.

“I think often that they worry more about the party than they do about the people,” she said.

In recent years, Parton said she had turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom due to personal reasons after it was offered multiple times by both former President Biden and President Trump.

“I couldn’t accept it because my husband was ill and then they asked me again about it and I wouldn’t travel because of the COVID,” Parton said in 2021 of the country’s highest civilian honor.

Despite the polarized political climate, Parton appeared to be universally adored.

A 2019 New York Times headline proclaimed, “Is There Anything We Can All Agree On? Yes: Dolly Parton.”

In the Parton family’s statement delivered by Seaver on Tuesday, he said his aunt lived “a rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see.”

“Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place. Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact,” Seaver said.

In a statement posted to Truth Social, Trump called her “one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER.”

“In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM. Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you,” he wrote.

The Parton family asked that in lieu of flowers, donations be made to Parton’s Imagination Library .

“Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness,” Seaver said.

“Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones,” Seaver said, “she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”

articles.title: Live updates: Trump teases ‘Lake America’ as Canada sets retaliatory tariffs; SC voters set to pick Graham or Norman
articles.summary: Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs against U.S. products, including steel and aluminum. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada would match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8. Since the trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada came to a halt, President Trump and Canadian Prime…
articles.body:
Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs against U.S. products, including steel and aluminum. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada would match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8.

Since the trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada came to a halt , President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have turned to taunting. On Tuesday morning, the president suggested the U.S. could start referring to Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Tuesday’s South Carolina Republican Senate runoff election between Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman will test President Trump’s endorsement power.

MAGA Inc., a super PAC that backs Trump, has invested in Graham’s election , and Trump touted an Oval Office meeting with the senator Monday night.

Norman trailed Graham in the state primary two weeks ago, with 24.6 percent and 32.7 percent of the vote, respectively, according to Decision Desk HQ . But Graham fumbled a question on Taiwan last week, which caused a wave of backlash . Polls close at 7 p.m. EDT.

Oklahoma’s primary elections are also Tuesday.

The president has nothing public on his schedule.

articles.title: Jury sides with Louisiana Supreme Court justice in rare defamation win for public official
articles.summary: A jury sided with Louisiana Supreme Court Justice Jefferson Hughes on Monday, finding a local newspaper and two former editors defamed him in a 2019 editorial. The Iberville Parish jury awarded Hughes $300,000 in damages for an investigative editorial published in Baton Rouge-based newspaper, The Advocate, according to WWL Louisiana, a New Orleans-based CBS affiliate.…
articles.body:
A jury sided with Louisiana Supreme Court Justice Jefferson Hughes on Monday, finding a local newspaper and two former editors defamed him in a 2019 editorial.

The Iberville Parish jury awarded Hughes $300,000 in damages for an investigative editorial published in Baton Rouge-based newspaper, The Advocate, according to WWL Louisiana, a New Orleans-based CBS affiliate . The justice originally sought $10 million in damages for the piece, which highlighted a custody battle that took place 20 years prior to the editorial’s publication. The custody battle sparked an FBI probe into Hughes and his handling of the case as a Livingston Parish district judge in the late 1990s.

Hughes’s win suggests the justice was able to prove the outlet acted with “actual malice,” a legal standard of proof needed in defamation cases where a public figure is the defendant. The standard is difficult to meet , as it places the legal burden on the plaintiff to show a respondent either knew a statement was false or recklessly failed to verify it.

“We are pleased that justice was served and Jeff was able to clear his name from this unfortunate defamation,” an attorney for Hughes said following the ruling, as reported by WWL Louisiana.

The case stemmed from a joint investigation by The Advocate and WWL Louisiana with the headline, “Our Views: Before Jeff Hughes landed on Louisiana Supreme Court, he made a mockery of justice.”

The editorial stated that Hughes failed to recuse himself from an abuse-related custody case in the late 1990s. The paper went on to argue that the move was a conflict of interest, alleging he was “romantically involved” with Berkley Durbin — a lawyer for the child’s mother — during these proceedings. At the time, he was acting as a state judge.

Hughes argued this timeline was inaccurate, adding that it “took years” for The Advocate to issue a clarification.

“This editorial has been revised to clarify that the attorney Judge Jeff Hughes was dating withdrew before he made his final ruling in the Nicholson custody case,” a later editor’s note clarified.

The investigation also mentioned a 2004 FBI probe into Hughes’s potential conflict of interest in the custody case. The agency uncovered a letter the judge wrote to the child’s grandmother — who had been on the other side of the custody battle with the child’s mother — where Hughes “appeared to apologize for his conduct.”

In the note, Hughes reportedly wrote that “because of my actions, justice suffered. For this, I am deeply remorseful.”

During the last day of arguments, WWL Louisiana reported that former editorial board member Danny Heitman said he did everything he could to ensure the editorial’s accuracy.

articles.title: Agriculture secretary says beef import plan still under discussion
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s plan to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports is still under discussion, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Tuesday. “I am not privy to talk about that,” Rollins said when asked by reporters outside of the White House about the details of the decision. “I think the conversations are still going…
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s plan to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports is still under discussion, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Tuesday.

“I am not privy to talk about that,” Rollins said when asked by reporters outside of the White House about the details of the decision.

“I think the conversations are still going on, and that’s Ambassador Greer who’s finalizing what exactly that looks like, and I think the president’s involved in that as well,” the secretary added, referring to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The secretary’s comments follow backlash among some Republicans over the proposed plan to temporarily pause “out-of-quota” tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef. President Trump announced the decision Friday, saying these imported products would be sold at 25 percent below market price.

Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) said he had advised the Trump administration “against this course of action for a year,” citing concerns about negative impacts on American ranchers.

“But the reality is this action will make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild our herd and bring prices down for the American people,” the senator wrote on social media . “And most importantly, this will harm our ranching families who feed the nation.”

Trump lashed out at former Georgia Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R) and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R) after they challenged his plan .

The Kentucky Republican slammed the move as a “slap in the face to American cattlemen & consumers.”

“Worse than socialism! Dumping foreign beef in U.S. markets can temporarily lower prices but it won’t incentivize American farmers to raise more beef. Bring back Country Of Origin Labels & pass my PRIME Act,” he wrote in a social media post .

Greene similarly accused the administration of putting “American beef LAST and foreign beef FIRST.”

“Now they will be undercut by foreign imported beef, as they have been hit financially with high cost of fertilizer and diesel from Trump’s war with Iran,” she wrote on social media .

The Trump administration has pointed to a historically small U.S. cattle population and the New World screwworm outbreak as driving forces behind rising domestic beef prices.

Trump defended his move to reporters before boarding Air Force One on Friday, saying it was “what the voters want.” The issue of affordability has been a central theme across Republican and Democratic campaigns this midterm election cycle.

“I love the ranchers,” Trump told reporters. “They’ve done a fantastic job, but they admit that we need a little help in order to get the prices down, so that is what we’re doing.”

articles.title: DOJ to monitor Charleston polling sites for South Carolina primary runoff
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) will monitor polling sites in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday as voters cast their ballots in the South Carolina Senate GOP runoff. The DOJ will send four attorneys from its Civil Rights Division, one assistant U.S. attorney from South Carolina and one staffer within the office of the U.S. attorney for…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) will monitor polling sites in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday as voters cast their ballots in the South Carolina Senate GOP runoff.

The DOJ will send four attorneys from its Civil Rights Division, one assistant U.S. attorney from South Carolina and one staffer within the office of the U.S. attorney for South Carolina to monitor polls in the Palmetto State’s largest city, the department noted in a release .

Through its monitoring efforts, the DOJ will “ensure transparency, ballot security, and compliance with federal law” in Charleston. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 allows federal observers to monitor procedures in polling places.

Voters in South Carolina on Tuesday will decide whether Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) or Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) will take the place of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) on the ballot opposite Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election.

Polls opened at 7 a.m. and will close at 7 p.m. EDT. Under state law, South Carolinians must bring a valid photo ID to cast a ballot.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said the DOJ’s monitoring efforts in Charleston mark the “next stop in our ongoing effort to ensure election transparency.” The DOJ noted it has sent more than 80 monitors to 200-plus polling locations in seven states this primary season.

“We appreciate the cooperation of the State of South Carolina, the County of Charleston, and the South Carolina United States Attorney’s Office in helping make this monitoring effort an exemplary one for promoting trust,” added Dhillon, who heads the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division.

In addition to South Carolina, the DOJ has sent monitors to Arizona, Florida , Michigan, Minnesota , Virginia and Wyoming for primary races. The department will also send monitors to polling places in Massachusetts and New Hampshire, with the respective primaries in those states set for Sept. 1 and 8.

“This monitoring initiative is aimed at promoting transparency and an open flow of communication between poll observers and election monitors,” the DOJ added in Tuesday’s release, noting it enforces statutes such as the Voting Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Civil Rights Act.

During the 2022 primary season, the DOJ sent monitors to nine states, the department noted. Dhillon told Bloomberg last week the department plans to deploy a record 1,000 monitors for this fall’s midterms.

articles.title: Trump administration threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if renovations are blocked
articles.summary: The Trump administration has threatened to demolish the Kennedy Center if a judge determines that the renowned performing arts center cannot close for a two-year renovation. In court filings on Monday, Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers repeatedly referred to the Kennedy Center as a “decrepit” structure in dire need of renovations led by the…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has threatened to demolish the Kennedy Center if a judge determines that the renowned performing arts center cannot close for a two-year renovation.

In court filings on Monday, Justice Department attorney Brantley T. Mayers repeatedly referred to the Kennedy Center as a “decrepit” structure in dire need of renovations led by the Trump administration.

Mayers said without renovations, the site will “deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years.”

He also argued that if President Trump is not given recognition for updating the center, it would cause “donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop.”

“There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure. The Trump Administration is ready to go but, without it, the Kennedy Center cannot be saved,” Mayers added.

His comments echo those of the federal government against a lawsuit filed by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member of the center, who argued it was illegal to add Trump’s name to the building without explicit permission from Congress.

She said his efforts to overhaul the Kennedy Center during a two-year closure were not clearly presented to the board.

Her office did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on the threat to demolish the building.

Earlier this year, a judge ruled that the president’s name could not legally be added to the building and ordered signage recognizing Trump to be removed.

Instead of removing the lettering on the building, it was covered with a tarp . The board, largely appointed by Trump, voted to add an inscription underneath the Kennedy Center’s name that reads: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.”

The next court hearing regarding the Kennedy Center’s future is scheduled for Thursday.

articles.body:
President Trump has ordered all American flags to be flown at half-staff in memory of Dolly Parton, who died Tuesday at the age of 80 .

“Very sad to report that Dolly Parton, one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER, has just passed away,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , adding her death is a “true loss for millions of people.”

The president added, “There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM.”

“Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you,” he concluded.

Parton, a country music legend and philanthropist whose work spanned generations, died peacefully in Nashville, Tenn., her publicity team announced.

“A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family,” the statement from True Public Relations added.

Bryan Seaver, Parton’s nephew and former head of security, said his aunt “never saw a door she couldn’t open” during her life.

“The doors she opened made and changed history,” Seaver said in a video message . “My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you. She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not.

“Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever.”

During her storied career, Parton won 11 Grammy Awards, three Emmy Awards and an honorary humanitarian Oscar last year. She was also nominated for six Golden Globes, two Academy Awards and a Tony Award.

In 2006, she was one of five Kennedy Center honorees. Parton reportedly declined the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times — twice during Trump’s first term, citing the illness of her late husband Carl Dean and the COVID-19 pandemic, and once during former President Biden’s term.

On the latter occasion, Parton noted her preference to avoid the appearance of partisanship.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) praised Parton on Tuesday, writing on social platform X , “Rare is the one who climbs to the pinnacle of fame, then scoffs at its allure only to retain the genuine humility that defines them.

“Dolly Parton was one of a kind, who loved people, her work, her family, and her Lord. Tennessee has forever been changed — enhanced — by her, and will never be quite the same without Dolly.”

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) also said his state will “lower our flags” in honor of Parton.

Progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called Parton “one of the great entertainers of our era.”

“She was not only a talented musician & songwriter, but a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief,” Sanders wrote on X . “Her music and humanity touched millions. She will be sorely missed.”
